column1: What are the three layers of the bladder detrusor muscle?
column2: Inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal — though detrusor is functionally a syncytial meshwork rather than discrete layers. Key for cystotomy closure planning.

column1: What is the trigone embryologic origin?
column2: Mesodermal (from incorporated mesonephric/Wolffian ducts and ureteric buds), unlike the endodermal bladder dome. Explains why trigone is non-distensible and densely innervated.
Approximately 400–600 mL with first sensation at ~150 mL, strong desire at ~300 mL. Capacity <300 mL on UDS raises low-compliance / contracted-bladder concern.
Superior and inferior vesical arteries (branches of anterior division of internal iliac); contributions from obturator, inferior gluteal, and in females, vaginal/uterine arteries.

column1: Sympathetic innervation of the bladder — origin and effect?
column2: T10–L2 via hypogastric nerve; beta-3 receptors on detrusor cause relaxation, alpha-1 on bladder neck cause contraction. Storage phase dominant.
S2–S4 via pelvic splanchnic nerves; M3 muscarinic receptors cause detrusor contraction during voiding.

column1: Somatic innervation of the external urethral sphincter?
column2: S2–S4 via pudendal nerve (Onuf's nucleus); spared in many neurodegenerative conditions like MSA.

column1: What is the space of Retzius?
column2: Prevesical (retropubic) space between pubic symphysis and bladder, bounded by transversalis fascia anteriorly. Accessed for retropubic suspensions, MMK, Burch.

column1: What anatomic structure is at risk in space-of-Retzius dissection?
column2: Aberrant obturator vessel (corona mortis) crossing superior pubic ramus in ~30%; dorsal venous complex anteriorly.
Primarily external iliac and obturator nodes; dome drains to common iliac, trigone to internal iliac. Important for invasive cancer staging.
Fibromuscular sheath investing the intramural ureter as it traverses the bladder wall; reinforces antireflux mechanism.
Mucosa (transitional epithelium), lamina propria, inner longitudinal + outer circular muscle, adventitia carrying blood supply.
UPJ, crossing of iliac vessels (pelvic brim), UVJ. Sites of stone impaction and iatrogenic injury.

column1: Ureteric blood supply — medial vs lateral?
column2: Abdominal ureter receives medial branches (renal, gonadal, aorta); pelvic ureter receives lateral branches (internal iliac, vesical, uterine). Dictates mobilization plane.

column1: Why mobilize the ureter laterally in the abdomen?
column2: Medial blood supply arises medially in the abdomen; preserve adventitial vessels by leaving them attached to the ureter and mobilizing on the lateral side.
Approximately 3–4 cm; entirely within the urogenital diaphragm distally and supported by pubourethral ligaments.
Sympathetic from hypogastric (T11–L2), parasympathetic from pelvic (S2–S4), somatic to rhabdosphincter from pudendal/levator branches.

column1: Female urethra histology — proximal vs distal?
column2: Proximal: transitional epithelium. Mid/distal: stratified squamous (estrogen-responsive). Submucosa rich in vascular plexus contributes ~30% of resting urethral pressure.

column1: Three layers of female urethral sphincter (DeLancey)?
column2: Inner longitudinal smooth muscle, middle circular smooth muscle, outer striated urogenital sphincter (rhabdosphincter — slow-twitch type 1 fibers).

column1: DeLancey's three levels of vaginal support?
column2: Level I (apical — uterosacral/cardinal), Level II (mid-vaginal — paravaginal/ATFP), Level III (distal — perineal body/urogenital diaphragm).
Urethra is compressed against a stable hammock of anterior vaginal wall + endopelvic fascia + levator ani during increased abdominal pressure. Failure causes SUI.

column1: Length of male urethra and its segments?
column2: ~18–22 cm; segments: prostatic, membranous (~1–2 cm), bulbar, penile, fossa navicularis, meatus.
Membranous urethra, surrounded by external striated sphincter and located at the urogenital diaphragm. Site of post-prostatectomy continence.
Transition between membranous urethra (within UG diaphragm) and bulbar urethra (within corpus spongiosum). Common site for pelvic-fracture urethral injury.
Pseudostratified columnar epithelium with patches of stratified squamous distally; fossa navicularis is non-keratinized stratified squamous.
Mucous glands along penile urethra. Site of gonococcal colonization; chronic inflammation contributes to LS-related stricture and pseudodiverticula.
Within UG diaphragm, ducts open into proximal bulbar urethra. Visible as opacification on RUG; can be confused with diverticulum.
Bulbar artery (branch of internal pudendal) supplies bulb/proximal spongiosum; dorsal arteries supply distal spongiosum retrograde via glans circumflex branches.

column1: Why is dorsal-onlay BMG safer than ventral for bulbar?
column2: Preserves bulbar artery and spongiosum vascularity; ventral spongiotomy can compromise the bulbar arterial supply, especially after prior urethroplasty.
Apical, anterior superior, anterior inferior, posterior, lower segmental arteries; Brodel's avascular line lies 1 cm posterior to lateral convex border.
Left renal vein receives gonadal, adrenal, and lumbar tributaries; right does not. Influences gonadal vein ligation in varicocele.
Anterior (Toldt) and posterior (Zuckerkandl) layers fusing laterally; encloses kidney and perirenal fat. Plane of dissection in nephrectomy and pyeloplasty.
G1 ≥90, G2 60–89, G3a 45–59, G3b 30–44, G4 15–29, G5 <15. Diversion requires consideration of metabolic acidosis risk at G3b or worse.

column1: Compartments of the corpus spongiosum vs corpora cavernosa?
column2: Spongiosum is low-pressure, surrounds urethra, lacks sinusoidal trabeculae; cavernosa are high-pressure trabecular sinusoids enclosed by tunica albuginea.
Two layers: inner circular (~0.5 mm) and outer longitudinal; outer is absent ventrally at the 6 o'clock urethral position. Site of Peyronie plaque preference dorsally.
Deep fascia investing the corpora and dorsal NVB; contains Colles fascia extension. Limits superficial urethral injury extravasation to penis; rupture allows tracking to scrotum/abdomen.
Single dorsal vein (midline), paired dorsal arteries lateral, paired dorsal nerves (most lateral); cavernosal nerves run posterolateral within Buck fascia, key for nerve-sparing.
Internal pudendal artery → common penile → terminal branches: cavernosal (deep), bulbourethral, dorsal arteries. Accessory pudendal in ~30% can be sole supply post-RP.
Neurogenic (NO release), vascular (cavernosal artery dilation), and venoocclusive (subtunical venule compression). Failure of any → ED phenotype.
Compressed against tunica albuginea during sinusoidal expansion to occlude outflow (venoocclusive mechanism). Failure = venous leak ED.
NANC neurons release NO → activates guanylate cyclase → ↑ cGMP → ↓ intracellular Ca²⁺ → smooth muscle relaxation. PDE5 degrades cGMP.
Skin, dartos (smooth muscle), external spermatic fascia, cremasteric fascia/muscle, internal spermatic fascia, tunica vaginalis.
Testicular artery from aorta (just below renal); collateral from cremasteric (inferior epigastric) and deferential (vesical) arteries — supports testis-sparing in vasectomy.
Countercurrent heat exchange around testicular artery; coalesces to single testicular vein. Dilation = varicocele, left-side predominant due to LRV anatomy.
Peripheral (~70% mass, cancer origin), central (~25%, surrounds ejaculatory ducts), transition (~5%, BPH origin), anterior fibromuscular stroma.
Inferior vesical artery (branch of anterior internal iliac) — divides into urethral and capsular branches. Selectively embolized in PAE for BPH.

column1: Where do the ejaculatory ducts enter the urethra?
column2: At the verumontanum (prostatic urethra), flanking the prostatic utricle. Landmark for TURP and TUIED.
Paired lobulated structures posterior to bladder base; duct joins vas deferens to form ejaculatory duct. Tip points cephalad-laterally — sentinel for prostatectomy dissection.

column1: Vulvar blood supply — anterior vs posterior?
column2: Anterior labial branches from external pudendal (femoral); posterior labial branches from internal pudendal — key for axial flap design (Singapore, lotus petal).
Dorsal nerves of clitoris run along dorsal surface at 11 and 1 o'clock under Buck fascia, on the tunica of paired corpora cavernosa. Avoid in clitoroplasty.
4 and 8 o'clock of vestibule, deep to bulbocavernosus; duct opens at posterior vestibule. Marsupialization preserves duct function.
Female homolog of prostate; periurethral glands draining at meatus. Source of female ejaculate and site of paraurethral cysts/abscesses.
Upper 2/3 — autonomic (uterovaginal plexus, less sensate). Lower 1/3 — pudendal (somatic, highly sensate). Influences fistula repair pain mapping.
Apical support of cervix/upper vagina (Level I); contains pelvic autonomic fibers — ureter runs 0.9–5 cm lateral. USL suspension stitch risk for ureteral kink.
Fan-shaped condensation containing uterine artery and pelvic plexus; supports cervix laterally. Resected in radical hysterectomy.
Predominantly fibrous (collagen) with only ~10–15% smooth muscle, distinguishing it from corpus. Explains rigid feel and post-conization stenosis risk.
Uterine appendages: fallopian tubes, ovaries, broad ligaments and their contents (round ligament, ovarian/utero-ovarian vessels).
From uterine cornu through inguinal canal to labia majora; female homolog of gubernaculum; carries artery of Sampson.
S2–S4; exits through greater sciatic foramen, around ischial spine through lesser foramen, into Alcock canal. Block target at ischial spine.

column1: Three terminal branches of pudendal nerve?
column2: Inferior rectal, perineal, dorsal nerve of penis/clitoris. Damaged in obstetric trauma, prolonged lithotomy, cycling neuropathy.
Lateral to rectum, deep to uterosacral/rectovesical fascia at the pelvic sidewall; receives hypogastric (sympathetic) and pelvic splanchnic (parasympathetic). Damage causes neurogenic bladder.
Vesicovaginal area defined by ureteric orifices and bladder neck — site of supratrigonal VVF and the Latzko colpocleisis repair.
Fibromuscular nodal point where bulbospongiosus, superficial/deep transverse perineal, external anal sphincter, and levator fibers converge. Reconstructed in 4th-degree obstetric repair.
Levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus) and coccygeus; innervated by direct branches of S3–S5 and pudendal.
Lateral attachment line for pubocervical fascia from pubic bone to ischial spine; site of Level II support and paravaginal repair.
Tendinous insertion of levator ani on obturator fascia; target for high uterosacral and apical suspensions; passes superior to ATFP.
Apical vault suspension target (Richter procedure); pudendal nerve and inferior gluteal vessels lie within 2 cm — caution with deep needle pass.
Bounded by parietal presacral fascia anteriorly, Waldeyer's fascia posteriorly; contains middle sacral vessels, presacral venous plexus — risk in sacrocolpopexy.
Avoid direct cautery (retracts into bone); use sterile thumbtacks, bone wax, or muscle weld. Massive bleeding can be fatal.
Internal anal sphincter (smooth, involuntary, autonomic); external anal sphincter (striated, voluntary, pudendal). Conjoined longitudinal muscle between.
Embryologic junction of endoderm/ectoderm; above — visceral autonomic innervation (painless); below — somatic pudendal (painful). Lymphatic drainage diverges here.
Midline aponeurotic raphe of bilateral rectus sheaths; avascular plane for midline laparotomy.
Midway between umbilicus and pubis; below this line the posterior rectus sheath is absent — all aponeuroses pass anteriorly. Key for component separation.
Superior epigastric (from internal thoracic) above umbilicus, inferior epigastric (from external iliac) below; pedicled inferior for VRAM flap.
Bounded by inferior epigastric vessels, lateral border rectus, inguinal ligament; site of direct inguinal hernias.
Inguinal ligament (superior), sartorius (lateral), adductor longus (medial). Contains NAVEL: nerve-artery-vein-empty-lymphatics, lateral to medial.
Medial circumflex femoral artery (dominant) enters proximal third; Mathes-Nahai type II — supports rotation flap with reliable proximal pivot.
Anterior to medial malleolus, ascends medial leg to join femoral vein 4 cm inferolateral to pubic tubercle. Harvest for grafts and shunts.

column1: Common peroneal nerve injury — positioning risk?
column2: Compression at fibular head during lithotomy / lateral decubitus → foot drop. Pad fibular head; check pulses and dorsiflexion postop.
Branch of lumbar plexus exiting under inguinal ligament near ASIS; compressed in prone/lithotomy → meralgia paresthetica.
Stensen duct opens opposite 2nd upper molar; harvest stays ≥1 cm from duct and 1 cm from oral commissure; preserves a mucosal collar at gingival margin.
Submandibular (Wharton) duct opens at ventral tongue base; harvest from lateral undersurface avoiding duct and avoiding lingual nerve laterally.
Inner aspect of lower lip; harvest <3 cm length and avoid vermilion to prevent eversion deformity; mental nerve runs at oral commissure.
Skin posterior to auricle; provides thin pliable graft for meatal or fossa-navicularis reconstruction; donor closes primarily.

column1: Sympathetic afferent referred-pain map for kidney?
column2: T10–L1 sympathetic — flank and groin referral; explains scrotal/labial radiation of renal colic.

column1: Continence mechanisms in the female — DeLancey three?
column2: (1) Pelvic floor reflex contraction, (2) urethral support hammock, (3) intrinsic sphincter function (rhabdosphincter + vascular cushion + mucosal seal).
Bladder filling → afferent S2–S4 → pontine storage center → sympathetic T10–L2 (β3 relaxes detrusor) and somatic (pudendal contracts sphincter).
Bladder fullness → spinobulbospinal reflex through pontine micturition center (Barrington nucleus) → parasympathetic S2–S4 contracts detrusor + relaxes sphincter via NO.

column1: Definition of detrusor overactivity on UDS?
column2: Involuntary detrusor contractions during filling phase, of any amplitude, with or without leak. Diagnosed on UDS, not by symptoms alone.

column1: Bladder compliance — normal value and formula?
column2: ΔV/ΔPdet; normal >20 mL/cm H₂O. Low compliance (<12.5) is upper-tract threat — augmentation indication.

column1: Detrusor leak point pressure threshold of concern?
column2: >40 cm H₂O (McGuire) predicts upper tract deterioration in neurogenic bladder; absolute indication for management escalation.
<60 cm H₂O suggests ISD; >90 cm H₂O suggests pure urethral hypermobility. Guides sling vs bulking choice.
Male Qmax >15 mL/s, female >20 mL/s on adequate volume (>150 mL). Below threshold raises BOO concern.
Plots Pdet@Qmax vs Qmax to grade BOO (0–VI) and detrusor contractility (very weak → strong). Standard for male UDS interpretation.
BOOI = PdetQmax − 2(Qmax); >40 obstructed, 20–40 equivocal, <20 unobstructed.
BCI = PdetQmax + 5(Qmax); >150 strong, 100–150 normal, <100 underactive. Predicts post-TURP voiding.
Endoderm of urogenital sinus; dome from allantois remnant (becomes urachus). Patent urachus = persistent communication to umbilicus.
Prostatic and membranous from urogenital sinus (endoderm); penile from urethral folds (endoderm) which fuse; fossa navicularis from ectodermal ingrowth of glans.
Failure of urethral fold fusion (weeks 8–14); androgen-dependent. Distal forms most common; severity tracks ventral curvature and chordee.
Epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicle, ejaculatory duct. Trigone is partial mesonephric origin.
Fallopian tubes, uterus, upper 2/3 vagina; appendix testis in males (Müllerian remnant); prostatic utricle is Müllerian remnant.
Failure of cloacal membrane mesodermal ingrowth; persistent cloaca, omphalocele, exstrophy of bladder + bowel, ambiguous genitalia. OEIS complex.
Sertoli: AMH (regresses Müllerian), inhibin B, supports spermatogenesis. Leydig: testosterone under LH stimulation.
Vaginal artery (branch of internal iliac/uterine), with anastomoses from middle rectal and internal pudendal; supports flap viability in pudendal-thigh and lotus-petal harvests.
Rectoprostatic / rectovaginal fascial layer between prostate or vagina and rectum; surgical plane in prostatectomy and rectocele repair.
Continuous visceral fascia investing pelvic organs; condensations form pubocervical fascia anteriorly, rectovaginal fascia posteriorly, USL/cardinal complex apically.

column1: What is the genitofemoral nerve and risk?
column2: L1–L2; genital branch innervates cremaster and labial/scrotal skin. Damaged in low transverse / inguinal exposure → numb scrotum/labia.
From L1; travels between transversus and internal oblique, through inguinal canal anterior to cord, to scrotal/labial skin. Entrapped by Pfannenstiel closure.
L1; lateral cutaneous to gluteal skin, anterior cutaneous to suprapubic skin. Pfannenstiel entrapment classic.

column1: Internal iliac artery anterior division branches?
column2: Umbilical (with superior vesical), obturator, inferior vesical, middle rectal, uterine/vaginal, internal pudendal, inferior gluteal. Hypogastric ligation spares these via collateral.
Iliolumbar, lateral sacral, superior gluteal. Spared in hypogastric ligation for hemorrhage control.

column1: Mathes-Nahai flap classification — type I vs V?
column2: Type I: single vascular pedicle (e.g., TFL). Type V: one dominant + secondary segmental (e.g., latissimus). Predicts rotation arc and harvest reliability.

column1: Anatomy of the male pelvic plexus?
column2: Lateral to seminal vesicles and prostate (5 and 7 o'clock); inputs from hypogastric + pelvic splanchnics; cavernosal nerves run on posterolateral prostate.

column1: Bladder neck circular vs trigonal smooth muscle?
column2: Bladder neck: distinct circular collar (sympathetic alpha-1, internal sphincter). Trigone: triangular muscle continuous with intramural ureter, dense alpha-1, contributes to closure.

column1: Three sources of urethral resting pressure?
column2: Smooth muscle tone (alpha-adrenergic ~30%), striated rhabdosphincter (~30%), submucosal vascular plexus and mucosal coaptation (~30%). Estrogen-responsive.

column1: What is the conjoint longitudinal muscle?
column2: Continuation of rectal longitudinal layer + puborectalis fibers between IAS and EAS; supports anal canal lengthening and helps continence.

column1: Where does the ureter cross the uterine artery in females?
column2: Water under the bridge — ureter passes posterior and inferior to uterine artery ~2 cm lateral to cervix; key landmark in hysterectomy.

column1: Renal pelvis vs intrarenal pelvis significance?
column2: Intrarenal pelvis: more challenging dismembered pyeloplasty exposure; extrarenal: easier transposition for crossing vessel.
Glans is dilated cap of corpus spongiosum; covered by stratified squamous epithelium; sensory innervation via dorsal nerves and terminal pudendal branches.
Dartos: superficial smooth muscle of scrotum. Colles: deep membranous layer of superficial perineal fascia, continuous with Scarpa abdominally and dartos in scrotum.

column1: Why does urethral injury below UG diaphragm spread to scrotum?
column2: Extravasation contained by Colles fascia inferiorly, Scarpa abdominally, dartos in scrotum — but not into thigh (fascia lata attachment).
Pudendal nerve + internal pudendal artery and vein in fascial split of obturator internus, on lateral wall of ischiorectal fossa.
Lateral: obturator internus + ischium. Medial: levator ani + EAS. Apex: where these meet. Filled with fat. Posterior approach for sacral nerve roots possible.

column1: Vagal afferents — proximal vs pelvic afferents from kidney/bladder?
column2: Renal pelvis and proximal ureter: T11–L2 sympathetic afferents (flank pain). Bladder: pelvic splanchnic + hypogastric afferents (suprapubic vs flank).
Loss of pubourethral support → urethra falls below pelvic floor → fails to be compressed against hammock during cough → leak.
Low MUCP (<20 cm H₂O) and/or low VLPP (<60 cm H₂O); urethra non-coapting at rest. Bulking and AUS rather than midurethral sling.

column1: What is the urethral pressure profile?
column2: Catheter pull-through measurement of pressures along urethra; functional length and MUCP derived. Used historically; less common since pad weight + UDS available.
Onuf's nucleus in S2–S4 anterior horn; somatic motor via pudendal nerve. Spared in MSA, lost in spinal cord injury below the level.

column1: Female pelvic floor — anterior vs posterior compartment definitions?
column2: Anterior: bladder/urethra. Apical: cervix/vault. Posterior: rectum/perineum. Defines POP-Q quantification system.
Stage 0: no prolapse. Stage IV: complete eversion (Aa, Ba, C all at +TVL or beyond). Stage II ≥ −1 cm from hymen.
Urorectal septum descends week 4–6 to divide cloaca into urogenital sinus (anterior) and anorectal canal (posterior). Failure → cloacal anomalies.
From sacral position at week 6 to T12–L3 by week 9; ascent failure = pelvic kidney; fusion = horseshoe (caught on IMA).
Ureter, renal pelvis, calyces, collecting ducts. Errors → duplications, ectopic ureter (often draining upper moiety in females → continuous incontinence).
In complete duplex system: upper-pole ureter inserts inferomedially (often ectopic, obstructed), lower-pole ureter inserts superolaterally (refluxes).
Subcutaneous, superficial, deep — classically described; functionally continuous. EAS injury graded by OASIS depth.
3a: <50% EAS thickness. 3b: >50% EAS. 3c: EAS + IAS. 4th degree: through anorectal mucosa. Repair within 12 hr if possible.

column1: Pelvic floor type 1 vs type 2 fibers?
column2: Type 1 (slow-twitch): tonic continence — 70% of levator. Type 2 (fast-twitch): reflex contraction at cough/sneeze. Both addressed in PFMT.
U-shaped opening anteriorly in pelvic diaphragm transmitting urethra, vagina, rectum. Widening in childbirth → POP.
Anterior vaginal wall over urethra-corpus spongiosum complex; corresponds to clitoral root + Skene-paraurethral tissue.

column1: Clitoral anatomy — root vs body vs glans?
column2: Paired crura attach to ischiopubic rami (root); converge into body angled posteriorly under symphysis; glans is the only externally visible part.
Erectile tissue flanking vaginal introitus deep to bulbocavernosus; engorge with arousal; preserved in vulvar reconstruction.
Strong fibrous band on superior pubic ramus; anchor for Burch colposuspension and femoral hernia repair (McVay).
Three arteries (testicular, cremasteric, deferential), three nerves (genital branch of GF, ilioinguinal, sympathetic), three other (vas, pampiniform, lymphatics).
Anterior: external oblique aponeurosis (+ internal oblique laterally). Posterior: transversalis fascia + conjoint tendon medially. Floor: inguinal ligament. Roof: arching IO/TA.
Fundiform (from linea alba) and suspensory proper (from symphysis pubis); release in penile lengthening adds visible length (~2 cm).
Superior rectal (IMA) above dentate, middle rectal (internal iliac) and inferior rectal (internal pudendal) below — anastomoses form internal hemorrhoidal cushions.

column1: Why is the rectal blood supply forgiving in low anterior resection?
column2: Rich submucosal anastomoses between superior and middle rectal arteries — but watertight at IMA ligation; key for anastomotic leak risk.

column1: Iliac vein anatomy — danger in pelvic node dissection?
column2: External iliac vein lies medial to artery and is thin-walled; common site of avulsion. Use atraumatic vascular control; compress proximally and distally for repair.

column1: What is the obturator internus muscle role in pelvic anatomy?
column2: Lateral wall of true pelvis; obturator NVB passes anteriorly through obturator canal; ischiorectal fossa lies medial.
Direct branches from S4–S5; with iliococcygeus forms posterior pelvic floor. Site for sacrospinous suspension stitch.

column1: Penile cavernosal nerve injury — anatomic mechanism in RP?
column2: Apical and lateral prostatic attachments tear cavernous fibers; nerve-sparing dissects within prostatic fascia plane to preserve potency.
Hemostasis (immediate), inflammation (days 1–4), proliferation (days 4–21), remodeling (3 weeks–1 year). Tensile strength peaks at ~70–80% of pre-injury.

column1: Wound tensile strength at 1 week vs 6 weeks?
column2: ~3–5% at 1 wk, ~50% at 6 wk, ~80% by 6 mo. Never returns to baseline.

column1: Primary vs secondary vs tertiary intention?
column2: Primary: clean wound closure. Secondary: granulation + contracture. Tertiary (delayed primary): closed after 4–5 days when contamination resolved.

column1: Why is wound contraction problematic in GU reconstruction?
column2: Myofibroblast-driven contraction is unwanted in mucosal substitution (urethra, vagina) — STSG contracts up to 40%, FTSG ~10–20%. Drives stricture recurrence.

column1: STSG vs FTSG composition and behavior?
column2: STSG: epidermis + partial dermis, takes more readily, contracts more. FTSG: epidermis + full dermis, takes less reliably, contracts less, better cosmesis.
Imbibition (24–48 hr, plasma nutrition), inosculation (48–72 hr, capillary alignment), neovascularization (>72 hr, in-growth).

column1: Why does buccal mucosa take so well on urethra?
column2: Thick non-keratinized epithelium, dense thin lamina propria with high panlaminar vascular plexus → efficient inosculation; resistant to urine.
Tacks graft to bed at multiple points, eliminating shear and dead space; allows imbibition and prevents hematoma/seroma uplift. Key for BMG urethroplasty.
Ensures continuous contact pressure between graft and bed during inosculation; reduces hematoma and shear; leave 5–7 days.

column1: Random pattern vs axial pattern flap?
column2: Random: supplied by dermal/subdermal plexus, length:base ratio 1.5:1 to 2:1. Axial: named artery within fascial pedicle, longer reach (e.g., Singapore flap).
Type A: multiple fasciocutaneous perforators (random-like). Type B: single perforator. Type C: segmental perforators along septum (used in radial forearm).
Muscle flap classification by vascular anatomy (I single pedicle → V dominant + secondary); predicts reliability and rotation arc.
Skin paddle supplied by named muscle/septocutaneous perforators with intramuscular dissection sparing the muscle (e.g., DIEP vs TRAM, ALT, SCIP).
60° limbs gain ~75% length along central limb; 45° ~50%, 30° ~25%. Used for scar contracture release.
V-shaped incision advances toward defect; donor closes as Y. Used for vulvar reconstruction and meatal advancement.
60°/120° rhombus; flap transposes from adjacent tissue along the short diagonal axis. Closes donor primarily.
Posterior labial branches of internal pudendal artery; axial fasciocutaneous flap from medial thigh/groin for vaginal reconstruction.
Labial fat-pad ± bulbocavernosus, pedicled on posterior labial branches inferiorly or anterior obturator superiorly; interposed in fistula repair.
Medial circumflex femoral artery — Mathes-Nahai II; reliable rotation flap for perineal, urethral, fistula coverage.
Fasciocutaneous flap on radial artery, thin pliable skin, sensate via lateral antebrachial cutaneous; workhorse for phalloplasty urethra and shaft.
Descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery; perforators from septocutaneous or musculocutaneous; large pliable skin paddle for phalloplasty.
Both based on deep inferior epigastric perforators. TRAM sacrifices rectus muscle; DIEP preserves muscle by intramuscular perforator dissection — lower abdominal morbidity.
Mobilize from greater curvature, preserve right or left gastroepiploic; long pedicle for vesicovaginal, rectovaginal fistula interposition; lymphangiogenic.
Vascularized layer for VVF interposition or as vaginal lining in robotic vaginoplasty; preserves the omentum.
Lateral femoral circumflex transverse branch; Mathes-Nahai I; reach to groin/perineum but distal third unreliable.
Axial fasciocutaneous flap from gluteal fold based on internal pudendal perforators; pivots into vulvoperineal defect.
Inferior gluteal artery perforator (IGAP) or descending branch of profunda; long sensate flap from posterior thigh for perineal defects.
1.5:1 or 2:1 meshing increases coverage and drains exudate but increases secondary contraction and produces visible pebbling. Avoid for visible scrotum unless necessary.

column1: Why use saphenous vein graft in priapism shunts?
column2: Reliable autologous conduit (Grayhack, Barry); large caliber, accessible, long pedicle for cavernovenous anastomosis.
Thin friable graft with high contraction; largely abandoned for buccal but historical option for hypospadias salvage.

column1: Tissue-engineered scaffolds in GU — current status?
column2: Decellularized matrices and synthetic polymer scaffolds investigational for urethral substitution; no scaffold matches autologous BMG outcomes to date.

column1: Radiation tissue effect — chronic vs acute?
column2: Acute: mucositis, dermatitis, edema (weeks). Chronic: endarteritis obliterans, fibrosis, vessel dropout, hypoxia, hypocellularity. Reconstruction needs vascularized non-radiated tissue import.
Hypoxia, hypocellularity, hypovascularity (3 H's); progressive obliterative endarteritis. Rationale for HBOT and flap interposition.
Hyperoxygenation drives angiogenesis, stimulates fibroblast/osteoclast function, increases stem-cell mobilization; Marx 20/10 protocol common.

column1: Marx HBOT protocol for radiation cystitis?
column2: 20 preop + 10 postop sessions at 2.0–2.4 ATA for 90 min daily; evidence supports symptomatic relief in 60–80% of refractory hemorrhagic cystitis.
Secondary intention → primary closure → STSG → FTSG → local flap → regional flap → distant flap → free flap. Modern "elevator" jumps rungs for best result.
Skin hooks, fine forceps, tension-free closure, layered approximation, eversion of edges; minimize crush and ischemia.
Gentle tissue handling, meticulous hemostasis, anatomic dissection, asepsis, tension-free closure, accurate approximation, dead-space obliteration.
Monofilament: low tissue drag, less bacterial harborage, weaker knot security (more throws). Braided: handles well, secure knots, higher infection risk.

column1: Absorption half-life — Vicryl vs PDS vs Monocryl?
column2: Vicryl: 50% strength at 21 d, absorbed 56–70 d. PDS: 50% at 6 wk, absorbed 6 mo. Monocryl: 50% at 7 d, absorbed 90–120 d.

column1: Why is PDS preferred for urinary tract closure?
column2: Long absorption, monofilament (low encrustation), retained strength for healing; avoid permanent suture in lumen to prevent stones.

column1: Why avoid permanent suture in urinary lumen?
column2: Nidus for stone formation, encrustation, biofilm, chronic infection. Use absorbable (Vicryl, Monocryl, PDS).
V-Loc: unidirectional barbs with terminal loop. Quill: bidirectional. Both eliminate knot tying; reduce closure time but caution on running tension distribution.

column1: Barbed suture concern in vesicourethral anastomosis?
column2: Generally safe and faster; some series link to migration if exposed at mucosa. Lock with backthrow at end and bury knots/tails.

column1: Needle taper vs cutting vs reverse cutting?
column2: Taper: round body, atraumatic — fascia/bowel/vessel. Cutting: triangular point inward — skin, tough fibrous. Reverse cutting: triangle outward — preferred skin to reduce cut-out.

column1: Knot security — number of throws by suture?
column2: Monofilament (Prolene/PDS): 6–7 throws. Braided (Vicryl/silk): 3–4 throws. Always more throws for slippery suture.
Double-throw first knot increases friction to hold while second throw is set; helpful for high-tension closure.
Lag phase 0–4 d (loss of preexisting collagen), fibroplasia 4–14 d (new collagen synthesis), maturation >14 d. Anastomotic leak typically POD 5–7.

column1: Why is the submucosa the holding layer in bowel anastomosis?
column2: Highest tensile strength; collagen-rich; full-thickness bites that include submucosa give durable closure.

column1: Hand-sewn vs stapled bowel anastomosis — outcomes?
column2: Equivalent leak rates in meta-analyses; stapled faster, hand-sewn cheaper. Stapled preferred in robotic/laparoscopic; both valid in open.
Abbreviated laparotomy: control hemorrhage and contamination, temporary closure, ICU resuscitation, return for definitive repair when triad reversed.
Hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy — self-perpetuating. Damage control aims to interrupt before definitive repair.
1 unit PRBC : 1 FFP : 1 platelet (PROPPR trial) — better hemostasis, lower 24-hr death from exsanguination. TXA within 3 hr.
Within 3 hours of injury; CRASH-2 showed mortality benefit; loading 1 g over 10 min then 1 g over 8 hr.
Clamping of portal triad (hepatic artery + portal vein) at foramen of Winslow to control hepatic bleeding; tolerated up to 60 min intermittently.

column1: Exposure principle for retroperitoneal hematoma — zone 1?
column2: Central / pancreaticoduodenal — explore in trauma (proximal vascular control via supraceliac aorta or left medial visceral rotation).
Lateral (renal) — explore only if pulsatile, expanding, or penetrating; blunt non-expanding can be observed if imaging adequate.
Pelvic — do NOT explore in blunt trauma (release of tamponade); preperitoneal packing + angioembolization preferred.
Mattox: left medial visceral rotation (exposes supraceliac aorta, left renal vessels, IMA). Cattell-Braasch: right (exposes IVC, right renal hilum, duodenum).
Choose flap to optimize outcome, not the lowest rung that closes; free flap may be best primary choice in radiated or complex defects.
Neutral wrist, elbow at 90–120°, shoulder adducted/relaxed; reduces musculoskeletal injury and microsurgical tremor.
2.5–4.5× for urologic anastomoses (urethra, vasovasostomy ~6×). Operating microscope 10–25× for microsurgery (vas, lymphatic).

column1: Why preserve adventitial blood supply on ureter?
column2: Adventitia carries longitudinal anastomotic plexus; stripping → ischemia → late stricture/breakdown.
Psoas hitch (gains 5 cm), Boari flap (10–15 cm), ipsilateral nephropexy, downward kidney mobilization (extra 2 cm); transureteroureterostomy as alternative.

column1: Why is detubularization required in continent diversion?
column2: Spheroid >> tubular for compliance and capacity (Laplace law); reduces unit pressures and protects upper tracts.
Adhesion-dense fields → risk of enterotomy; consider preop imaging, adhesiolysis time, and segment selection (mid ileum if terminal previously used).

column1: Bowel segment functional differences — ileum vs colon?
column2: Ileum: better compliance, lower mucus, B12/bile salt absorption. Colon: thicker wall, electrolyte reabsorption (hyperchloremic acidosis risk). Choose by reconstruction goal.
Through rectus, in supine/sitting/standing positions, away from scars/folds/belt line, patient can visualize; ideally marked by stoma nurse preop.

column1: Wound healing factors — modifiable risk reduction?
column2: Smoking cessation (4 wk preop), glucose <180 mg/dL, normothermia, oxygenation, nutrition (prealbumin >18), no NSAIDs in early phase.
Reduces edema and exudate, increases granulation tissue, microdeformation stimulates angiogenesis, decreases bacterial load (debated), bridges to closure.
Slow expansion stimulates "biologic creep" with epidermal hyperplasia and dermal thinning; net tissue gain for scrotal/penile shaft coverage in burns.

column1: What is delayed primary closure indication?
column2: Contaminated wound (penetrating bowel, Fournier's stage); pack open, observe 3–5 d, close when no infection. Tertiary intention.

column1: Why does urine cause poor healing?
column2: Urea, salts, and pH disrupt fibroblast and angiogenesis; chronic urine extravasation → fibrosis and fistula persistence. Divert + drain + interpose flap.
Typically ≥1 mm; smaller (perforator-to-perforator) uses supermicrosurgery (≤0.8 mm) with 11-0 nylon.
8–10 sutures (12 o'clock first, equally spaced, back-wall in/out from inside the lumen) ensures circumferential approximation without leak.

column1: Cold ischemia vs warm ischemia tolerance for flaps?
column2: Warm ischemia: muscle 4–6 hr, skin/fasciocutaneous up to 8 hr. Cold (4 °C): 12–24 hr in selected cases. Plan for prompt revascularization.
Color (pink → pale = arterial; dusky/purple = venous), capillary refill (1–2 s normal), turgor, Doppler signal, temperature, pinprick bleed quality.

column1: Salvage of failing flap — venous vs arterial?
column2: Venous congestion: medicinal leeches (Hirudo) buy 24–48 hr; arterial: emergent re-exploration, thrombectomy, anastomotic revision.

column1: Why are flaps preferred over grafts in radiated beds?
column2: Grafts require local neovascularization (impossible in obliterative endarteritis); flaps bring their own blood supply. Cornerstone of post-radiation reconstruction.

column1: Penile preputial graft vs flap utility?
column2: Preputial skin: classic donor for hypospadias graft or pedicled island flap; supplied by dartos pedicle. Avoid in circumcised patients.
Superficial circumflex iliac artery perforator; thin pliable groin flap; used in genital lymphedema (3R/LFT) and resurfacing.
Reorients scars to align with relaxed skin tension lines; gains length perpendicular to scar; used for meatal stenosis and urethral lengthening.
Perineal scrotal skin advancement (inverted-U) for perineal urethrostomy in long-segment / panurethral stricture not amenable to substitution.
Anterior bladder wall flap with base:apex ratio ≥3:1, base ≥4 cm, length up to 15 cm; tubularized over stent for distal ureteral reconstruction.
Perforator pedicle as pivot; skin paddle rotated up to 180° around perforator. Avoids microsurgical anastomosis for distant flap reach.
Vertical rectus abdominis musculocutaneous flap on inferior epigastric pedicle; volume + skin paddle for major pelvic-exenteration defects.
Internal and external pudendal artery perforator flaps; respectively from internal pudendal (gluteal-fold) and external pudendal (mons/labial) supply.
Profunda femoris perforator propeller flap from medial thigh; rotates into perineal/scrotal defects on perforator pivot.
Clean, clean-contaminated, contaminated, dirty. SSI risk: 1–2%, 5–10%, 15–20%, >30% respectively. Drives prophylactic antibiotic choice.
Dehiscence: fascial closure failure (~POD 5–10). Evisceration: contents through fascia. Pink serosanguineous "salmon fluid" precedes both — return to OR.
Δ pressure (DBP − compartment) <30 mm Hg or absolute >30; emergency fasciotomy. Risk after prolonged lithotomy (well-leg compartment syndrome).
Transfixion stitch with double-loop wrap around a Heaney clamp on a large pelvic pedicle; clamp unwound while tightening, providing transfixion + coaptation + double-loop lock.

column1: Heaney stitch — three mechanisms preventing slippage?
column2: (1) Transfixion through pedicle tissue, (2) clamp coaptation of pedicle, (3) double-loop wrap. No simpler ligature is as reliable on large pelvic pedicles.
Vaginal hysterectomy pedicle control: uterine artery, cardinal and uterosacral ligaments, ovarian pedicle. Also used for USL suspension anchor stitches.
Inverting closure of a divided bowel end without staplers: clamp-guided continuous Connell-type seromuscular bites slid off the clamp, then a second Lembert layer.
Closure of open bowel ends in hand-sewn anastomosis (e.g., Hartmann pouch, blind stump in continent diversion), Roux-en-Y limb stumps. Useful when staplers unavailable or contraindicated.
Parker-Kerr uses a Connell-pattern (inverting) running stitch sequentially "rolled off" a clamp; differs from open hand-sewn Connell only in that the clamp guides inversion.
Tacks graft (BMG, FTSG) or flap to underlying bed at multiple interior points; eliminates dead space and shear, supports imbibition.

column1: Quilting stitch — typical material and spacing?
column2: Fine absorbable (5-0 or 6-0 PDS/Vicryl) placed every 5–8 mm in lattice; full-thickness through graft into vascular bed.

column1: Quilting stitch — risk if too aggressive?
column2: Strangulates graft vascularity; pull stitches snug but not tight; over-suturing concentrates ischemia and worsens take.
Reduces grip tackiness, eases instrument handling, decreases inadvertent suture snag and tissue trauma during microsurgery; demonstrated in vasovasostomy and microsurgical training.
Sterile saline or water; avoid antiseptics (chlorhexidine/iodine) which may degrade latex. Re-wet periodically.

column1: Glove perforation — rate in long urologic case?
column2: Roughly 10–25% perforation by 2 hr; double-gloving reduces inner-glove perforation by ~70%. Change at standard intervals during exposure.
Reduces drag and memory in monofilament (PDS, Prolene); decreases tissue cheesewiring on running fascial closure.
Sterile saline, lubricated suture coatings (factory), or surgeon-applied "running through wet gauze" pass before high-tension closure.

column1: Common knot-tying error — granny vs square knot?
column2: Granny: both throws same direction (slips). Square: opposing directions. Always confirm reversed throws to lock.
Two-handed: precise placement (deep pelvis, vascular). One-handed: speed (skin, fascia). Both must yield square knots.
Microsurgery, fine vessel anastomosis, when economizing on suture length. Limits knot security versus two-handed.
First throw deep, subsequent throws lock at depth, tail cut short; used for subcuticular and intracorporeal scenarios to avoid extrusion.

column1: Why are surgeon's loupes set at fixed working distance?
column2: Bifocals matched to surgeon's preferred posture (40–50 cm); fixed declination ~30–40° avoids cervical flexion strain.
Forearms supported, wrists in slight extension, fine movements from thumb-index pinch with intrinsic muscle control. Damp tremor with breathing rhythm.
In anastomosis, completing the posterior (deep) wall first while exposure is best, then rotating to anterior wall — used in ureteroureterostomy and vesicourethral anastomosis.

column1: Van Velthoven anastomosis — what is it?
column2: Continuous double-armed running vesicourethral anastomosis (RARP); two sutures tied together at 6 o'clock, run up to 12 o'clock and tied. Speeds closure.
In anastomosis where mucosa-to-mucosa apposition needed (ureter, urethra), evert edges with through-and-through bites to prevent inversion and stricture.
Pressure → bipolar/monopolar → ligation → clip → suture-ligature → packing/hemostatic agent → vascular control proximal/distal. Choose by vessel size and tissue type.

column1: Bipolar vs monopolar safety in pelvic surgery?
column2: Bipolar: current local to tips, safer near nerves/ureter. Monopolar: stray current and lateral thermal spread up to 5 mm; avoid near vital structures.

column1: Stitch interval rule for fascial closure (4:1)?
column2: Suture length 4× wound length (Jenkins rule) with 1-cm bites at 1-cm spacing reduces incisional hernia incidence.

column1: Small-bite vs large-bite fascia closure (STITCH trial)?
column2: Small bites (5 mm × 5 mm with 2-0 monofilament) reduce incisional hernia at 1 yr vs 1-cm × 1-cm bites (13% vs 21%).
Continuous inverting U-stitch entering and exiting on the same side; used for bowel/inner-layer closure; achieves mucosal inversion.
Interrupted or running seromuscular inverting stitch outside the mucosa; classic second-layer of two-layer bowel anastomosis.
Continuous horizontal mattress seromuscular inverting stitch; used for bowel closure outer layer alternative to Lembert.
0–1 very low, 2 low, 3–4 moderate, ≥5 high. ≥5 indicates pharmacologic prophylaxis ± mechanical; AUA pelvic surgery typically uses Caprini-based stratification.
Enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily or UFH 5,000 U TID, plus mechanical SCDs. Extended prophylaxis 28 days for major pelvic/oncologic surgery.

column1: Extended VTE prophylaxis indications in urology?
column2: Open or robotic radical pelvic surgery, pelvic LND, prior VTE; 28-day enoxaparin reduces VTE without significant bleeding excess.
2.5 mg PO BID; investigated in PROPS trial after major cancer surgery. Convenient oral alternative to LMWH.

column1: RCRI (Lee revised cardiac risk index) — components?
column2: High-risk surgery, IHD, CHF, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated DM, Cr >2.0. ≥2 = elevated MACE; obtain functional capacity + further workup.
≥4 METs (climb a flight, walk briskly) sufficient for most non-cardiac surgery; below threshold consider stress testing if it changes management.
30 days mandatory; surgery deferred for 30 days when possible. Continue aspirin perioperatively for any cardiac stent unless bleeding prohibitive.
6 months elective surgery deferral; aspirin continued; bridge clopidogrel cessation 5–7 days preop if surgery cannot wait.
Mechanical mitral valve, recent VTE <3 mo, AF with CHADS₂ ≥5; bridge with LMWH. Otherwise hold 5 d, restart 24 hr postop.

column1: DOAC perioperative hold — apixaban high-bleed-risk procedure?
column2: Hold 48 hr preop (CrCl >30); 72 hr if CrCl <30. No bridging needed.
Specific reversal of dabigatran (humanized Fab fragment); 5 g IV. Andexanet alfa reverses apixaban/rivaroxaban.

column1: PCC vs FFP for warfarin reversal?
column2: 4-factor PCC (Kcentra) preferred for emergent reversal: faster INR correction, less volume, lower TRALI; FFP reserved for unavailable PCC.
>5 mg prednisone equivalent for >3 wk in last 6 mo with major surgery; give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV then 50 mg q8h × 24 hr.

column1: Low-dose chronic steroids and surgical infection risk?
column2: Increases SSI ~2× and impairs wound healing; cannot stop perioperatively without precipitating crisis. Optimize glycemic control and nutrition.
<7% ideal; <8% acceptable. >8% associated with increased SSI; postpone elective surgery if reasonable.
140–180 mg/dL intra/postop; tight control (<110) increases hypoglycemia without benefit (NICE-SUGAR).
Hold weekly formulations (semaglutide) 1 week preop, daily 24 hr — anesthesia aspiration risk from delayed gastric emptying (ASA 2023).
Hold 3–4 days preop (per duration); risk of euglycemic DKA, especially with prolonged NPO and surgical stress.
Hold day of surgery; resume when normal renal function and PO intake. Lactic acidosis risk in AKI.
Hgb <13 g/dL men, <12 g/dL women: iron studies (ferritin <30 = deficiency); IV iron 4–6 wk preop reduces transfusion.
1 g IV over 10 min, repeat 1 g over 8 hr; reduces transfusion in major surgery; avoid in thromboembolic history if alternatives exist.
Hopkins Frailty Phenotype (5 criteria: weight loss, exhaustion, low grip, slow gait, low activity); Modified Frailty Index (5 or 11 items). Predicts complications and mortality.
4–6 wk preop exercise + nutrition + smoking cessation + psychosocial support reduces complications in major urologic surgery.
Hold biologics 1 dosing cycle preop; continue baseline immunosuppressants (tacrolimus, MMF) for transplant patients. Coordinate with transplant team.
Maintain target trough; oral can be IV-converted at 1/3 dose. Avoid nephrotoxins; monitor levels every 1–2 d.

column1: ERAS — core components for urologic surgery?
column2: Carb loading, no prolonged fasting, no MBP (often), opioid-sparing analgesia, normothermia, early feeding, early ambulation, early Foley removal, multimodal antiemesis.
Clear liquids up to 2 hr preop, light meal 6 hr; carb drink at 2 hr reduces insulin resistance.

column1: Mechanical bowel prep — current cystectomy practice?
column2: Generally omitted in cystectomy (no clear benefit, increased dehydration/AKI); selective use for colon-based diversions or per individual practice.
Peripheral mu-opioid antagonist; accelerates return of bowel function after cystectomy with diversion (POBE study); decreases ileus and LOS by ~1 day.
Within 60 min of incision (120 min for vancomycin/fluoroquinolones); redose if surgery >2× drug half-life or blood loss >1.5 L.

column1: AUA prophylaxis for cystoscopy with manipulation?
column2: Single dose TMP-SMX or fluoroquinolone or cephalexin; not routinely needed for simple diagnostic cystoscopy in low-risk patients.

column1: AUA prophylaxis for clean vaginal surgery?
column2: First-generation cephalosporin (cefazolin 2 g, 3 g if >120 kg) within 60 min; metronidazole added if anaerobe risk.
Vancomycin + gentamicin (or aminoglycoside) within 60 min; addresses staph + gram-negative skin flora; controversial but standard.

column1: Postoperative pulmonary embolism — first-line diagnostic imaging?
column2: CT pulmonary angiogram. V/Q scan if contrast contraindicated. D-dimer rarely useful postop (universally elevated).
Hemodynamic compromise → systemic thrombolytics (tPA 100 mg over 2 hr) or catheter-directed; surgical embolectomy if contraindicated to lytics.

column1: SCD vs IPC — what's the difference?
column2: Sequential compression device = intermittent pneumatic compression; same modality. Reduces stasis component of Virchow triad.

column1: Postop nutrition — when start oral feeds?
column2: Early enteral within 24 hr if tolerated (ERAS); reduces ileus, infection, LOS. Even in bowel anastomosis early feeds are safe.
Severe malnutrition, alcohol use, weight loss >10%. Watch phosphate (drops first), magnesium, potassium. Replete before/with refeeding; advance slowly.
Glycine absorption during TURP → dilutional hyponatremia + hyperammonemia (glycine metabolism); confusion, seizures. Switch to bipolar saline TURP eliminates risk.
SIADH: euvolemic, restrict water. CSW: hypovolemic (urinary Na high), replete saline. Both occur post-pelvic surgery.
≤8–10 mEq/L per 24 hr to avoid osmotic demyelination; emergent (seizing) 3% saline 100 mL bolus.
Common in ileal/colonic conduit and continent diversions; longer bowel segments worsen. Treat sodium bicarbonate; consider nicotinic acid (chloride co-transporter).
With terminal ileum >60 cm resected; deficiency emerges 3–5 yr after stores depleted. Annual screening; lifelong IM B12 1,000 µg monthly.
Stop opioids (use NSAID/regional), alvimopan, ambulation, gum chewing, nasogastric decompression only if severe, electrolyte correction (K, Mg).
Senna + docusate scheduled, lactulose PRN; advance with PO intake; assess opioid contribution; avoid bisacodyl in fresh anastomosis.
Scheduled acetaminophen + NSAID (where safe) + gabapentin (selected) + regional (TAP, epidural, intrathecal) + opioid-sparing rescue.
T7–L1 dermatomes (abdominal wall); lateral midaxillary or subcostal approach; spares visceral pain — adjunct, not sole analgesia for laparotomy.
Posterior abdominal wall block providing somatic + some visceral analgesia for nephrectomy/cystectomy; longer duration than TAP.
Ischial spine palpated transvaginally or transperineally; local 10–20 mL injected near pudendal canal; provides perineal/vulvar surgical analgesia.
Spinal: rapid onset, single shot ~2 hr (bupivacaine). Epidural: continuous infusion, hours-days; preferred for major open abdominal/pelvic.
Common peroneal palsy (fibular head compression), femoral neuropathy (excessive hip flexion), well-leg compartment syndrome (>4 hr), DVT.

column1: Lithotomy duration risk for compartment syndrome?
column2: >4 hours; reposition every 2 hours if possible. SCDs OFF the elevated leg (calf compression in lithotomy ineffective).
Brachial plexus stretch, eye compression (POVL), chest wall hypoventilation; pad axillae and head; check eyes regularly.
Steep Trendelenburg (>30°) for RARP/sacrocolpopexy raises IOP — POVL risk. Limit duration when feasible; head-up "breaks" if long case.
QT prolongation (max 16 mg IV); use with caution with other QT drugs. Dexamethasone 4 mg + ondansetron is standard ERAS pairing.
Female, nonsmoker, history of PONV/motion sickness, postop opioids. ≥3 = high risk, multimodal prophylaxis.

column1: Foley removal timing in ERAS cystectomy?
column2: Diversion-dependent: stents 2–3 wk, Foley/urethral catheter per anastomosis. Avoid prolonged urethral catheter in ileal conduit (not needed).
Output <50 mL/d, low creatinine (matches serum), no chylous appearance. Routine prolonged drainage discouraged.
Drain Cr > serum Cr (typically >2× serum); ratio ≥1.1 raises concern. Direct urethrography / cystography if leak suspected.
POD 1: Wind (atelectasis). POD 3: Water (UTI). POD 5: Walking (DVT/PE). POD 7: Wound (SSI). Anytime: Wonder drugs / lines.
↑Cr ≥0.3 mg/dL in 48 hr or ≥1.5× baseline in 7 d, or UOP <0.5 mL/kg/hr × 6 hr. Stage I–III.
Stroke-volume-variability or pulse-pressure-variability guided fluid bolus to optimize cardiac output; reduces both over- and under-resuscitation in ERAS.
4–8 weeks optimal; even 4 weeks reduces SSI and pulmonary complications; <4 wk may transiently increase secretions but still net benefit.
Age, surgery type (AAA highest), albumin, BUN, functional dependence, COPD; predicts respiratory failure within 30 days.
≥3 yes = intermediate risk; ≥5 high risk. Pre-existing CPAP brought to hospital; postop monitoring for opioid-induced respiratory depression.
Reduces SSI, blood loss, transfusion, arrhythmia; forced-air warming + warmed fluids. Target >36 °C.
Platelet dysfunction and reduced enzymatic clotting cascade <34 °C; reversible with warming. Avoid in massive transfusion (lethal triad).
0.5 mL/kg/hr adult; 1 mL/kg/hr peds; <0.3 sustained → oliguria, evaluate volume + obstruction (kink, clot, missed catheter occlusion).

column1: Anesthetic implications of spinal cord injury T6 or above?
column2: Autonomic dysreflexia — paroxysmal hypertension from bladder/bowel stimulus; pretreat with adequate anesthesia, avoid noxious stimuli at awakening.
Volatile anesthetics (sevoflurane, isoflurane) and succinylcholine; dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV is treatment.

column1: Local anesthetic max dose — lidocaine plain vs with epi?
column2: Plain 4.5 mg/kg (max 300 mg); with epinephrine 7 mg/kg (max 500 mg). Bupivacaine: 2 mg/kg (max 175 mg).
Stop injection, ABC, benzodiazepines for seizure, 20% lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg bolus + infusion 0.25 mL/kg/min. Avoid vasopressin/calcium channel blockers.
Male, age >50, BPH history, opioid use, regional anesthesia, prolonged surgery, gynecologic/anorectal surgery. Trial of void protocol postop.
Cephalic phase stimulation accelerates return of bowel function modestly; cheap and safe adjunct.
Hair clip (not shave), CHG bath, normothermia, glucose control, prophylactic antibiotic timing/redose, supplemental O₂, wound protector for bowel.

column1: CHG skin prep vs povidone iodine?
column2: Chlorhexidine-alcohol (Hibiclens) superior to povidone in clean-contaminated surgery (Darouiche NEJM 2010); avoid in eyes/mucosa.
I: healthy. II: mild systemic. III: severe systemic non-incapacitating. IV: incapacitating life-threatening. V: moribund <24 hr without surgery. E suffix = emergency.
Procedure-specific 30-day mortality, MACE, SSI, pneumonia, AKI, VTE, return to OR, LOS. Used for informed-consent and risk-mitigation planning.
5 variables: age, dependent status, creatinine, ASA, procedure-specific risk. Outputs MICA — perioperative MI or cardiac arrest probability.
Non-selective antimuscarinic (M1–M5); highest CNS penetration → cognitive impairment risk in elderly. Avoid in frail/dementia.

column1: Oxybutynin IR vs ER vs transdermal — comparison?
column2: IR: highest dry mouth (active metabolite N-desethyl). ER: smoother; transdermal/gel: bypass first pass, less metabolite, less xerostomia.
Non-selective antimuscarinic but more bladder-selective than oxybutynin clinically; LA form 4 mg once daily.
M3-preferential antimuscarinic; 5–10 mg daily; lower xerostomia vs oxybutynin; QT caution at 10 mg.
M3-selective antimuscarinic; less CNS penetration (less anticholinergic burden); useful in cognitively vulnerable.
Quaternary amine — minimal CNS penetration (does not cross BBB); renally excreted; preferred in dementia. Take on empty stomach.
Hydrolyzed by nonspecific esterases to 5-HMT (active metabolite of tolterodine); avoids CYP variability; 4 or 8 mg daily.
Narrow-angle glaucoma, gastric retention, severe UC; relative — myasthenia, severe constipation, urinary retention without catheter.
Cumulative anticholinergic exposure linked to dementia risk (Gray JAMA 2015) — minimize in elderly, prefer trospium or beta-3.
Selective beta-3 adrenergic agonist; 25 or 50 mg daily; relaxes detrusor during filling without affecting voiding contraction.

column1: Mirabegron — main side effect of clinical relevance?
column2: Hypertension elevation (~1–3 mm Hg); avoid uncontrolled HTN. Limited tachycardia; QT change minimal. Inhibits CYP2D6.
Newer beta-3 agonist 75 mg daily; comparable efficacy with less HTN signal and no major CYP2D6 interaction; less DDI burden.
Synergistic efficacy in refractory OAB (BESIDE, SYNERGY trials) — modest additive UUI reduction without major safety signal.

column1: OnabotulinumtoxinA bladder dose for idiopathic OAB?
column2: 100 U intradetrusor in 20 sites; refractory OAB after antimuscarinics. Risk: PVR/CIC ~5%, UTI 25%.

column1: OnabotulinumtoxinA dose for neurogenic detrusor overactivity?
column2: 200 U intradetrusor (30 sites); higher than idiopathic; CIC almost universally required after.
Cleaves SNAP-25 → blocks acetylcholine release at parasympathetic terminals → reduces detrusor contraction; effect 6–9 months.
Nocturnal polyuria (>33% urine output overnight); ddAVP 0.2 mg PO or sublingual 27.7 µg (women) / 55.3 µg (men) nightly.
Baseline + 7-day + 30-day sodium; risk highest in age >65, baseline Na <135, concomitant diuretics. Hold if Na <130.
Heart failure (volume retention), uncontrolled HTN, baseline hyponatremia, polydipsia, SIADH, CrCl <50, age >65 with risk factors.
Selective alpha-1A/1D blocker; lower cardiovascular effects than non-selective; main side effects: ejaculatory dysfunction, IFIS, orthostasis (less).
Highly alpha-1A selective; least orthostasis but highest retrograde/anejaculation (~28%).
Non-subtype-selective alpha-1 blocker but functionally uroselective; once daily; lower ejaculatory dysfunction than tamsulosin.
Non-selective alpha-1 blockers; lower cost, more orthostatic hypotension; used for BPH + HTN dual benefit historically (ALLHAT raised CV concerns).
Tamsulosin (highest risk) > other alpha-1A blockers; warn ophthalmologist before cataract surgery; effect persists months after stopping.
Selective type-2 5-alpha reductase inhibitor; reduces DHT ~70%; ~25% prostate volume reduction over 6–12 mo; 5 mg daily.
Dual type-1 + type-2 5-ARI; DHT reduction >90%; comparable BPH efficacy; long half-life (5 wk).
Reduces PSA ~50% at 6–12 months; double measured PSA for cancer screening interpretation. Time to symptomatic benefit: 6 months.
Decreased libido, ED, ejaculatory dysfunction (~5–10%); rare persistent post-finasteride syndrome described.
A PSA that does not halve after 6 mo of finasteride/dutasteride raises cancer concern; reverse the doubling rule.
Alpha-blocker + 5-ARI reduces clinical progression more than either alone in moderate-large prostates (>40 g) with elevated PSA.
FDA-approved for LUTS/BPH; improves IPSS via smooth muscle relaxation; effective in ED + LUTS overlap; do NOT combine with alpha-blocker if not stable.
Muscarinic agonist; oral 10–50 mg TID-QID. Limited evidence; rarely used; impotency of detrusor underactivity has no strong pharm fix.
Skeletal-muscle relaxant acting on ryanodine receptor; reduces SR Ca²⁺ release; used in MH and rarely for DSD.
GABA-B agonist; oral and intrathecal (ITB pump) — spastic neurogenic bladder, especially MS/SCI with DSD.
GABA-A modulator; reduces pelvic floor tone and pain in high-tone PFD; vaginal suppositories used off-label.
Alpha-1 agonist increases urethral tone (~5–15% leakage reduction); limited efficacy; HTN/tachycardia limit chronic use.
100–200 µg every 3–5 min (max 1 mg/hr); reverses ischemic priapism by alpha-1 vasoconstriction. ECG monitoring, BP check.
Inhibit cGMP breakdown in cavernosal smooth muscle → prolonged smooth muscle relaxation → erection. Require NO/sexual stimulation to initiate.
Onset 30–60 min, peak 1–2 hr, duration 4 hr; reduced by high-fat meal. 25, 50, 100 mg.
Onset 30 min, half-life 17.5 hr — 36 hr window. 5 mg daily, 10 or 20 mg on demand. Food-independent.
Vardenafil similar to sildenafil. Avanafil: rapid onset 15–30 min, shorter half-life (~5 hr); fewer visual side effects.
Nitrate use (any form, within 24 hr sildenafil/vardenafil, 48 hr tadalafil) — fatal hypotension. Severe hepatic disease, hypotension.
Symptomatic hypotension risk; start at lowest dose, stable alpha-blocker first; tamsulosin/silodosin lowest risk pairing.
Blue-tinted vision (PDE6 cross-reaction in retina); rare NAION reports — caution in non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy history.
FDA-required warning for sudden sensorineural hearing loss; rare; discontinue and evaluate.
Test dose 2.5–5 µg titrate to 60 µg; warns to seek care if erection >4 hr (priapism risk).
Papaverine + phentolamine + PGE1; compounded; lower pain than alprostadil alone; effective when monotherapy fails.
125–1,000 µg pellet; bioavailability lower than injection; success ~40%; allows non-injectors; risk of urethral burning/syncope.
Negative pressure draws blood into corpora; ring at base maintains erection (≤30 min); useful post-RP rehab and combined with PDE5i.
Symptomatic hypogonadism + 2 confirmed AM total T <300 ng/dL; rule out reversible causes (opioid, OSA, obesity); shared decision-making on CV/prostate risk.
Untreated prostate or breast cancer, severe LUTS (AUA-SS >19), Hct >50%, untreated severe OSA, recent MI/stroke <6 mo.
Topical gel (daily, transfer risk), IM cypionate/enanthate (q1–2 wk peaks/troughs), undecanoate IM (q10 wk), pellets q3–6 mo, oral undecanoate (Jatenzo).
Total T at 3, 6, 12 mo then yearly; PSA + DRE; Hct (hold/dose-reduce >54%); evaluate symptoms; AUA 2018 / 2024 guideline.
SERM blocking hypothalamic estrogen feedback → ↑LH/FSH → ↑endogenous T; preserves spermatogenesis vs exogenous T. Off-label.

column1: HCG for fertility preservation on TRT?
column2: Mimics LH, maintains intratesticular T and spermatogenesis; 1,500–3,000 IU SQ 2–3× weekly with exogenous T.
Aromatase inhibitor 0.5–1 mg 1–3× weekly; used in obese males with E2 >50 pg/mL and persistent symptoms despite TRT.
Melanocortin receptor agonist (MC4R) injected SC for HSDD in premenopausal women; FDA 2019.
5HT1A agonist / 5HT2A antagonist for HSDD; daily oral; alcohol restrictions; hypotension/syncope risk. FDA 2015.
Off-label transdermal patch ~300 µg/d targets premenopausal upper range; benefit on sexual function modest; long-term safety unknown.
Intralesional injection in plaque; FDA-approved for stable phase with palpable plaque, curvature 30–90°; series of 4 cycles.
Corporal rupture/fracture (~0.5–1%), penile hematoma, pain. Mandatory modeling protocol; counsel on fracture risk.
Mixed evidence; AUA does not strongly recommend; off-label; used in acute-phase pain reduction with limited curvature impact.
Off-label PDE inhibitor with TGF-β reduction in animal studies; trials suggest stabilization in acute phase; limited evidence (~400 mg TID).

column1: Acute vs chronic Peyronie's — therapeutic window?
column2: Acute: <12 mo, pain, evolving curvature — medical therapy. Chronic: stable >12 mo, painless, calcification — surgical correction.

column1: Etiology of priapism — ischemic vs non-ischemic?
column2: Ischemic (low-flow): compartment-syndrome physiology, painful, dark cavernous blood, emergency. Non-ischemic: arterial fistula, painless, bright red blood, not emergent.
Aspirate cavernosa → irrigate saline → intracavernosal phenylephrine 100–200 µg q3–5 min; failure → surgical shunt (Winter → distal shunt → MPP).
PDE5i daily (paradoxical), pseudoephedrine, hormonal suppression (GnRH analog), digoxin, baclofen — variable evidence; SCD-related has hydroxyurea / transfusion.

column1: TMP-SMX prophylaxis dose for recurrent UTI?
column2: 40/200 mg PO nightly continuous, or post-coital single dose; reduces UTI by ~85%. Watch sulfa allergy/SJS.
50–100 mg nightly; avoid if CrCl <60 (now <30 per 2015 update). Pulmonary fibrosis risk with chronic use — monitor.
Hydrolyzes to formaldehyde in acidic urine (pH <5.5); ALTAR trial showed non-inferior to antibiotic prophylaxis. Co-administer vitamin C or cranberry to acidify.

column1: Topical vaginal estrogen for recurrent UTI?
column2: Postmenopausal women — reduces recurrent UTI; restores vaginal microbiome; AUA 2022 recommendation; cream/tablet/ring.
2 g daily; inhibits E. coli FimH adhesion; comparable to nitrofurantoin in one trial; safety profile favorable. Modest evidence.
Routine prophylaxis NOT recommended for clean UDS in low-risk; consider for instrumented neurogenic or recent UTI (AUA 2019 BPG).
Single dose fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX (or cephalosporin); continued only if bacteriuria documented; resistance-aware regional choice.
~1–3% infection; high stakes (explant). Vancomycin + aminoglycoside coverage; minimize OR traffic; iodine-soaked antibiotic dip.
Photodynamic agent improving NMIBC detection (~30% additional CIS detected); urology-specific aid.
Amitriptyline 10–50 mg nightly; anticholinergic + Na-channel + sodium and serotonin/NE; helps urgency, sleep, pain.
Duloxetine 30–60 mg daily (SUI in EU only); reduces neuropathic pain via DRN/LC modulation; nausea major early side effect.
Start 100–300 mg nightly, titrate to 900–1,800 mg/d; targets α2δ subunit of VGCC. Renally dose-adjust.
More predictable absorption, BID dosing, faster titration; same α2δ target; controlled substance (Schedule V).
Inhibit prostaglandin → renal vasoconstriction (avoid in AKI); GI bleed; some data on bowel anastomotic leak — pause perioperatively if concerning.

column1: Local anesthetic differences — lidocaine vs bupivacaine?
column2: Lidocaine: rapid onset, short duration (1–2 hr), low cardiotoxicity. Bupivacaine: slower, longer (4–8 hr), higher cardiotoxicity risk (LAST).
Ropivacaine: lower cardiotoxicity, slightly less motor block at same sensory level; preferred for epidurals.
Lidocaine 5% + amitriptyline 2% + gabapentin 6% (variable formulations) for vulvodynia/perineal pain; off-label.
GAG-layer restoration hypothesis; modest efficacy; maculopathy risk (Pearce 2018) limits long-term use — annual ophthalmology screening.
50% DMSO 50 mL retained 15 min; weekly × 6 sessions; gives smelly breath; AUA second-line; declining use.
Heparin 40,000 U + alkalinized lidocaine + sodium bicarb retained 30–60 min; symptomatic relief in IC/BPS flares.
GAG replacement therapy; weekly × 4–6 then monthly; common in EU; modest US adoption.
Off-label oral immunomodulator; reserved for Hunner-lesion phenotype non-responders; nephrotoxicity and HTN monitoring.
Endoscopic fulguration or triamcinolone injection; durable symptom relief; central tenet of phenotype-driven IC therapy.
UUI/OAB refractory to medical therapy, non-obstructive urinary retention, fecal incontinence. Two-stage placement preferred.
30-min sessions weekly × 12, then monthly maintenance; 60–80% improvement; non-invasive alternative to SNM.
Subcutaneous tibial nerve neuromodulator (nickel-sized) implanted in distal medial leg; FDA-approved for UUI; activates per programmed schedule.
Wireless implant in lower leg over tibial nerve, externally controlled; longer-duration alternative to in-office PTNS.
Reduce mucus formation and stone risk in ileal/colonic diversions; vitamin C, ammonium chloride; methenamine prophylaxis enhancement.
Daily bicarbonate irrigation, generous hydration, urease-acidifying agents; severe mucus → N-acetylcysteine bladder irrigation.
1,000 µg IM monthly indefinitely; oral 1,000–2,000 µg daily can suffice in some. Annual B12 screen recommended.
2% lidocaine jelly 10 min preinstrumentation; high-volume (10 mL) into urethra; basis of comfortable cystoscopy.
Conjugated estrogen 0.625 mg/g cream nightly × 4–6 wk shrinks caruncle and treats associated GSM; surgery only if symptomatic post-medical.
0.05% ointment nightly × 4–6 wk then taper; ongoing maintenance; reduces SCC risk in adherent cohort (4.7% vs 0%). First-line.

column1: Topical estrogen for GSM — AUA 2025 first-line?
column2: Low-dose vaginal estrogen first-choice; cream, tablet, ring; minimal systemic absorption; safety even in breast-cancer survivors with shared decision-making.
6.5 mg vaginal insert nightly; locally converted to estrogen/androgen; minimal systemic; option in breast cancer survivors.
SERM (oral 60 mg daily) for moderate-severe dyspareunia of GSM; estrogen agonist on vagina, neutral elsewhere; hot flashes possible.
20 U in 60 mL saline injected into myometrium reduces blood loss; rare reports of bradycardia/cardiac event; brief reduced bleeding window.
100–500 mg in 1 L saline for refractory hematuria; reduces clot burden; not for upper-tract bleeding (clot obstruction risk).
Surgicel: oxidized cellulose (mechanical/oxidative). FloSeal: gelatin+thrombin matrix. Tisseel: fibrin sealant. Each for different bleeding patterns.
Granules may persist as stones if intraluminal; flush thoroughly; do not use directly in urinary lumen.
50–100 mL in saline for cystotomy or VVF leak testing; alternative to fluorescein/indigo carmine (discontinued).
Fluorescence imaging — 2.5–5 mg IV bolus shows perfusion, lymphatic mapping, sentinel nodes; widely adopted in robotic urology.

column1: Bowel prep before urinary diversion — current evidence?
column2: Mechanical bowel prep generally OMITTED (no benefit, increased dehydration/AKI); oral antibiotics (neomycin + metronidazole) selectively used.
12 mg PO 30 min preop + 12 mg PO BID × max 7 days or discharge; accelerates GI recovery; restricted to inpatient REMS.
0.15 mg/kg SC every other day; peripheral mu-opioid antagonist; reverses opioid constipation without compromising analgesia.
Dexamethasone 4–8 mg IV — PONV prophylaxis + adjunct analgesia + reduced inflammation; safe in non-diabetic patients.
1 mg protamine neutralizes 100 U heparin in last hour; over-rapid administration causes hypotension/anaphylactoid; max 50 mg.
INR 2–4: 25 U/kg; INR 4–6: 35 U/kg; INR >6: 50 U/kg; max 5,000 U. Faster INR correction than FFP.
Reverses apixaban/rivaroxaban; FDA-approved 2018; very expensive; off-label edoxaban; risk of post-reversal thrombosis.
Sugammadex selectively encapsulates rocuronium/vecuronium; faster, complete reversal; neostigmine + glycopyrrolate for non-aminosteroid agents.
Subanesthetic 0.1–0.5 mg/kg bolus or infusion reduces opioid use; useful in chronic-pain patients; psychomimetic side effects at higher doses.
1–2 mg/kg/hr IV reduces postop opioid requirement and ileus; LAST monitoring; off-label in many institutions.
Selective alpha-2 agonist for sedation/analgesia adjunct; lowers opioid need, may reduce delirium; bradycardia/hypotension risks.
Ileal Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchanger reabsorbs urinary chloride for bicarb → hyperchloremic acidosis; mitigated by short segment + bicarb supplementation.

column1: Why ileum over jejunum for urinary diversion?
column2: Jejunum causes severe hyponatremic-hyperkalemic acidosis (loss of Na/Cl, absorb K/H); ileum and colon far safer profiles.

column1: Antimuscarinic effect on cognition — Beers criteria?
column2: Strongly anticholinergic agents (oxybutynin IR) on Beers list as potentially inappropriate in elderly — prefer trospium, darifenacin, beta-3.
Hydroxyurea induces fetal hemoglobin, reduces recurrent ischemic priapism; transfusion exchange in acute setting; warn re: PDE5i conversion.

column1: Bicalutamide use in urology beyond cancer?
column2: Off-label for gender-affirming feminization (androgen blockade); also part of CAB in advanced prostate cancer (out of pure-recon scope, but anti-androgen properties referenced).
Oral (first-pass), transdermal patch (lower VTE), IM ester. Transdermal preferred >40 yo or VTE-prone.
100–200 mg daily; androgen receptor blockade + aldosterone; hyperkalemia, hypotension, breast tenderness; check K+.
Leuprolide/triptorelin suppress endogenous gonadotropins; reversible; used in adolescents (puberty blockade) and adults with refractory androgens.
650 mg–1,300 mg PO TID titrated to bicarb 22–26; or potassium citrate alternative. Adjust to BMP weekly initially.

column1: Loop diuretic considerations in CKD urology patient?
column2: Furosemide 20–40 mg IV/PO; titrate to UOP and weight; ototoxicity at high IV doses; combination with thiazide overcomes diuretic resistance.
Hydrochlorothiazide 25–50 mg daily reduces urinary calcium ~50%; effective for hypercalciuric stone formers; monitor potassium and uric acid.
10–20 mEq PO TID; alkalinizes urine to pH 6–7; reduces calcium oxalate and uric acid stones; GI intolerance limits dose.
100–300 mg daily; inhibits xanthine oxidase; complementary to urinary alkalinization; rash/SJS risk especially in HLA-B*5801.
Thiol drugs cleave cystine disulfide bond increasing solubility; tiopronin preferred (lower toxicity); used when alkalinization + fluid fail.

column1: Indigo carmine alternative for ureteral patency?
column2: Discontinued from market; methylene blue or fluorescein IV are alternatives; ICG also used for ureteral mapping.
Symptomatic urinary analgesic for dysuria; 100–200 mg TID × 2 days; orange urine/stool; G6PD hemolysis risk; methemoglobinemia in overdose.
Partial agonist with ceiling effect; can blunt analgesic response from full agonists; many ERAS protocols continue buprenorphine perioperatively to avoid withdrawal.
QT prolongation, variable half-life; continue maintenance dose, supplement with short-acting opioids; coordinate with addiction medicine.
0.04–0.4 mg IV titrated for respiratory depression; preserve some analgesia; expect short half-life — observation/re-dosing.
Non-selective alpha-blocker (irreversible); used historically for BOO in neurogenic bladder; mostly replaced by uroselective alpha-1A agents.
TCA with anti-muscarinic + central effects; reduces nocturnal enuresis short-term; cardiotoxicity in overdose limits modern use.
Older non-selective antimuscarinic; useful as sublingual rescue; same CNS/dry mouth profile concerns.
Quaternary amine antimuscarinic with limited CNS penetration; mostly displaced by trospium; cheap legacy option.
Smooth muscle relaxant marketed for OAB; minimal/no efficacy in modern trials; obsolete recommendation.
Postop urinary retention; no UDS-proven detrusor stimulation; class largely abandoned. AUA guidelines do not endorse.
Vanilloid TRPV1 agonists desensitizing C-fibers; experimental neurogenic detrusor overactivity treatment; not FDA-approved.
Reverses HA fillers (penile/labial); 150–300 U injected; recognize early to dissolve before granuloma; allergy testing if available.
Used post-cystoscopic stricture incision or pyeloplasty as anti-fibrotic adjunct; alkylating agent reducing fibroblast proliferation; off-label in benign disease.
40 mg in 5 mL saline injected submucosally around lesion at cystoscopy; durable symptom relief over fulguration alone in some series.
Bevacizumab intravesical or systemic for refractory hemorrhagic radiation cystitis; limited evidence; reserved for select cases.
40 mg in 50 mL weekly × 4 then monthly; GAG-layer restoration; common European IC/BPS regimen.
NK1 antagonist for PONV in high-risk; long duration (~40 hr); add to ondansetron + dexamethasone in Apfel ≥3.
1.5 mg transdermal q72hr; for high-PONV-risk; anticholinergic side effects (cognitive in elderly).
UFH 5,000 U TID — cheap, reversible, renal-safe. LMWH (enoxaparin 40 mg daily) — better bioavailability, less HIT, contraindicated CrCl <30 unprotected.
Thrombocytopenia magnitude, Timing 5–10 d, Thrombosis, no oTher cause; ≥4 = intermediate, ≥6 high. Confirm with PF4/serotonin release.
Stop ALL heparin, switch to argatroban or bivalirudin; do NOT use LMWH or warfarin alone initially (warfarin only after platelet recovery).
Continue for secondary cardiac prevention through most urologic surgery if bleeding-acceptable; benefit/risk balance per case.
Cefazolin has minimal cross-reactivity with PCN allergy (<1%); for true severe allergy: clindamycin + aztreonam or vancomycin + gentamicin.
15–20 mg/kg actual weight; infuse 1–2 hr before incision; redose >6 hr; troughs not required for prophylaxis.

column1: Pip-tazo dose for sepsis from urinary source?
column2: 4.5 g IV q6–8h; covers most gram-negatives and pseudomonas; renal-adjusted; common empiric pyelonephritis with risk factors.
Ertapenem: once daily, no pseudomonas coverage. Meropenem: q8h, broader (pseudomonas, anaerobes). Carbapenem reserved for ESBL.
3 g single oral dose for uncomplicated cystitis; rising resistance; useful in MDR cystitis and pregnancy.
Tedizolid once daily oral, less hematologic toxicity short-term; linezolid q12h, longer track record. Both for MRSA SSTI and VRE.
Use the narrowest effective regimen, document indication and duration, avoid prolonged prophylaxis post-procedure, treat colonization only in pregnancy or pre-procedure.
Use adjusted body weight (IBW + 0.4 × [TBW − IBW]); avoid actual weight to prevent toxicity. Renal monitoring essential.
Not direct, but planning around microsurgery; common postop ED protocols include trial of PDE5i; not first-line during reversal.

column1: Aromatase inhibitor for high estradiol in male?
column2: Anastrozole 0.5–1 mg 2× weekly when E2 >50 pg/mL with symptoms despite TRT; monitor bone density on chronic use.
SERM derivative of clomiphene; stimulates LH/FSH; preserves spermatogenesis in hypogonadism; superior tolerability vs clomiphene (no estrogenic isomer).
Topical gels can transfer to partners/children — wash hands, cover application site, shower before contact. Pellets/injections avoid this.
200 mg doxycycline within 72 hr of condomless sex reduces STI risk in MSM/trans women; CDC 2024 guideline; not for general population.

column1: Pelvic floor PT and pharmacotherapy synergy?
column2: Combined PFPT + topical analgesics in vulvodynia/PFD outperforms either alone; pillar of multimodal pelvic pain.
Alpha-blocker tried for outlet relaxation in early IC; superseded by mechanism-targeted therapy; legacy reference only.
Caustic agents used historically for intractable bladder bleeding; supplanted by alum, formalin, embolization, HBOT.
1% solution continuous irrigation; aluminum encephalopathy rare; reserve for refractory bleeding. Less toxic than formalin.
1–10% concentration under anesthesia (severe end-stage hemorrhagic cystitis); protect upper tracts (ureteric catheters), avoid extravasation; high morbidity.

column1: PRP injection in genitourinary use — evidence summary?
column2: Modest evidence for SUI, ED, vulvodynia; lichen-sclerosus histologic improvement; investigational without FDA-cleared device for GU indication.
PRP: centrifuged platelets + plasma. PRF: solid fibrin matrix with platelets/leukocytes — sustained growth factor release; PRP+PRF combinations studied.

column1: Estradiol vs estriol topical for GSM?
column2: Estriol (E3): weaker, less systemic; popular EU. Estradiol (E2): higher potency; minimal systemic at low dose. Both effective.
Local conversion; no endometrial hyperplasia signal in trials; appropriate for postmenopausal dyspareunia.
Selective androgen receptor modulators — experimental for hypogonadism with minimal prostatic effect; not FDA-approved; supplement market caution.
Watch additive HTN (mirabegron) + dry mouth/anticholinergic burden; BESIDE showed acceptable safety in elderly with monitoring.

column1: Daily PDE5i for post-RP penile rehab?
column2: Tadalafil 5 mg or sildenafil 50 mg nightly; aim to maintain corporal oxygenation; some RCT evidence; AUA endorses penile rehab broadly.
Patient knows to seek care at 4 hr; prescribe phenylephrine kit selectively; recognize signs of impending priapism (rigid >4 hr, painful).
Preop dose 600 U/kg weekly × 3 + iron, in selected patients refusing transfusion or undergoing high-loss procedures; thrombosis risk.

column1: IV iron — ferric carboxymaltose vs iron sucrose?
column2: FCM: 750–1,000 mg/dose, one-two doses. Sucrose: 200 mg per dose, 5 doses. FCM preferred for rapid preop repletion.
