Standard contraindication: malignancy (theoretical seeding); modern leukoreduction filters mitigate; case-by-case in oncologic resections.
Continue aspirin if cardiac indication; hold DOAC per agent (apixaban 48 hr, rivaroxaban 24–48 hr) — manage individually.

column1: Anticoagulation in mechanical heart valve — bridging?
column2: Mandatory LMWH bridge for warfarin hold around major surgery; restart per bleeding risk; antidote (vit K + 4F-PCC) emergent.
1 g PO TID for 5 days at menses onset; useful in heavy menstrual bleeding, including post-myomectomy.
Sulfate 1–4 g bolus for refractory arrhythmia, perioperative analgesia adjunct, eclampsia prophylaxis; monitor reflexes/respiratory rate.

column1: Glycine vs saline irrigation — TURP risk?
column2: Glycine (monopolar TURP) — TURP syndrome risk; saline used in bipolar TURP/HoLEP — eliminates TURP syndrome.

column1: Why avoid bowel-prep + ERAS together routinely?
column2: Mechanical prep causes dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, AKI; modern ERAS for urinary diversion typically omits MBP except colon-based cases.
100–200 µg SC TID; somatostatin analog reduces lymphatic flow; adjunct to dietary medium-chain TG and drain management.
Smooth muscle relaxation transiently used in stone passage / instrumentation; modest evidence; nausea common.
Medical expulsive therapy for distal ureteral stones 5–10 mm; ~25% absolute increase in passage; SUSPEND trial muted but meta-analyses positive for larger stones.
Spasmolytic used in Europe for renal/ureteral colic; limited US use; oral or IV.
No reliable contractility benefit; cease use; manage with intermittent catheterization, sacral neuromodulation for non-obstructive retention.
Excess parasympathetic from anticholinesterase or muscarinic agonist overdose; SLUDGE syndrome; reverse with atropine.
Up to 30 mL of 2% (600 mg lidocaine) topically/intraurethrally — well below toxic mucosal absorption; absorption increases with damaged mucosa.

column1: DOAC reversal — when to use 4F-PCC empirically?
column2: Life-threatening bleeding on apixaban/rivaroxaban without immediate andexanet — 50 U/kg 4F-PCC; off-label but supported by guidelines.
2.5 mg BID per FDA label; limited renal-failure data; many institutions prefer warfarin in dialysis though apixaban gaining acceptance.
1 g IV q6h reduces opioid use; expensive vs oral with equivalent bioavailability if PO tolerated. Hepatic dose cap 4 g/d (3 g elderly).
15–30 mg IV q6h; ≤5 days total to limit GI/renal; avoid in CKD, peptic ulcer, fresh anastomosis if concern.
1–2 mg/kg IV for refractory vasoplegic shock; inhibits guanylate cyclase; G6PD caution.
Curved-jaw needle holder allowing deep pelvic suture placement at angle; designed for vaginal hysterectomy pedicle ties.
Spring-loaded fine-tip microsurgical driver; for 8-0 to 10-0 sutures in micro-vascular and vasovasostomy.
Needle holder with integrated scissor blades — speeds skin closure but risks accidental suture cut; popular in office procedures.
Specialized long curved needle driver for deep pelvic urethral anastomosis (urethroplasty); slender shaft for confined spaces.
Self-retaining elastic-stay-hook retractor for perineal/vaginal exposure; replaces hand-held retractors; surgeon flexibility for stay placement.
Modular ring fixed to operating table with adjustable retractor blades; perineal Bookwalter provides hands-free deep pelvic exposure.
Right-angle smooth-blade vaginal retractor for pedicle exposure; complements Heaney clamp and needle holder in vaginal hysterectomy.
Long thin lateral vaginal retractor for sacrospinous suspension and deep vault dissection.
Self-retaining posterior vaginal retraction by mass; standard for office and OR vaginal procedures; lifts perineum.
Self-retaining angled-blade retractor for shallow perineal/scrotal/inguinal access.
Fine 1×2 toothed forceps for skin; gentle grip with minimal trauma; standard for plastic-style closure.
Atraumatic vascular forceps with parallel ribbed jaws; used for ureter, vessels, bowel handling without crush.
Russian: star-tip atraumatic, broad grip on fascia/skin edges. Bonney: heavier toothed gripping; both for fascial closure in gyn.
Toothed grasping clamp for skin edges, tough tissue, vagina cuff; crushing — not for bowel or ureter.
Atraumatic curved-jaw broad grasper for tubular structures (bowel, ureter, vas); less crush.
Heavy crushing toothed clamp with 1×2 tip; for tough fascia, secured before division; not for delicate tissue.
Angled narrow-tip suction for fine dissection (microsurgery, ENT, deep pelvis); thumb-occluded for flow control.
Rigid wide-bore tip for high-volume oropharyngeal/abdominal suction; not for fine dissection.
Multi-fenestrated tip for large fluid evacuation (ascites, irrigation); does not occlude on tissue.

column1: Van Buren sound — what is it?
column2: Curved metal urethral sound for diagnostic/therapeutic urethral dilation; sized 8–30 Fr; historical for stricture screening, now largely replaced by cystoscopy.
Urethrotome with adjustable blade for blind urethrotomy; calibrates urethra and incises stricture; legacy device.
Hand-held thin-skin-graft harvester; calibrated 0.005"-0.020"; for small STSG donor.
Both electric/air-powered dermatomes for STSG; differ in head design and calibration; Zimmer common in US OR.
Hand-operated long-blade dermatome for FTSG harvest (e.g., abdominal donor); manual calibration.
Carrier sheet mechanism to perforate STSG (1.5:1 or 3:1) for surface expansion and drainage.
Disposable transvaginal suture-passer for sacrospinous suspension; loads suture, deploys through ligament for apical fixation.
Curved needle carrier for transvaginal McCall culdoplasty and uterosacral suspension; deep pelvic stitch placement.
Long single-prong ligature carrier for needle suspension (Pereyra, Raz, Stamey) — largely historical for SUI; supplanted by midurethral sling.
Aneurysm-needle for passing suture around deep structures (sacrouterine, broad ligament) in vaginal surgery.
Endoscopic suturing aids that automate needle pass through closing jaws; useful in robotic/laparoscopic enclosure.
Third channel for continuous bladder irrigation (CBI) after TURP/clot retention; 22–24 Fr typical for irrigation.
Angled tip for BPH/false-passage navigation; rotate tip anteriorly along urethral curve. Latex or silicone.
Open-tip catheter passable over guidewire; useful for difficult catheterization, post-prostatectomy.
Two finger-breadths above pubic symphysis, midline, bladder distended >300 mL or under US/cystoscopic guidance.
Q4–6 hr maintaining residuals <500 mL; reduces UTI vs indwelling; preferred for chronic retention/neurogenic bladder.
Polyurethane: stiff, longer indwelling. Silicone: softer, less encrustation but harder to deploy. Coated/hydrogel — lubricious.
Self-expanding nickel-titanium stent (Memokath, Resonance) for malignant/recurrent obstruction; indwell months-years.
NT: external drainage only. NU stent: external + internal across UVJ — option for upper tract diversion with downstream patency.
JP: flat fenestrated bulb-suction. Blake: round channel-grooved bulb-suction; less tissue ingrowth, easier removal. Both closed-suction.
Passive open drain; surface-tension drainage; used for fluid collections where active suction unwanted (e.g., bulbar urethroplasty closure).
Type I monofilament macroporous (>75 µm); allows fibroblast and immune cell ingress; favored for hernia/prolapse over heavier multifilament.
Type I: macroporous monofilament. Type II: microporous (sintered PTFE). Type III: macroporous multifilament. Type IV: submicroscopic. Type I = best for hernia.

column1: Why is transvaginal mesh banned for POP (FDA 2019)?
column2: Erosion, dyspareunia, infection, chronic pain led to FDA 2019 ban on transvaginal POP mesh (mid-urethral sling for SUI unaffected).
Acellular biological scaffold; urethroplasty patch graft and incontinence/POP biological alternative; limited durability vs mesh.
Biological grafts for AUS cuff reinforcement, complex rectus fascia replacement, abdominal wall reconstruction; encapsulate/integrate over months.
Non-particulate bulking agent for SUI; transurethral injection at midurethra; durable to 7 yr in series; FDA 2020.
Solid silicone elastomer particles in carrier gel; transurethral periurethral bulking; durable but irreversible.
Calcium hydroxylapatite microspheres in gel carrier; bulking for SUI; radio-opaque on imaging.
Dextranomer/hyaluronic acid copolymer (NASHA/Dx); endoscopic STING/HIT injection at UVJ for primary VUR.
Pyrolytic carbon-coated zirconium beads in gel; bulking agent; persistent radio-opaque artifact on imaging.
Both sacral neuromodulators (S3 lead); Axonics rechargeable miniaturized device (~15 yr battery), MRI conditional; InterStim X non-rechargeable.
da Vinci SP — three articulating instruments + camera through single 25 mm cannula; advantageous in transperineal/transvaginal access; reduced port footprint.

column1: vNOTES — vaginal natural orifice transluminal endoscopic surgery?
column2: Hybrid laparoscopic/vaginal access through vaginal cuff; emerging for hysterectomy and adnexal procedures; scarless.

column1: IPP — three-piece vs two-piece vs malleable?
column2: Three-piece (cylinders + pump + reservoir): best concealment/rigidity. Two-piece: smaller reservoir within pump. Malleable: rod, lowest mechanical complication.
Cuff (around urethra/bladder neck), pump (scrotal/labial), pressure-regulating balloon (retropubic); 6–8 wk activation delay.
3.5 cm transcorporal/female bladder neck up to 11 cm; male bulbar usually 4.0–4.5 cm; tight cuff → erosion.

column1: Penile pearls / foreign body cultural practice?
column2: Subcutaneous beads/pearls implanted for sexual practice; complications: erosion, infection, granuloma; removal counseled.
Polyethylene glycol gel injected between prostate and rectum to spare rectum during prostate radiation; absorbed at 6 mo.
Permanent transurethral implants compress lateral prostatic lobes — minimally invasive BPH option preserving ejaculation; no tissue removal.
Holmium:YAG laser 2,100 nm; absorbed in water; used for prostate enucleation and ureteroscopy stone lithotripsy. Saline irrigation safe.
Holmium: pulsed, dual function (lithotripsy + tissue). Thulium fiber laser (TFL): continuous wave, finer dust, less retropulsion; emerging.
LigaSure: bipolar vessel sealing (≤7 mm). Harmonic: ultrasonic shears (cavitation cuts, coag at 55 °C). Lateral spread differs — choose by anatomy.
As Low As Reasonably Achievable: minimize time, maximize distance, use shielding; lead apron, thyroid shield, eyewear; dosimeter monitoring.

column1: Optical aid — surgical headlight LED vs xenon?
column2: LED: cooler, lighter, longer life. Xenon: brighter spectrum, classic for plastic surgery; LED predominates new units.
30–40° downward declination keeps cervical spine in neutral; reduces neck pain in long microsurgery cases.
Long thin-jaw cutting biopsy for prostate fragments, bladder stone removal, sinus/skull base tissue. Versatile in reconstructive cases.

column1: SHIM/IIEF-5 score range and severity cutoff for severe ED?
column2: 1–25 total; severe ED 1–7, moderate 8–11, mild-moderate 12–16, mild 17–21, no ED 22–25. 6-month recall.

column1: What is the FSFI-19 cutoff for female sexual dysfunction?
column2: Total score ≤ 26.55 (conventional); stricter DSM-5-TR cutoff is ≤ 23.1. Six domains: desire, arousal, lubrication, orgasm, satisfaction, pain.
How often did you feel bothered by low sexual desire? — added to enhance HSDD sensitivity; the most common distress endpoint in HSDD trials (flibanserin, bremelanotide).
Total score ≥ 11 on the 12-item FSDS (0–4 per item, 30-day recall); ICC > 0.74, Cronbach's α > 0.86.

column1: What is the DSDS and its sensitivity for HSDD?
column2: Decreased Sexual Desire Screener — 5-item ISSWSH-endorsed tool for generalized acquired HSDD; sensitivity 83.6–96.0%, specificity 87.8%; ~2 minutes.

column1: FDA-endorsed coprimary endpoints for HSDD trials?
column2: FSFI-desire domain + FSDS-R Item 13. Used in pivotal flibanserin and bremelanotide trials.

column1: Unique scales in PROMIS SexFS v2.0 not in other female sexual function instruments?
column2: Dedicated scales for vaginal discomfort, clitoral discomfort, and labial discomfort — ~1 in 5 US women endorse vulvar discomfort with sexual activity.

column1: PISQ-IR — what makes it unique for pelvic-floor cohorts?
column2: Uniquely captures sexually inactive women (12 items inactive, 21 items active) — important because FSFI excludes inactive patients; useful in POP/SUI/OAB outcome research.

column1: POP-Q reference plane and sign convention?
column2: The hymen = 0 cm. Negative values are proximal/above (normal support); positive values are distal/below (prolapsed).

column1: What are POP-Q points Aa and Ba?
column2: Aa: anterior vaginal wall 3 cm proximal to urethral meatus (fixed −3 to +3 cm). Ba: most dependent point of the anterior wall between hymen and Aa (range −3 to +TVL).

column1: POP-Q point D — purpose and when omitted?
column2: D = posterior fornix at uterosacral attachment; omitted post-hysterectomy. Compare C vs D: a large C−D difference signals cervical elongation rather than true uterine descent.
Most distal point >+1 cm below the hymen but less than (TVL − 2) cm. Stage IV is ≥ (TVL − 2) cm = essentially complete eversion.

column1: POP-Q gh and pb normal values?
column2: Genital hiatus 2–4 cm; perineal body 2–4 cm. gh > 4 cm suggests levator deficiency / avulsion; pb < 2 cm suggests obstetric perineal damage.

column1: Which POP-Q measurements are NOT used in staging?
column2: gh, pb, and TVL are descriptors only. Staging is determined by the most distal single point among Aa, Ba, C, D, Ap, Bp.

column1: Why use sustained Valsalva, not cough, for POP-Q?
column2: Cough produces a brief pressure spike that may not represent maximum descent. Sustained Valsalva (≥3 seconds) reproduces maximum prolapse extent.
Lithotomy underestimates prolapse; at least 50% of symptomatic women stage higher on standing. Always reassess standing if lithotomy disagrees with symptoms.

column1: PERFECT scheme components for pelvic floor assessment?
column2: Power (Modified Oxford 0–5), Endurance (sec), Repetitions, Fast contractions, Every contraction quality, Co-contraction absence, Timing (pre-cough reflex). Laycock 1994.

column1: Q-tip test deflection threshold for urethral hypermobility?
column2: ≥30° deflection (straining − resting angle) = urethral hypermobility. <30° in an incontinent woman suggests ISD as primary mechanism.

column1: Urodynamic criteria for intrinsic sphincter deficiency?
column2: MUCP < 20 cm H2O OR VLPP/ALPP < 60 cm H2O. ISD predicts inferior response to retropubic sling; favors bulking agent or autologous pubovaginal sling.

column1: 1-hour vs 24-hour vs 7-day pad test — best use?
column2: 1-hour: ICS-standardized initial diagnosis (less reproducible). 24-hour: treatment-outcome gold standard. 7-day: captures peak leakage; correlates with ICIQ-SF.
>15 g pad-weight gain defines abnormal pad test.

column1: MSIGS — how is it performed and clinical utility?
column2: Male Stress Incontinence Grading Scale via standing cough test, grades 0–4. Adds prognostic value to pads-per-day for male transobturator sling selection (Shakir nomogram).

column1: Validated bladder-diary duration per AUA/SUFU OAB guideline?
column2: 3-day ICIQ bladder diary is validated standard; records time/volume of voids, fluid intake, incontinence episodes, pad use. Part of standard OAB workup.
Length, Segment (anatomic location), Etiology — predicts operative complexity, recurrence, and complication risk.
Palpate bilaterally along posterior pubic rami at the pubovisceral insertion (10 o'clock and 2 o'clock). Defect = soft tissue rather than firm muscle. ~80–90% sensitivity vs MRI.

column1: Bulbocavernosus reflex absent — is it always pathologic?
column2: No — absent in up to 30% of neurologically normal women. Absence alone without other findings is not diagnostic of neuropathy.
Dorsal clitoral/penile nerve → pudendal nerve → S2–S4 → bulbocavernosus + EUS contraction. Tests sacral reflex arc integrity.
Cauda equina emergency until proven otherwise — urgent MRI spine. Sacral root S3–S5 territory.

column1: Cough Stress Test — supine negative, next step?
column2: Repeat standing with one foot elevated; standing increases sensitivity ~30%. Never conclude negative CST without standing assessment.

column1: Delayed leakage 2–10 s after cough on CST — interpretation?
column2: Cough-induced detrusor overactivity (not stress incontinence). Manage differently — anti-incontinence surgery is inappropriate.

column1: Occult SUI prevalence in advanced prolapse?
column2: 40–80% of women with advanced anterior or apical prolapse. Demonstrated by reducing the prolapse during CST. Counsel re: concurrent anti-incontinence procedure.
Dysuria, dyspareunia, post-void dribbling ("3 Ds"). Positive milking sign = expression of fluid from meatus on anterior-to-posterior urethral compression.
MRI pelvis with urethral protocol (T2 sagittal and axial, small FOV). VCUG may show contrast if the neck is patent.
Inability to pass 14 Fr catheter through the urethral meatus — pathognomonic for female urethral stricture.

column1: Male meatal caliber thresholds — when is stenosis confirmed?
column2: <14 Fr = meatal stenosis (meatotomy/meatoplasty likely). <10 Fr = severe stenosis, high likelihood of proximal extension. ≥18 Fr = adequate.

column1: Why avoid forceful dilation in male LS / BXO?
column2: Friable scarred tissue splits, bleeds, and promotes further scarring. Definitive management requires excision + buccal mucosal graft, not dilation.

column1: Penile LS / BXO — proximal urethral extension rate?
column2: 20–40% of cases extend into the urethra. Extension beyond navicular fossa requires formal urethroplasty with BMG.

column1: Lifetime SCC risk at site of penile LS?
column2: 4–8% lifetime risk of penile squamous cell carcinoma at the site of LS. All excised tissue must go to histopathology.
Grade I: palpable only with Valsalva. Grade II: palpable at rest, not visible. Grade III: visible "bag of worms" through scrotal skin.
Should prompt evaluation for right-sided retroperitoneal pathology (caval or renal vein compression by mass). 90% of clinical varicoceles are left-sided or bilateral.
12–16 cm (mean ~13.5 cm). SPL <10 cm in Peyronie's indicates significant disease-related shortening.
<30°: conservative (traction, pharmacotherapy). 30–60° without shortening: plication. >60° or shortening/indentation: incision/excision + grafting; IPP if comorbid ED.
Plication procedures contraindicated. Incision and grafting (or penile prosthesis) required.

column1: Peyronie's plaque distribution — most common location?
column2: Dorsal (~70%). Ventral plaques (<5%) must be distinguished from spongiofibrosis of urethral stricture.

column1: Bougie-à-boule vs urethral sound — preferred for calibration?
column2: Bougie-à-boule preferred — spherical tip palpates narrowings more sensitively and causes less mucosal trauma than cylindrical sound.
Never advance against resistance. Forcing through obstruction creates false passages, splits the urethra, and complicates reconstruction.
Pathognomonic for bulbar urethral disruption until proven otherwise. Retrograde urethrogram mandatory before any urethral instrumentation.
≥24 Fr. <18 Fr confirms stricture; <14 Fr likely obliterative; <10 Fr severe / near-obliterative.
Malignant germ cell tumour until proven otherwise. Do not aspirate. Urgent scrotal ultrasound + AFP, β-HCG, LDH + urologic oncology referral.
15–25 mL. Unilateral atrophy <10 mL suggests prior torsion, mumps orchitis, varicocele effect, or post-inguinal surgery.

column1: Normal perineal body length in males?
column2: 3–4 cm (posterior scrotal raphe to anterior anal verge). <2 cm limits posterior perineal urethroplasty approach and bulbar mobilization.

column1: What does RUG image (and not image)?
column2: RUG shows the urethral lumen — the contrast column traces patent channel, not corpus spongiosum or periurethral fibrosis. Spongiofibrosis is invisible on RUG.

column1: By how much does RUG underestimate stricture length?
column2: ~1 cm at each shoulder margin. McAninch 1988: RUG underestimated length in 78% vs intraoperative measurement. Add buffer; correlate with SUG.
Right posterior oblique (RPO) 45°. Inadequate obliquity (<40°) causes penile and bulbar urethra to overlap, obscuring bulbar pathology.
50:50 Omnipaque 240 with saline (~120 mg I/mL). Full-strength obscures mucosal detail. Do not dilute below 120 mg I/mL.

column1: Pulsed fluoroscopy frame rate for urethrography?
column2: 7.5 fps pulsed mode — 50–70% dose reduction vs continuous fluoro with no diagnostic penalty.

column1: Membranous urethral narrowing on RUG — pathologic?
column2: Almost always normal — caused by external sphincter spasm during retrograde injection. Only call a stricture if narrowing persists on VCUG voiding phase with caliber <16 Fr.
Wine-glass (champagne-flute) sign: proximal urethra dilates above the stricture (bowl); stricture forms the narrow stem. Pathognomonic for intrinsic female urethral stricture.
<14 Fr on calibration or VCUG. Normal female caliber 18–24 Fr.
<1 cm: perineal anastomosis. 1–3 cm: perineal + adjunctive (inferior pubectomy, corporal separation). >3 cm: complex transpubic / abdominoperineal.

column1: Combined RUG + VCUG — how performed for PFUI?
column2: SPC bladder filled antegradely with 200–300 mL diluted contrast; simultaneous retrograde 60 mL via meatal Foley; image both columns; measure gap between distal antegrade and proximal retrograde.
Moderate ureteral + pelvicalyceal dilatation; complete obliteration of sharp calyceal angles; moderate ureteral tortuosity. Usually surgical correction.
Gross ureteral and pelvicalyceal dilatation/tortuosity; intrarenal reflux; risk of renal scarring → urgent surgical correction + nephrology co-management.
3 months — urethral anastomoses mature over 6–12 weeks; captures initial healed state and early recurrence.
20 mSv/year averaged over 5 years (revised down from 150 mSv/yr). Eye lens is the rate-limiting organ in high-volume endourology.
20 mSv/yr averaged over 5 yrs; ≤50 mSv in any single year.

column1: ICRP fetal dose limit during declared pregnancy?
column2: 1 mSv during gestation (ICRP); NCRP 0.5 mSv/month after declaration. High-dose PCNL usually reassigned.

column1: 0.5 mm lead apron — scatter attenuation at 70 kVp?
column2: ~95% scatter absorption. Thyroid collar with apron roughly halves effective dose.
Reduces eye exposure by a factor of 19. Only ~50% of endourology centers use protective eyewear.

column1: Under-table lead drape — operator-trunk dose reduction?
column2: Combined table-end + under-table lead shield reduces trunk dose 95%, genital dose 99%, leg dose 97%.

column1: Sitting vs standing in lithotomy — radiation impact?
column2: Sitting increases surgeon median dose by 17%; genital dose up 78% vs standing.

column1: FLASH UK reference DAP for ureteroscopy / stent insertion?
column2: Stent 2.3 Gy·cm² (49 s); URS 2.8 Gy·cm² (57 s). PCNL is the outlier at 24.1 Gy·cm² / 431 s.
Direct visualization of spongiofibrosis — depth, extent, calcification — that is invisible on fluoroscopy. SUG length matches intraop in nearly all cases vs RUG underestimating in 78%.

Echogenic plaque + obliterative full-thickness destruction of corpus spongiosum ± calcification. Requires substitution urethroplasty (BMG augmentation, staged Johanson, or perineal urethrostomy). EPA/simple onlay will fail.
High-frequency linear array 7.5–15 MHz. 12–15 MHz optimal for penile urethra; 7.5–10 MHz for bulbar transperineal approach.
Grade 3: AP diameter 15–20 mm; severely dilated calyces; mild parenchymal thinning. Grade 4: >20 mm; severe cortical loss. Grade 3–4 → MAG3 indicated.
Renal artery PSV >180–200 cm/s suggests >60% stenosis. Renal-to-aortic ratio >3.5 = hemodynamically significant.

column1: PDUS normal PSV and EDV for adequate cavernosal inflow?
column2: PSV >30 cm/s (some series >35); EDV <5 cm/s; RI >0.90 in full erection. Acceleration time <110 ms.
PSV ≥30 cm/s (preserved arterial inflow) with EDV >5 cm/s and/or RI <0.75. Continuous deep dorsal vein flow with peak velocity >3 cm/s adds specificity.
PSV <30 cm/s. PSV <25 cm/s = definite arterial insufficiency; 25–30 cm/s borderline. Cavernosal artery diameter <0.7 mm post-injection less reliable.

column1: Most common cause of false-positive PDUS / DICC for VOD?
column2: Incomplete cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation. Mitigate with redosing protocol and visual sexual stimulation (VSS).

column1: Standard ICI agent for PDUS testing?
column2: Alprostadil 10–20 µg (start 10 µg) — only FDA-approved agent for diagnostic ICI. Trimix if insufficient response. Re-dose at half initial after 10–15 min if needed.

column1: Persistent rigid erection >1 hour post-PDUS — management?
column2: Intracavernosal phenylephrine 100–500 µg diluted, repeated q5–10 min. If refractory → corporal aspiration.
Pressure drop over 30 sec from 150 mmHg should be <45 mmHg. Greater drop indicates veno-occlusive dysfunction.
Normal <3 mL/min. Mild VED 3–15; moderate 15–50; severe >50 mL/min at 90–100 mmHg corporal pressure.
Ischemic: absent / severely diminished cavernosal artery flow; no diastolic flow. Non-ischemic: normal to high cavernosal velocities with turbulent flow + color aliasing at A-V fistula.
Contractions, Compliance, Continence, Capacity, Sensation, Contractility, Coordination, Complete emptying, Clinical obstruction.
All transducers zeroed to atmospheric pressure and positioned at the level of the pubic symphysis (per ICS Good Urodynamic Practices 2016).
Pdet = Pves − Pabd. Pves from bladder catheter; Pabd from rectal/vaginal catheter. Removes abdominal-pressure artifact from intrinsic detrusor activity.
BOOI = Pdet@Qmax − 2(Qmax). ≥40 = obstructed; <20 = unobstructed; 20–40 equivocal.
BCI = Pdet@Qmax + 5(Qmax). <100 = underactive detrusor; 100–150 normal; >150 strong.
Sustained storage Pdet >40 cm H2O in neurogenic bladder = high-risk for upper-tract damage / renal failure (McGuire 1981 in myelodysplastic patients).

column1: Stress UI on UDS — defining tracing finding?
column2: Leakage during filling cystometry with cough/Valsalva → simultaneous rise in Pves and Pabd; Pdet unchanged. Distinguishes from urgency incontinence (DO contraction).
Involuntary EAS contraction coinciding with detrusor contraction during voiding; identified on EMG, anatomically confirmed by videourodynamics. Pathognomonic for suprasacral cord lesion.
Sphincter needle EMG showing complex repetitive discharges and decelerating bursts. Young women with painless retention; responds to sacral neuromodulation.

column1: VALUE trial — preoperative UDS in uncomplicated female SUI?
column2: Nager NEJM 2012: basic office evaluation was non-inferior to UDS for 1-year surgical outcomes. ACOG 2015: UDS not necessary before primary anti-incontinence surgery in uncomplicated SUI.

column1: AUA/SUFU 2024 on UDS in initial OAB evaluation?
column2: Should NOT be routinely performed — no pathognomonic urodynamic findings confirm OAB diagnosis.

column1: When is UDS indicated in NLUTD per AUA/SUFU 2021?
column2: Unknown-risk or high-risk neurogenic LUTD — multichannel UDS with DLPP required. Low-risk NLUTD does not need routine UDS.
≥3%. Klingler 1998: 19% complication rate in men vs 1.8% women; 4.8% post-study retention in men with BOO; 6.2% significant UTI.

column1: AUA Urotrauma Guideline 2020 — imaging in penile fracture?
column2: Diagnosis is clinical; imaging not routinely required. US may be performed for equivocal cases (Grade C). MRI is alternative if US equivocal/unavailable.

column1: MRI plus RUG for PFUI — what does MRI add?
column2: Bladder neck integrity, prostatic stump position, fibrotic bridge characterization (T2/DWI), pubic symphysis injury (STIR), pelvic floor muscle status. MRI tissue gap exceeds fluoroscopy gap by 3–8 mm.

column1: Pubococcygeal line on dynamic MRI — where is it drawn?
column2: From inferior pubic symphysis to last coccygeal joint. All organ descent is measured perpendicular to or vertical drop below this line. Normal: bladder base at/above PCL.
Complete detachment from inferior pubic ramus. Bilateral grade 3 → highest POP recurrence risk; favors mesh augmentation discussion vs native-tissue repair.

column1: Horseshoe sign on MRI — what does it indicate?
column2: Pathognomonic for urethral diverticulum — T2 hyperintense fluid-filled sac wrapping around the urethra on axial imaging; neck typically posterior at mid-urethra.

column1: Solid enhancing component in urethral diverticulum — workup?
column2: Mandates biopsy before surgical planning — carcinoma in UD (most commonly adenocarcinoma, clear-cell or mucinous) until proven otherwise.
Proximal tubular secretion via organic anion transporters (OAT1/OAT3). ~90% albumin-bound limits glomerular filtration. ERPF extraction ~40–50% per pass.

column1: Why MAG3 over DTPA in reconstructive urology?
column2: Tubular secretion is preserved until late-stage renal failure — usable renogram curves when DTPA is flat/uninterpretable due to reduced GFR.

column1: F+20 furosemide dose for diuretic renogram in adult?
column2: 0.5 mg/kg IV (max 40 mg). Pediatric 1 mg/kg max 40 mg. F+20 is the SNMMI/BNMS-preferred protocol.

column1: T½ obstruction thresholds on MAG3 diuretic renogram?
column2: <10 min unobstructed; 10–20 min equivocal; >20 min obstructed pattern (intervention indicated).
3a: rise + partial fall, washes out with diuretic — dilated but unobstructed. 3b: rise + plateau/rise despite diuretic — mechanical obstruction confirmed.
Severely reduced (functionally solitary contralateral). Intervention critical; discuss nephrectomy vs reconstruction. <15% near-nonfunctioning — reconstruction unlikely to recover function.

column1: Why is serum creatinine insensitive for unilateral obstruction?
column2: Contralateral compensatory hypertrophy maintains normal creatinine until affected kidney loses >60% of its function. Use serial MAG3 SRF trending instead.

column1: Routine preoperative labs in healthy ASA 1–2 — recommended?
column2: No — AAFP/ACP/Choosing Wisely. Samsel 2025 (n=634 urogynecology): 74% had labs; meaningful abnormalities were rare and did NOT change management. ACOG PB 214 also does not recommend routine bloodwork.
<8% per ADA 2026 + Endocrine Society. Class 2a per 2024 AHA/ACC: reasonable to test if not obtained within 3 months. >8% elevates SSI risk — defer elective surgery if feasible.
Discontinue 3–4 days before surgery to reduce risk of perioperative euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis.
Total testosterone <300 ng/dL on two separate morning fasting blood draws with consistent clinical symptoms. Single low value insufficient (diurnal variation 30–40%).
Baseline >48% relative contraindication; on-therapy >54% mandates dose reduction / formulation switch / phlebotomy; persistent >54% requires discontinuation. Check baseline, 3–6 mo, annually.

Decreased SHBG: obesity, T2DM, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, exogenous androgens/glucocorticoids → falsely "normal" total T. Increased SHBG: aging, hyperthyroidism, cirrhosis, HIV, estrogen → falsely low total T. Use free T.

column1: PSA in patient on 5-ARI — correction rule?
column2: Traditionally multiply measured PSA by 2 (~50% suppression). Unreliable — only 35% have expected 40–60% decrease; 30% have >60% decrease. More discriminating trigger: any rise ≥0.3 ng/mL from on-therapy nadir.

column1: PSA in trans women on estrogen GAH?
column2: Median PSA falls to ~0.02 ng/mL. Standard 4.0 ng/mL cutoff does NOT apply. Use patient's own baseline; any detectable rise above pre-estrogen baseline (or >0.1 ng/mL without baseline) should prompt evaluation.
≥3 RBCs/HPF on microscopic examination of spun sediment — NOT on dipstick alone. Positive dipstick must be confirmed microscopically.
~16.5% — always warrants urgent urologic evaluation with cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging.

column1: Urine culture threshold in diversion patients?
column2: By 12 months post-cystectomy, virtually 100% have positive UA (LE, hemoglobin, bacteria) and culture. Polymicrobial more common in neobladders (81%) vs conduits (67%). Treat only with systemic symptoms.

column1: Meares-Stamey 4-glass test diagnostic threshold for chronic bacterial prostatitis?
column2: Bacterial colony count in EPS or VB3 exceeds VB2 by ≥10-fold. Modified 2-glass (VB2 vs VB3): sensitivity 44–54%, specificity 100%, accuracy 96–98%. Prostate massage contraindicated in acute bacterial prostatitis.
Any growth (≥10² CFU/mL) may be significant — gold standard with minimal contamination. Counts as low as 200 CFU/mL can be clinically significant.

column1: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in CIC neurogenic bladder — screen / treat?
column2: No — extremely common and should NOT be screened for or treated. Treatment does not improve outcomes and promotes resistance (AUA/SUFU NLUTD guideline).

column1: Two populations where IDSA recommends ASB treatment?
column2: Pregnancy and endoscopic procedures with mucosal trauma. All other populations: do not treat ASB.

column1: 24-hour urine — dominant variables for stone risk?
column2: Calcium, volume, citrate (dominance analysis per AUA). Real-world testing is poor: only 4.8% of stone patients had 24-h urine. Nephrology consult increased OR 6.09.

column1: AUGS recommendation re intraoperative cystoscopy in POP repair?
column2: Universal cystoscopy at all POP reconstructive operations (except posterior-only). Detects unsuspected lower-tract injuries in ~4%. Confirm ureteral efflux bilaterally.
Symptomatic obstruction with inability to pass a 17 Fr cystoscope. Treat with DVIU + low-dose mitomycin C (0.3–0.4 mg/mL); 90% nonradiated, 76% radiated success (Rozanski).

column1: Iatrogenic ureteral stricture risk after ureteroscopy?
column2: 2.9% develop ureteral stricture (Sunaryo population study) — about 2× the rate from stone disease alone (1.5% after SWL). Independent risk factors: access sheath (OR 4.6), perforation (OR 11.8), op time >60 min (OR 5.7).

column1: Endoscopic vs open ureteral stricture management — 60-month patency?
column2: Open revision 69% vs endoscopic 27% (Van Son 27-yr experience). Open remains gold standard; endoscopic offers safer less-invasive alternative.

column1: Antegrade endoscopic management of ureteroenteric stricture — success?
column2: Katims: 83.3% success at median 30 months with laser incision + triamcinolone + balloon dilation to 24 Fr + parallel double-J stents. Antegrade through PCN tract is preferred approach.

column1: Defecatory disorder Rome IV — diagnostic requirement?
column2: At least 2 abnormal anorectal tests (ARM, balloon expulsion, defecography). ACG/ASCRS: interpret modalities together — no single gold standard.

column1: ARM rectoanal gradient — performance for defecatory dysfunction?
column2: Sensitivity 36%, specificity 85% for prolonged balloon expulsion. Resting anal pressure reflects IAS tone (~70% of resting continence); squeeze pressure reflects EAS + puborectalis.

column1: Paradoxical pelvic-floor contraction in asymptomatic women?
column2: Up to 37% of healthy women demonstrate paradoxical contraction during evacuation — clinical correlation is essential before diagnosing dyssynergia.
IAS is the hypoechoic ring; EAS is the hyperechoic ring. IAS tears = hyperechoic defects in hypoechoic muscle; EAS tears = hypoechoic defects in hyperechoic muscle.

column1: Occult OASIS prevalence on EAUS after vaginal delivery?
column2: Up to one-third of primiparous women have occult sphincter defects. With 3D ultrasound, significant defects in ~10%.
~100° at rest, narrows to ~70° during Kegel, widens to ~120° during evacuation in healthy women. Paradoxical narrowing during evacuation is the hallmark of dyssynergia.

column1: Defecography — fluoroscopic vs MRI position effect?
column2: Fluoroscopic is seated (most physiologic — greatest construct validity). MRI is supine — may underestimate rectal intussusception and rectocele.
~4.9 mSv — approximately half of an abdominal/pelvic CT.

column1: Posterior vaginal bulging — proportion that is enterocele rather than rectocele?
column2: Approximately one-third of women with posterior wall bulging have enteroceles or sigmoidoceles rather than rectoceles. Defecography essential to distinguish.

column1: Bladder augmentation surveillance after gastrocystoplasty — frequency?
column2: Annual cystoscopy more strongly recommended (vs other bowel segments) given higher malignancy incidence. Standard ileal: AUA/SUFU recommends annual H&P + BMP + imaging; routine cystoscopy debated.

column1: Post-urethroplasty surveillance — what does small-caliber recurrence on cystoscopy predict?
column2: Cystoscopic recurrence <17 Fr predicts higher rate of secondary intervention (Amend, TURNS n=304). Goonesinghe: 96% of recurrences detected in first year; 7/11 had Qmax >15 mL/s (missed by flow alone).
Costamagna et al.: side-viewing duodenoscope to access ureteroileal anastomosis; 79.2% technical success with satisfactory outcomes in all successfully treated at mean 43 months.

column1: 24-hour collection — primary hyperparathyroidism screen in stone formers?
column2: PHPT prevalent in 3–5% of recurrent stone formers. Obtain serum intact PTH when serum calcium is high or high-normal. Critically: do NOT start thiazides for hypercalciuria in undiagnosed PHPT — can unmask hypercalcemia.
Hexagonal → cystinuria. Coffin-lid → struvite. Envelope-shaped → calcium oxalate. RBC casts → glomerulonephritis; WBC casts → pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis.
Dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts suggest glomerular (upper-tract) source. Isomorphic RBCs suggest lower-urinary-tract origin. Dipstick alone does not define microhematuria.
Ineffective in preventing bacteriuria. Bacteriuria should NOT be treated without systemic symptoms. Hydronephrosis is independently associated with infectious complications (OR 4.2) — investigate.

350–400 mL of dilute water-soluble contrast via Foley by gravity (~40 cm above patient). Bladder full when patient reports discomfort, spontaneous void around catheter, or target volume reached. Post-void NOT necessary for CT.

column1: Why is passive antegrade filling inadequate for cystography?
column2: Insufficient intravesical pressure → high false-negative rates. Active retrograde filling is mandatory. Critical principle — never rely on clamping the Foley during routine trauma CT.

column1: Conventional cystography drainage films — why required?
column2: Up to 10–15% of injuries are only visible on drainage films when the contrast pool no longer obscures the leak. Posterior wall injuries may be missed on AP if lateral view not feasible.

column1: Female sexual dysfunction — DSDS sensitivity vs SIDI-F purpose?
column2: DSDS: 5-item ISSWSH HSDD diagnostic tool, ~2 min, sens 83.6–96.0%/spec 87.8%. SIDI-F: 13-item clinician-administered scale for measuring HSDD severity (not general FSD); preferred for treatment-response monitoring.

Bottom-up: treat escape points and extra-pelvic varicosities first (foam sclerotherapy or ligation). Escalate to ovarian-vein embolization or iliac-vein stenting only for refractory or pelvic-symptom development.

PSV is highest at the crura (52.9 ± 20.2 cm/s) and decreases distally to mid-penis (21.6 ± 10.6; p<0.001). EDV does not vary significantly. Arteriogenic ED better diagnosed at mid-penis; non-arteriogenic at crura. No standardized guideline location.
Expanded Prostate Cancer Index Composite — post-prostate-cancer urinary, sexual, and bowel function. Widely used in prostate-cancer reconstruction research.
ICIQ-Satisfaction — validated satisfaction measure after urological surgery. Useful for postoperative outcome reporting across reconstructive procedures.
Bristol: comprehensive female-specific LUTS instrument. ICIQ-UI-SF: 4 items; frequency, volume, bother, circumstance; heavily validated all-adults short form.

Multiple urethrocutaneous fistula openings in severely scarred perineum, often from untreated periurethral abscess or long-standing severe urethral stricture disease. Indicates need for complex multistage reconstruction.

column1: DICC — sites of venous leak identified on cavernosography?
column2: Deep dorsal vein system (most common); cavernosal (crural) veins; spongiosal system; combined patterns. 46% with abnormal FTM have normal cavernosogram (Mulhall 2004) — limits utility of the radiographic component.
Definitive arterial anatomy assessment. Reserved for young men with post-traumatic ED being considered for penile revascularization surgery. NOT used as screening tool due to invasiveness.
Detects arteriovenous shunting; venous leak localization. 85.2% concordance with PDUS. Requires contrast + ICI; limited availability.

2026 single-center retrospective (n=275): impaired PSV (<30 cm/s) associated with elevated cardiovascular risk profile. Supports PDUS as early sentinel test for occult atherosclerosis in men presenting with ED.
Urethral Stricture Surgery PROM. Validated by BAUS section; combines LUTS, health status (EQ-5D), treatment satisfaction. Baseline + longitudinal tracking before and after urethroplasty.
Pelvic-floor-disorder cohort (POP, SUI, OAB), including sexually inactive women. Uniquely captures sexual inactivity due to PFD. The FSFI excludes inactive patients.
USS-PROM includes EQ-5D as the generic HRQoL component. Disease-specific tracking before and after urethroplasty has largely replaced ad-hoc symptom scoring at high-volume centers.

column1: PCN-tract retrograde + antegrade combined endoscopy for ureteroenteric stricture — advantage?
column2: Through-and-through access enables rapid identification of stenotic segments hidden by mucosal folds; allows larger endoscopes with better irrigation (Delvecchio).

column1: Most important risk factor for prolapse recurrence on POPQ + MRI?
column2: Bilateral grade 3 levator avulsion — favors mesh augmentation discussion vs native-tissue repair. Detectable by digital exam (~80–90% vs MRI) or by dynamic MRI.
Incomplete cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation is THE most common cause. Mitigate with redosing protocol + visual sexual stimulation (VSS).

column1: Foley balloon inflation site during RUG?
column2: Fossa navicularis with 1.5–2 mL water/saline. Insert tip 2–3 cm. Do NOT advance past fossa or use more volume — overdistension is painful and causes meatal/fossa trauma.

column1: Lichen sclerosus and SCC — adherent vs non-adherent topical clobetasol cohorts?
column2: 0% vs 4.7% SCC in adherent vs non-adherent — indefinite ultra-potent topical corticosteroid is the central long-term recommendation across LS surgical-ladder pages.

~50% reduction. Multiply measured PSA by 2 as traditional doubling rule, BUT only 35% have expected 40–60% decrease (Marks VA cohort); 30% have >60% decrease. Better trigger: any rise ≥0.3 ng/mL from on-therapy nadir.

column1: Sarkar VA study — clinical impact of missing 5-ARI PSA correction?
column2: Longer time to diagnostic biopsy, higher Gleason grade at diagnosis, greater probability of nodal/metastatic disease at presentation, higher prostate-cancer-specific mortality. Most common cause of missed prostate-cancer diagnoses in chronic 5-ARI users.

column1: TRAVERSE trial — cardiovascular safety of TRT?
column2: 2023 NEJM n=5,246: non-inferiority for major adverse cardiovascular events. Signals for atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism, and acute kidney injury — discuss in shared decision-making.

Recent ejaculation (within 48 h); prostatic instrumentation (DRE minor; cystoscopy/TURP/biopsy substantial); acute prostatitis or symptomatic UTI (retest in 4–6 wk); acute urinary retention; defer until catheter removed.

column1: 24-hour urine — collection adherence in stone formers?
column2: Real-world: only 4.8% of stone patients underwent 24-h urine; 0.6% had all 3 target measurements (calcium, oxalate, citrate). Nephrology consult OR 6.09 vs urology OR 1.95.

column1: Pre-existing DO on UDS — impact on continence surgery outcomes?
column2: Associated with increased post-operative OAB after continence surgery. Pre-existing voiding dysfunction predicts post-operative voiding difficulty. Findings have not been shown to improve outcomes when used to guide decisions (per EUGA 2024).

column1: Cochrane review on UDS-guided vs clinical decision-making in SUI?
column2: 8 trials, UDS changed clinical decision-making in 17% vs 3% (RR 5.07), but did NOT translate to improved continence outcomes at 1 year (37% vs 36% incontinent; NNT = 100).
Complex repetitive discharges + decelerating bursts. Young women with painless retention. Associated with PCOS. Sacral neuromodulation is the only specific treatment — >70% therapeutic effectiveness.

column1: Best test for "neurogenic" CIC patient with new symptoms?
column2: UA + culture — culture only when signs/symptoms suggest UTI. Do NOT screen ASB in CIC patients. AUA/SUFU NLUTD: culture-directed antibiotics given higher resistance rates.

column1: Pre-prosthetic hypogonadism — impact on IPP satisfaction?
column2: Untreated hypogonadism associated with lower satisfaction; correction before or alongside IPP improves outcomes. Testosterone is part of AUA-recommended initial ED workup.

column1: Endocrine evaluation for male infertility — primary vs secondary failure?
column2: FSH is most sensitive marker of spermatogenic failure. Elevated FSH + reduced sperm = primary testicular failure. Low FSH/LH/T = hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Karyotype + Y-chromosome microdeletion if sperm <5 million/mL.

column1: Pre-existing voiding dysfunction predicts what after continence surgery?
column2: Post-operative voiding difficulty. Identifying it does not improve outcomes when used to guide decisions, per EUGA 2024 position statement on complicated SUI.

column1: Bouger-à-boule calibration size for normal adult meatus?
column2: 18 Fr. Begin at 18 Fr; if expected stenosis begin at 10–12 Fr. Largest bougie that passes without resistance = caliber. 2 Fr increments confirm.

column1: Male urethral stricture caliber severity classification?
column2: Mild >15 Fr; moderate 10–15 Fr; severe <10 Fr; complete obliteration = 0 Fr. RUG severity influences counseling/consent but should not prevent operative planning.

column1: Lichen sclerosus on RUG — contour pattern?
column2: Moth-eaten / spicular — contrast enters crevices; ragged margins. Pattern of LS / BXO requires multistage reconstruction (substitution urethroplasty).
Fluctuant tender mass on exam; on RUG, may present as a fistulous tract — extravasation of contrast through periurethral tissue toward skin or rectum. Modify surgical approach.

column1: Foley balloon size in PFUI MRI protocol?
column2: No urethral catheter for MRI imaging. Suprapubic catheter clamped (allows posterior urethra to fill retrograde). Moderately full bladder (150–200 mL) for bladder-neck landmark.

Uroflowmetry Qmax ≥15 mL/s + PVR <50 mL + symptom score (IPSS/PROM-BUS) + RUG. Normal flow + low PVR + no symptoms does not need routine RUG beyond 3-month study. Rising IPSS with declining Qmax warrants RUG.

Pavlica 2003 (n=32): RUG mean error 1.1 cm (overestimation of lumen narrowing length but underestimation of fibrotic extent); SUG 0.3 cm. SUG also identified periurethral fibrosis and calcification not visible on RUG.
Trojan 2001 (n=41): SUG sensitivity 100%, specificity 96% for stricture detection. RUG sensitivity 84%, specificity 88%. SUG superior in identifying stricture multiplicity and extent.
RUG underestimated stricture length relative to intraoperative measurement in 78% of cases. SUG-measured length matched intraoperative in nearly all cases (mean discrepancy <0.5 cm).

20–30 supervised cases before consistent diagnostic accuracy. High operator dependence — no widely adopted standardized training pathway. Community and general urology settings may lack trained sonographers.
Not accessible with current SUG technique. Membranous and prostatic urethra cannot be visualized. PFUI evaluation requires RUG + VCUG ± MRI; SUG is NOT appropriate in this setting.
Sterile saline (primary) or sterile 2% lidocaine gel. 20–30 mL for distension; inject slowly continuously while scanning. Lidocaine gel provides analgesia but minor artifact.

column1: Adult LS-related obliterative distal disease — RUG vs SUG?
column2: RUG: moth-eaten/spicular distal contrast pattern. SUG: Grade 4 echogenic plaque with calcification (hyperechoic foci + posterior acoustic shadowing). Both suggest panurethral substitution urethroplasty (BMG or staged Johanson).
Normal intrarenal resistive index <0.70. Renal artery PSV >180–200 cm/s suggests >60% stenosis; renal-to-aortic ratio >3.5 = hemodynamically significant.
Detected on 3D / 4D pelvic floor ultrasound. ~80–90% concordance with MRI for experienced operators. Bilateral avulsion + wide hiatus predicts higher prolapse recurrence after native-tissue repair.

column1: Pre-existing voiding dysfunction prediction — clinical implication?
column2: Predicts post-op voiding difficulty. Pre-existing DO increases post-op OAB risk after continence surgery. UDS findings have not been shown to improve outcomes when used to guide decisions.
Clinical history with symptom scores, physical exam, 3-day voiding diary, uroflowmetry + PVR, cystometry with pressure-flow study. ICS Good Urodynamic Practices 2016 sets technical standards.

Physiologic anterograde filling (natural diuresis) and longer observation periods than retrograde-fill lab UDS. Indications: unexplained urinary symptoms with non-diagnostic standard UDS; suspected DO not captured in brief lab study. Limitations: calibration; longer duration; patient cooperation.
Wireless, catheter-free, battery-powered devices monitoring bladder pressure and volume during daily activities. Under active investigation — potentially transforms ambulatory UDS diagnosis.

Defines VUAS / BNC functionally — inability to pass 17 Fr cystoscope. Endoscopic management: DVIU + low-dose mitomycin C (0.3–0.4 mg/mL) at incision sites; balloon dilation; intralesional triamcinolone.

column1: Transurethral incision with transverse mucosal realignment for BNC?
column2: Novel cystoscopic technique using laparoscopic suturing device transurethrally — endoscopic Y-V plasty. 89% success after one procedure; 100% after two.
90% overall success in non-radiated patients; 76% in radiated patients at median 21-month follow-up. Success defined as ability to pass 17 Fr cystoscope postoperatively.

column1: Mostly-women-related sexual dysfunction screening at routine visits — ACOG?
column2: ACOG PB 213 (2019): initiate clinical discussion at routine visits. Brief PROMIS single-item screener at intake; FSFI and FSDS as useful adjuncts. Questionnaires NOT required for diagnosis or treatment.

column1: DSDS preferred for whom in primary care?
column2: 5-item ~2-minute non-specialist HSDD diagnostic tool. ISSWSH-endorsed. Sensitivity 83.6–96.0% / specificity 87.8% for HSDD. Non-expert clinicians considered DSDS adequate to diagnose HSDD in 92.9% of cases.

column1: Bicornual hourglass / hinge effect — Peyronie's surgical contraindication?
column2: Plication procedures contraindicated. Requires incision and grafting or penile prosthesis. Hinge effect: corpora buckle at narrowing during erection rather than deviating; patient describes "hinge" not curve.

Always in stable (quiescent) phase. Requires larger excision margins at grafting (calcified tissue cannot be sutured). Affects graft sizing — area of excised calcification must be measured precisely intraoperatively.

column1: IIEF-5 cutoff predicting good post-Peyronie's surgery outcome?
column2: Severe ED (<17) — counsel that incision-and-grafting procedures may worsen erectile function. Penile prosthesis implantation (with or without manual modeling) is preferred when comorbid ED present.
National Institutes of Health Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index. 0–43 scale measuring CP/CPPS severity. 6-point change is the clinically meaningful improvement threshold.
Bladder Contractility Index: Pdet@Qmax + 5(Qmax). <100 = underactive detrusor; 100–150 normal; >150 strong. Helps distinguish BOO (high Pdet@Qmax) from DUA (low Pdet@Qmax) when both produce low Qmax.

column1: Bull's eye finding on cystoscopy in fistula?
column2: Not standard terminology. Direct visualization of fistula opening in bladder mucosa (often surrounded by erythematous/edematous tissue). Confirms diagnosis and guides surgical planning.

column1: Penile-Doppler ICI test in Peyronie's — AUA recommendation?
column2: In-office ICI test with or without duplex Doppler ultrasound prior to invasive intervention. Provides plaque characterization (location, size, calcification) and vascular assessment.

column1: Up to 55–61% of Peyronie's patients on IIEF have what PDUS finding?
column2: Normal vascular parameters on PDUS — suggesting mechanical / psychological ED rather than vasculogenic. Questionnaire-based assessment often discordant with vascular findings.
<17 Fr recurrences on early surveillance urethroscopy had significantly higher rate of secondary intervention over long-term follow-up. Predictive of need for reintervention.

column1: Baradaran TURNS — quality-of-life and cystoscopic recurrence?
column2: Only 33.8% of small-caliber recurrences and 6.2% of large-caliber recurrences required secondary procedures. QoL not significantly different among groups — cystoscopy alone may be a poor screening test when defined by patient symptoms.
Endoscopic 51.6% success vs 95.7% reconstruction (p<0.001). Endoscopic best for proximal/distal strictures ≤2 cm with mild-to-moderate hydronephrosis. Median recurrence time 51 months.

column1: Pelvic floor MRI defecography — H-line and M-line?
column2: H-line: anteroposterior width of levator hiatus. M-line: descent of levator hiatus below PCL. Assess levator ani integrity. Anorectal angle ~100° at rest, 70° Kegel, 120° evacuation in healthy women.

Pre-contrast (calculi), arterial (~25–30 s; vascular), portal venous (~70 s; parenchymal), delayed/excretory (5–10 min; collecting system + ureteral injury). Standard split-bolus protocols combine to limit radiation.
~7–15 mSv depending on phases and protocol. Use selectively — explicit indication required; standard trauma CT (portal venous alone) misses most ureteral injuries.
Hematuria evaluation (after risk stratification), suspected ureteral injury, evaluation of upper-tract anatomy before reconstructive surgery, complex stone disease.
May augment pharmacologic response in patients with incomplete erection after ICI. Mitigates incomplete cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation — the most common cause of false-positive results.
7–15 MHz rotating endoanal transducer; provides 360° cross-sectional images. 3D EAUS provides volumetric data and improved defect characterization.

column1: Standing pad weight test - dwell time and capture?
column2: 24-hour pad test = treatment-outcome gold standard. 7-day captures peak leakage; strong correlation with 24-hour and moderate correlation with ICIQ-SF.

column1: PRO measures used in pivotal flibanserin trial?
column2: FSFI-desire domain + FSDS-R Item 13. These two are now FDA-endorsed coprimary endpoints for HSDD trials.
Spiculation / moth-eaten contour suggests lichen sclerosus. Smooth tapered: low spongiofibrosis. Irregular indistinct margins: dense spongiofibrosis — substitution likely needed.

column1: Cysto-Conray II vs Cystografin for cystography?
column2: Cysto-Conray II: iothalamate meglumine 17.2%, 200–400 mL adults. Cystografin: diatrizoate meglumine 30%, 25–300 mL. Both can be diluted; both emphasize avoiding excessive pressure.
Detects extent of cavernosal necrosis and fibrosis in delayed presentations (>36–48 h); informs early-implant decision. T2-weighted images detect cavernous body avulsions and separations.

column1: Tanner stage relation to testicular volume?
column2: Children: 4 mL volume at puberty onset. Tanner stage measured with Prader orchidometer (bead comparison). Normal adult volume 15–25 mL.
External penile clamp used in RUG when meatal/fossa stricture prevents Foley insertion. Alternative to Foley balloon technique; allows hands-free operation.

column1: DICC Phase III cavernosal artery occlusion pressure?
column2: Optional. Measures gradient between systemic systolic pressure and cavernosal artery pressure. Assesses arterial inflow adequacy. Mean gradient 42–43 mmHg in multi-institutional study.
Normal ~0.3–0.5 mm flaccid; >0.7 mm post-injection. Less reliable than velocity parameters. Asymmetric flow (significant PSV difference R vs L) suggests unilateral arterial disease.

column1: What is the bladder leak point pressure (LPP) classification — when used in incontinence?
column2: Valsalva LPP <60 cm H2O = ISD (genuine SUI). Detrusor LPP >40 cm H2O = upper-tract risk threshold (McGuire 1981). Different thresholds and clinical applications.

column1: Cardiac risk of TRT — TRAVERSE summary?
column2: Non-inferiority for MACE. Signals for atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism, acute kidney injury. Should be discussed in shared decision-making. n=5,246 hypogonadal men with CV risk.

column1: Routine cystoscopy at posterior-only POP repair?
column2: NOT recommended by AUGS — exception to universal cystoscopy rule. Anterior or apical repairs warrant universal intraoperative cystoscopy with ureteral efflux confirmation.
Limited supply. Alternatives: methylene blue, IV fluorescein, phenazopyridine to aid visualization of ureteral jets. Mannitol and lasix can also enhance diuresis.

column1: Diagnostic uncertainty after initial UDS — next step?
column2: Repeat UDS with optimized conditions (ensure no contractions are missed; consider AUM if standard study is non-diagnostic) or proceed to videourodynamics for anatomic localization.

column1: EAUS in obstetric setting — IUGA recommendation?
column2: EAUS after perineal repair to evaluate residual injury and guide management in subsequent pregnancies, including early referral to specialized units. Up to 1/3 primiparous women have occult OASIS.

column1: MRI vs EAUS for sphincter atrophy?
column2: MRI is superior to EAUS for distinguishing EAS tear from scar and for identifying external-sphincter atrophy. EAUS better visualizes the IAS.

column1: Transperineal ultrasound vs EAUS for OASIS detection?
column2: TPUS correlates well with EAUS (Spearman ρ 0.74–0.77). "Significant defects" on TPUS OR 46 for predicting anal incontinence (vs 38 for EAUS). Suitable for screening; defects should be confirmed with EAUS.
Pressure-perfusion study at the renal pelvis to differentiate obstruction from non-obstructive dilatation. Largely supplanted by MAG3 diuretic renogram. Whitaker test rare in modern practice.

RPO 45° oblique. SPC bladder filled antegradely with 200–300 mL diluted contrast; simultaneous retrograde 60 mL via meatal Foley balloon (1.5 mL). Two contrast columns fill toward obliteration from both ends.
FTM >50 mL/min at 90–100 mmHg corporal pressure. Mild 3–15; moderate 15–50. Resistance = pressure/flow normally >5 (mmHg·min)/mL.

column1: DICC equilibrium intracorporeal pressure (EIP) — normal vs disease?
column2: Normal EIP approaches mean arterial pressure (~80–100 mmHg). Multi-institutional DICC study mean EIP only 29.4 mmHg — reflects high prevalence of vascular disease in evaluated population.

column1: CT cystography vs conventional cystography sensitivity?
column2: Both have equivalent sensitivity (95–100%) and specificity (100%) for detecting bladder injury. CT cystography preferred — can be performed concurrently with trauma CT without patient transport.
Up to 10–15% of bladder injuries only visible on drainage films when contrast pool no longer obscures the leak. Mandatory step in conventional cystography protocol.
Fluoroscopic VCUG remains the gold standard for VUR diagnosis and grading. Radionuclide cystography (RNC) used primarily for follow-up surveillance — less radiation but less anatomic detail.
Contrast-enhanced voiding urosonography uses intravesical ultrasound contrast agents. Increasingly used in pediatric populations as radiation-free alternative to fluoroscopic VCUG.
Capacity (mL) = (age in years + 2) × 30. Bael et al.: relationship is logarithmic with wide 5th-95th-percentile range. Gender has no influence on capacity.

column1: ACS Best Practices retrograde-fill volume — adult?
column2: 350–400 mL. Bladder is full when patient reports discomfort, spontaneous voiding occurs around catheter, or target volume is reached. Standardized adult protocol.

column1: When to defer cystography in suspected pelvic hemorrhage?
column2: If pelvic hemorrhage amenable to angioembolization is suspected concurrently with bladder injury, postpone cystography until after angiographic procedure — extravasated contrast impairs angiographic accuracy.

Cystoscopy + vaginal exam + cystography or CT cystogram. Add double-dye (tampon) test for occult or ureteral involvement. MRI indicated when fistula not visualized endoscopically but symptoms present.
Discouraged for routine UTI diagnosis because of universal chronic colonization. By 12 months, virtually 100% positive for LE, hemoglobin, and bacteria. Treat only with systemic symptoms.
Polymicrobial more common in neobladders (81%) than conduits (67%) by 12 months. Both should not be screened for or treated unless systemic symptoms present.

column1: Posterior bladder wall on AP cystogram — pitfall?
column2: Injuries on posterior wall may be missed on AP views because lateral view rarely feasible in patients with pelvic fractures. Drainage films may reveal occult injuries.

column1: Cystoscopy in primary VUR work-up for surgery?
column2: Routine cystoscopy before reimplantation for primary VUR in children with adequate preoperative imaging yields little additional information (only 0.7% unsuspected anomalies) and adds 16.2% to OR costs. Reserve for suspicious imaging.

Chung et al. described laparoscopic ureteroneocystostomy with psoas hitch using cystoscopic injection of normal saline into submucosal plane — facilitates anti-reflux tunnel creation during minimally invasive reimplantation.
Patients unfit for ureteral reconstruction. 92% at 12 months for stricture bypass. Emerging technique with limited long-term data.
Papaverine 60 mg + phentolamine 1 mg, or alprostadil 20 µg. Two 19-gauge butterfly needles in corpora — one for infusion, one for pressure monitoring. Wait 10–20 min for max smooth muscle relaxation.

column1: Phase II DICC — pressure decay test?
column2: After raising intracorporeal pressure to 150 mmHg with heparinized saline (roller pump), stop and measure pressure decay over 30 sec. Normal: <45 mmHg drop. Greater drop indicates veno-occlusive dysfunction.

Simplified alternative using infusion set (gravity-driven). Diagnostic value comparable to pump cavernosometry with advantages of simplicity, lower cost, fewer complications. Maintenance flow remains most accurate parameter.

column1: Stenosis after URS — Ulvik risk factors?
column2: Independent risk factors: ureteral access sheath use (OR 4.6), ureteral perforation (OR 11.8), operative time >60 min (OR 5.7). Balloon dilation was effective first-line treatment in 75% of cases.

column1: Renal ultrasound — when to upgrade to MAG3?
column2: Grade 3+ hydronephrosis on any imaging; neurogenic bladder with worsening upper tract; post-urinary diversion (annual MAG3 after year 1); post-urethroplasty with new/worsening hydronephrosis; pre-pyeloplasty or reimplantation.

column1: Define stress urinary incontinence (SUI) per ICS.
column2: Involuntary leakage of urine on effort, exertion, sneezing, or coughing — a symptom, sign, and urodynamic observation distinct from urgency.

column1: What VLPP threshold suggests intrinsic sphincter deficiency (ISD)?
column2: VLPP < 60 cm H2O — historically used with MUCP < 20 cm H2O to define ISD in women.

column1: What MUCP threshold defines intrinsic sphincter deficiency in women?
column2: Maximum urethral closure pressure < 20 cm H2O on urethral pressure profilometry.

column1: What is the ICS definition of overactive bladder (OAB)?
column2: Urinary urgency, usually with frequency and nocturia, with or without urgency incontinence, in the absence of UTI or other obvious pathology.
Involuntary leakage associated with both urgency AND with effort, exertion, sneezing, or coughing.

column1: What is the AUA/SUFU first-line therapy for OAB?
column2: Behavioral therapy (bladder training, fluid management, pelvic floor exercises) before pharmacotherapy or third-line therapies.

column1: What is the AUA second-line therapy for OAB?
column2: Antimuscarinics or beta-3 agonists (mirabegron, vibegron); shared decision-making regarding side-effect profile.
PTNS, sacral neuromodulation (Interstim), and intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA injections.

column1: What is the standard onabotulinumtoxinA dose for idiopathic OAB?
column2: 100 U intradetrusor, ~20 injection sites; reserved 200 U dose for neurogenic detrusor overactivity.

column1: Maximum approved onabotulinumtoxinA dose for neurogenic detrusor overactivity?
column2: 200 U intradetrusor; expect higher CIC rates than at 100 U.
The complaint that the individual has to wake at night one or more times to void; each void preceded and followed by sleep.
Ratio of nocturnal urine volume to 24-h urine volume; >0.33 in elderly (>0.20 in younger) defines nocturnal polyuria.

column1: Most common reversible cause of nocturia in older men?
column2: Nocturnal polyuria, not BPH; addressed with fluid restriction, evening diuretic timing, OSA workup, and desmopressin if isolated.

column1: What is the diagnostic test of choice for SUI in women per AUA/SUFU guideline?
column2: History + cough stress test with comfortably full bladder; UDS is not required for index uncomplicated SUI before sling.

column1: When is preoperative urodynamics indicated before SUI surgery?
column2: Mixed symptoms, prior anti-incontinence surgery, neurogenic, elevated PVR, prolapse beyond hymen, suspicion of voiding dysfunction.
1–10 g — mild leakage.
11–50 g — moderate leakage.
>50 g — severe leakage.

column1: ValSalva leak point pressure measurement principle?
column2: Lowest abdominal pressure (via rectal/vesical) at which leakage occurs without detrusor contraction; uses 150–200 mL fill.

column1: What does abdominal leak point pressure > 90 cm H2O suggest?
column2: Hypermobility-predominant SUI rather than intrinsic sphincter deficiency; sling outcomes are generally better.

column1: Cotton-swab Q-tip test definition of urethral hypermobility?
column2: Resting-to-strain angle > 30° from horizontal — indicates urethral hypermobility supporting SUI mechanism.
Incontinence persisting beyond 12 months from RP; spontaneous improvement is unlikely after 1 year.

column1: First-line conservative therapy for post-prostatectomy SUI in the first year?
column2: Pelvic floor muscle training (Kegels) — start preoperatively if possible; majority of recovery within 12 mo.

column1: Threshold pad use that selects AUS vs male sling for PPI?
column2: Mild leakage (1–2 pads/day, <150 g/24 h) → male sling; severe leakage or radiation history → AUS.

column1: Why is AUS preferred over male sling after pelvic radiation?
column2: Radiated tissue has worse sling outcomes; AUS still works with compromised tissue; cuff erosion risk is higher and warrants discussion.

column1: What ICIQ-SF score range is considered severe incontinence?
column2: 16–21 — used to corroborate pad weight and counsel toward AUS vs sling.

column1: Most common cause of de novo SUI after POP repair?
column2: Unmasking of occult SUI after correction of urethral kinking from anterior prolapse.

column1: What percent of women with stage 3–4 POP have occult SUI on prolapse-reduction testing?
column2: Approximately 30–80% depending on reduction method; reduction stress test is the most useful preoperative screen.

column1: Preferred concomitant anti-incontinence strategy at sacrocolpopexy in continent women with occult SUI?
column2: Burch colposuspension (CARE trial) — reduces postoperative SUI from 44% to 24% at 3 months.
Involuntary urine leakage associated with urgency — the sudden compelling desire to pass urine that is difficult to defer.
Involuntary detrusor contractions during the filling phase, spontaneous or provoked.

column1: Threshold PVR concerning for retention before starting antimuscarinics for OAB?
column2: >200–300 mL — work up underlying obstruction or detrusor underactivity before pharmacotherapy.

column1: Antimuscarinic with the lowest CNS penetration (preferred in elderly)?
column2: Trospium — quaternary amine, does not cross BBB; preferred in cognitively vulnerable patients.

column1: Anticholinergic burden cognitive concern relevant to long-term OAB therapy?
column2: Cumulative anticholinergic exposure (oxybutynin especially) associated with increased dementia risk — favor mirabegron/vibegron or trospium in elderly.
Beta-3 adrenergic agonist; relaxes detrusor during storage without antimuscarinic side effects; watch BP.
75 mg PO once daily; no BP monitoring requirement per FDA labeling unlike mirabegron.

column1: Sacral neuromodulation typical response rate in refractory OAB?
column2: ~60–80% achieve ≥50% symptom improvement at 5 years; battery longevity now ~15 yr with rechargeable systems.
30 min sessions weekly × 12 weeks induction, then monthly maintenance; ~60% response.
Failure of at least one antimuscarinic or beta-3 agonist after adequate trial (4–8 weeks); qualifies for third-line therapy.

column1: Most common indication for revision of midurethral sling?
column2: Voiding dysfunction / urinary retention (1–10%) requiring sling loosening or transection.

column1: Timing window for early sling loosening for retention?
column2: Within 7–14 days postoperatively; later than that, mesh has fibrosed and formal urethrolysis is needed.

column1: Most common type of vaginal mesh exposure presentation?
column2: Vaginal discharge, dyspareunia (partner "hispareunia"), or palpable mesh on exam; partner symptoms are highly specific.

column1: What is the FDA position on transvaginal mesh for POP (2019)?
column2: Ordered manufacturers to stop selling transvaginal mesh kits for POP; midurethral slings for SUI remain available.

column1: Workup for de novo urgency after sling?
column2: PVR, UA, cystoscopy to exclude mesh perforation into bladder/urethra; UDS if mixed picture.
Involuntary loss of urine during sleep; in adults, evaluate for nocturnal polyuria, OSA, neurogenic detrusor overactivity.

column1: First-line evaluation tool for new urinary symptoms across phenotypes?
column2: 24–72 h bladder diary — captures functional capacity, voided volumes, fluid intake, nocturnal output, and leakage episodes.

column1: Define functional bladder capacity vs cystometric capacity.
column2: Functional capacity = largest voided volume on diary; cystometric capacity = volume at strong desire on UDS — diary capacity is usually lower and more clinically relevant.

column1: Define urgency on a validated PRO scale.
column2: Patient Perception of Intensity of Urgency Scale (PPIUS) grades 0–4; grade ≥3 = severe urgency or urgency incontinence.

column1: What is the Sandvik severity index?
column2: Combines frequency × amount of leakage from 2 questions; scores 1–2 slight, 3–6 moderate, 8 severe, 9–12 very severe.

column1: PGI-I "much better" threshold for treatment success?
column2: Patient Global Impression of Improvement score 1–2 (very much / much better) on a 7-point scale.

column1: What is the OAB-q SF MID (minimal important difference)?
column2: ~10-point change on the 100-point symptom-bother subscale defines clinically meaningful improvement.
Continuous or intermittent leakage from a chronically over-distended bladder, often with elevated PVR; manage underlying retention before targeting "incontinence".

column1: Continuous incontinence in a previously continent woman after surgery — most concerning diagnosis?
column2: Iatrogenic vesicovaginal or ureterovaginal fistula until proven otherwise — perform dye/tampon test.
Inflammation/skin breakdown from chronic moisture exposure; managed with barrier creams, scheduled toileting, and absorbent products.
Complete involuntary voiding triggered by laughter in otherwise continent children/adolescents; often improves with methylphenidate.

column1: Define coital incontinence and its typical phenotype.
column2: Leakage at penetration usually = SUI; leakage at orgasm usually = detrusor overactivity. Useful history shortcut.

column1: Threshold for "significant" PVR in women with mixed incontinence before surgery?
column2: >150–200 mL — may suggest BOO or DUA and modify surgical plan.

column1: What is the SISTEr trial main finding?
column2: Burch vs autologous fascial sling for SUI: fascial sling had higher continence rates (66% vs 49%) at 2 yr but more voiding dysfunction.

column1: TOMUS trial conclusion (retropubic vs transobturator MUS)?
column2: Equivalent objective success ~80%; transobturator had more groin/thigh pain, retropubic more voiding dysfunction and bladder perforation.

column1: ESTEEM trial — for women with MUI, what does combining sling + behavioral/pelvic floor therapy add?
column2: Greater reduction in UDI-6 scores at 12 mo vs sling alone; supports multimodal management of MUI.

column1: Predominant symptom rule for treating MUI?
column2: Treat the more bothersome component first; address other if persistent — avoid two simultaneous invasive therapies.

column1: First-line evaluation of male SUI with mixed symptoms after RP?
column2: UDS to confirm sphincteric incontinence vs DO; cystoscopy to rule out bladder neck contracture or stricture.

column1: What is the typical pad usage threshold defining "social continence" post-AUS?
column2: 0–1 pad/day; reported in ~80% of AUS recipients at 1 yr.

column1: AUS device-survival expectation at 5 and 10 years?
column2: ~75% at 5 yr, ~50% at 10 yr free of revision; lifetime explantation rate 7–17%.

column1: Most common cause of late AUS failure?
column2: Urethral atrophy under the cuff (loss of coaptation); next: erosion (catheter, instrumentation), mechanical failure.

column1: Why is AUS deactivated at night and reactivated to void?
column2: No — pump is always activated; AUS is deactivated only after surgery for 4–6 weeks to allow cuff site healing, then activated permanently.

column1: Why warn AUS patients against urethral instrumentation?
column2: Risk of cuff erosion is highest with catheterization on an active cuff; if needed, deactivate device first and use 14F or smaller.

column1: Female sling option for ISD without hypermobility?
column2: Pubovaginal autologous fascial sling — preferred over MUS in fixed urethra with ISD; bulking agents are an alternative.

column1: When are urethral bulking agents preferred over slings?
column2: Elderly, frail, anticoagulated, ISD without hypermobility, prior failed sling, or as bridge; lower success (~40–60%) but minimally invasive.

column1: Approved bulking agents currently in US?
column2: Macroplastique (silicone), Bulkamid (polyacrylamide hydrogel), Coaptite (calcium hydroxylapatite).
~70% subjective improvement at 7 yr; the most durable of the modern bulking agents.

column1: Triad suggesting urethral diverticulum in a woman with SUI workup?
column2: Post-void dribbling, dyspareunia, and dysuria — "the 3 D's"; confirmed on MRI.
