column1: Desmopressin contraindication in elderly with nocturnal polyuria?
column2: Hyponatremia risk — check baseline Na+, avoid if Na+ < 135 or in CHF/SIADH; female-specific 25-µg sublingual is FDA-approved.
Women 25 µg SL, men 50 µg SL once nightly — women have higher risk of hyponatremia at higher doses.
Detrusor underactivity or large PVR with preserved sensation — improves emptying without instrumentation.
Time from first urgency sensation to leakage; <2 min indicates poor urethral storage compensation.

column1: Most common cause of "transient" incontinence — DIAPPERS mnemonic?
column2: Delirium, Infection, Atrophy, Pharmaceuticals, Psychologic, Excess output, Restricted mobility, Stool impaction.

column1: First-line treatment of post-menopausal urinary urgency with GSM signs?
column2: Low-dose vaginal estrogen (per 2025 AUA/SUFU/AUGS GSM guideline) — first-choice in eligible women.

column1: Define "occult SUI" detection requirement before POP surgery?
column2: Reduction stress test (manual, pessary, speculum) with comfortably full bladder; positive = leak with prolapse reduction.

column1: OPUS trial conclusion for occult SUI at vaginal prolapse repair?
column2: Concomitant MUS reduced UI at 3 and 12 mo (27% vs 43% at 3 mo); offer MUS to women with positive occult SUI testing.

column1: Define bladder outlet obstruction (BOO) in men per ICS UDS.
column2: Generic term for obstruction during voiding evidenced by increased detrusor pressure and decreased flow; pressure-flow study is the diagnostic standard.
Grades 0–VI based on pdetQmax vs Qmax curve; grade ≥ III = obstructed in men.

column1: What is the Abrams-Griffiths (AG) number and obstruction cutoff?
column2: AG = pdetQmax − 2·Qmax; >40 = obstructed, 20–40 equivocal, <20 unobstructed in men.

column1: Bladder contractility index (BCI) formula and interpretation?
column2: BCI = pdetQmax + 5·Qmax; >150 strong, 100–150 normal, <100 underactive detrusor.
BVE = (voided volume / total bladder capacity) × 100%; <90% suggests incomplete emptying.

column1: IPSS score range and severity bands?
column2: 0–35: 0–7 mild, 8–19 moderate, 20–35 severe; QoL question scored separately 0–6.

column1: Definition of detrusor underactivity (DUA) per ICS?
column2: Contraction of reduced strength and/or duration resulting in prolonged or incomplete bladder emptying within a normal time span.

column1: Difference between detrusor underactivity and acontractile detrusor?
column2: Acontractile = no measurable contraction on UDS; DUA = reduced strength/duration but contraction present.

column1: Female BOO urodynamic criteria — Solomon-Greenwell nomogram?
column2: Uses pdetQmax and Qmax; classifies "no obstruction," "mild," "moderate," "severe" — supersedes Blaivas-Groutz for some.
Free Qmax <12 mL/s with pdet ≥20 cm H2O at any point during voiding; or Qmax <15 with pdet ≥25.

column1: Most common cause of female BOO after anti-incontinence surgery?
column2: Iatrogenic obstruction from a tight midurethral sling or pubovaginal sling.

column1: Differential of primary bladder neck obstruction (PBNO) in young man?
column2: Functional bladder neck non-relaxation on voiding; UDS shows high pdet with elevated bladder neck on VCUG; rule out neurogenic.
Alpha-1 blocker (tamsulosin, alfuzosin) — relaxes bladder neck smooth muscle; second-line is bladder neck incision.
Intermittent and/or fluctuating flow rate due to involuntary contractions of the external urethral sphincter during voiding in neurologically normal individuals.
Severe acquired dysfunctional voiding in children with high PVR, hydroureteronephrosis, recurrent UTIs, encopresis; normal neurologic exam.
Biofeedback-assisted pelvic floor relaxation training (urotherapy); +/- timed voiding, anticholinergics if DO.

column1: Distinguish hypospadias by meatal location categories?
column2: Glanular, coronal, distal penile, midshaft, proximal penile, penoscrotal, scrotal, perineal — with proximal subtypes more often associated with chordee.
Failure of mesenchymal migration with abnormal cloacal-membrane positioning; results in dorsal urethral defect.

column1: What is the Sachse classification of urethral stricture etiology?
column2: Idiopathic, iatrogenic (most common in developed world), inflammatory (LS), traumatic — guides management timing and recurrence risk.

column1: Most common cause of bulbar urethral stricture in adults?
column2: Idiopathic — accounts for ~30%; followed by iatrogenic (catheter trauma, TURP) and traumatic.

column1: Define recurrent bulbar urethral stricture after DVIU.
column2: Most strictures recur within 2 yr; success rate of repeat DVIU drops to <20% after second attempt — proceed to urethroplasty.

column1: Threshold stricture length where urethroplasty is preferred over DVIU?
column2: >2 cm in bulbar urethra or any penile stricture — urethroplasty success ~90% vs DVIU ~40%.

column1: Lichen sclerosus urethral stricture characteristic length and location?
column2: Long pan-urethral strictures involving meatus, fossa navicularis, and penile urethra; not amenable to local flap from involved skin.

column1: Define vesicourethral anastomotic stenosis (VUAS) post-RP rate?
column2: Historically 8–20%; lower with current robotic technique (~1–8%); presents at 3–6 mo post-op with worsening flow.
Endoscopic dilation or incision; consider injectable steroids; refractory cases need open reconstruction.

column1: Most common cause of bladder neck contracture after TURP?
column2: Coagulation injury at the bladder neck; risk increases with small prostate or extensive bladder-neck resection.

column1: Female urethral diverticulum classic symptoms (the "3 Ds")?
column2: Dyspareunia, dysuria, post-void dribbling; suburethral tender mass on exam.

column1: Imaging study of choice for female urethral diverticulum?
column2: MRI pelvis with endoluminal/surface coil — defines size, location, ostium, malignancy concern; replaces VCUG/DPUG.

column1: Most common histology in malignancy arising in a urethral diverticulum?
column2: Adenocarcinoma (especially clear cell); rarely SCC or urothelial carcinoma; mandates MRI on every case.
Urethral diverticulum, Skene gland cyst, urethral caruncle; less commonly leiomyoma or malignancy.
Reddish, friable, distal urethral mucosal prolapse in postmenopausal women; treat with topical estrogen.

column1: Skene gland cyst location and treatment?
column2: Paraurethral cyst from periurethral glands; if symptomatic, marsupialization or excision.
Prepubertal girls (often African American) and postmenopausal women; circumferential mucosal eversion at meatus.

column1: First-line treatment of pediatric urethral prolapse?
column2: Sitz baths + topical estrogen × 2–6 weeks; surgical excision if necrotic, refractory, or recurrent.

column1: Bladder neck stenosis post-radiation — preferred long-term management?
column2: Endoscopic incision with steroid injection; if refractory + radiated tissue → bladder neck reconstruction or urinary diversion.

column1: Most predictive UDS finding for failure of TURP for LUTS in elderly men?
column2: Absence of BOO (Schaefer ≤ II) and detrusor underactivity (BCI <100) — predicts persistent symptoms after outlet surgery.

column1: AUA BPH guideline absolute indications for surgery?
column2: Refractory urinary retention, recurrent UTIs from BPH, recurrent gross hematuria, bladder stones, renal insufficiency, large bladder diverticula.

column1: Prostate volume threshold above which simple prostatectomy/HoLEP preferred over TURP?
column2: >80 mL — TURP TUR-syndrome and bleeding risk rise; HoLEP size-agnostic but TURP becomes inferior.

column1: What is a Qmax <10 mL/s in a male LUTS workup most suggestive of?
column2: Bladder outlet obstruction OR detrusor underactivity — UDS needed if treatment decision hinges on distinction.

column1: What is a Qmax >15 mL/s in a male LUTS workup most suggestive of?
column2: Unobstructed flow — LUTS likely due to OAB or polyuria; outlet procedures unlikely to help.
Involuntary contraction of the striated urethral sphincter during a detrusor contraction; pathognomonic of suprasacral spinal cord lesion.

column1: Why is dysfunctional voiding NOT called DSD?
column2: DSD requires neurologic lesion; dysfunctional voiding occurs in neurologically intact patients via learned guarding.

column1: Anal wink reflex (S2–S4) screens what before incontinence surgery?
column2: Sacral nerve integrity; absent reflex suggests cauda equina or peripheral neuropathy and prompts neuro workup.

column1: What is the "sphincter behavior" pattern in Fowler's syndrome?
column2: Abnormal EMG activity with complex repetitive discharges in the urethral sphincter — young women with retention; SNM is treatment of choice.
Young women (20s–30s), often with PCOS; painless urinary retention with capacity >1 L and impaired sphincter relaxation.

column1: Treatment of choice for Fowler's syndrome?
column2: Sacral neuromodulation — restores voiding in ~70% of refractory cases; CIC otherwise.

column1: Define non-relaxing pelvic floor on exam?
column2: Inability to volitionally relax the puborectalis on Valsalva; supports myofascial component and biofeedback as therapy.

column1: Common phenotype of female BOO in young women without sling?
column2: Dysfunctional voiding from learned guarding; PBNO is rare in women; Fowler's syndrome in retention.

column1: Most common cause of de novo voiding dysfunction post-sling?
column2: Tight sling tension causing functional obstruction; up to 10% of MUS, most resolve with sling release within 2 wk.

column1: PVR concerning threshold in adults without sensation?
column2: >200 mL on repeated measurements warrants UDS or imaging; >300 mL risks upper-tract changes if chronic.
Deflected upward urinary stream in toilet-trained boy after circumcision; treatment is meatotomy if symptomatic.

column1: Lichen sclerosus genital prevalence in adult men?
column2: ~0.07–1%; underdiagnosed; presents with phimosis, meatal stenosis, or pan-urethral stricture.
Phimosis = inability to retract foreskin (chronic); paraphimosis = inability to reduce retracted foreskin (urologic emergency).

column1: Indication for circumcision in adult phimosis?
column2: BXO/LS, recurrent balanitis, voiding obstruction, refractory paraphimosis, malignancy concern; topical steroids first-line for non-LS.

column1: Topical steroid regimen for non-LS phimosis success rate?
column2: Clobetasol or betamethasone 0.05% BID × 4–8 wk: 70–95% resolution; avoid empirically in LS pediatric cases.

column1: What is the typical age and presentation of primary bladder neck obstruction?
column2: Young men (20s–40s) with LUTS, low Qmax, elevated PVR, but no detrusor overactivity — VCUG shows persistent BN closure during voiding.
Hesitancy, weak/intermittent stream, straining, incomplete emptying, terminal dribble, double voiding.
Frequency, urgency, nocturia, urgency incontinence — overlap with OAB.

column1: PSA velocity threshold concerning for cancer in BPH eval?
column2: >0.75 ng/mL/yr; consider biopsy or MRI; not used in isolation.

column1: What is the median lobe finding's impact on BPH therapy choice?
column2: Significant intravesical median lobe excludes UroLift and Rezum (relative), favors HoLEP/TURP/aquablation/simple prostatectomy.

column1: Anesthesia and sphincter implications of bladder neck incision (BNI)?
column2: Single deep incision at 5 or 7 o'clock through prostatic capsule; risk of retrograde ejaculation 30–50%; minimal SUI risk.

column1: Difference between urethral stricture and bladder neck stenosis on exam?
column2: Stricture = scar in penile/bulbar urethra ± LS; BNS = scar at posterior urethra/bladder neck post-RP/TURP/radiation.

column1: Most common organism in chronic prostatitis (CBP, NIH II)?
column2: E. coli (~80%); other Enterobacteriaceae, Enterococcus, P. aeruginosa.

column1: Treatment duration for chronic bacterial prostatitis?
column2: Fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim 4–6 weeks; consider intracellular penetration of prostatic fluid.
Chronic pelvic pain syndrome ≥3 mo without identifiable infection; subdivided into IIIA (inflammatory, leukocytes in EPS) and IIIB (non-inflammatory).
Pain (0–21), urinary symptoms (0–10), QoL (0–12); total 0–43; ≥15 = moderate, ≥30 = severe symptoms.
Urinary, Psychosocial, Organ-specific, Infection, Neurogenic, Tenderness — domain-directed individualized therapy.

column1: Imaging for adult urethral stricture preoperative planning?
column2: Retrograde urethrogram + voiding cystourethrogram to delineate length and location; ultrasound urethrography supplements.

column1: Recurrence rate of bulbar stricture after single DVIU?
column2: ~50% recur within 12 mo, >80% by 2 yr — proceed to urethroplasty after failed first DVIU.

column1: Maximum urethral stricture length amenable to excision and primary anastomosis (EPA) in bulb?
column2: ~2 cm; longer strictures require flap or graft urethroplasty due to chordee/shortening risk.
Maternal exposure to endocrine disruptors, ART/IVF, prematurity, family history; severe forms warrant DSD evaluation.
Ventral meatus, ventral chordee, dorsal hooded prepuce.

column1: Threshold of chordee severity that requires corporeal grafting?
column2: >30° residual curvature after degloving; Nesbit plication for ≤30°, dermal/SIS graft for severe.

column1: Most common BPH medical class with rapid symptom improvement?
column2: Alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin, alfuzosin, silodosin); onset 1–2 wk; mainly affect dynamic component.
Reduces PSA by ~50% at 12 mo — multiply observed PSA by 2 for cancer surveillance.

column1: Prostate volume threshold for 5-ARI clinical benefit?
column2: >30–40 mL; reduces AUR/surgery risk ~50% at 4 yr in CombAT/MTOPS-like data.

column1: Tadalafil approved for which LUTS indication?
column2: Daily 5 mg for ED + BPH-LUTS; modest IPSS improvement without Qmax change; useful in overlap phenotype.

column1: Anticholinergic/beta-3 add-on indication in male LUTS?
column2: Persistent storage symptoms (urgency, frequency) after alpha-blocker if PVR <250 mL; monitor for retention.
Severe coagulopathy, active UTI, prior radiation, prostate cancer requiring intervention; bleeding still requires post-op coagulation.

column1: Most common ejaculatory side effect of TURP/HoLEP?
column2: Retrograde ejaculation ~65–75%; counsel preoperatively, especially in younger men interested in fertility.
UroLift (PUL), Rezum (water vapor), iTind — preserve antegrade ejaculation in ~80–95%.

column1: First-line investigation for new gross hematuria in BPH patient?
column2: CT urogram + cystoscopy (AUA microhematuria framework); BPH bleeding is diagnosis of exclusion.

column1: Most common cause of acute urinary retention in older men?
column2: BPH precipitated by alpha-agonists, anticholinergics, UTI, constipation, fecal impaction, alcohol; trial of void with alpha-blocker after catheter.

column1: Trial of void after AUR — likelihood of success on alpha-blocker?
column2: ~50–60% with tamsulosin started immediately; lower if PVR>1 L or prostate >50 mL.
Painless retention with bladder volume >800 mL, elevated detrusor pressure, hydronephrosis, and renal dysfunction; needs prompt decompression then drainage long-term.
UOP >200 mL/h for ≥2 h after decompression; replace 75% with IV NS, monitor electrolytes Q4–6h.

column1: Pseudo-dyssynergia in non-neurogenic patients explained by?
column2: Voluntary or learned sphincter guarding during voiding; mimics DSD on UDS but EMG resolves with distraction.

column1: What is "deferred voiding" pattern in dysfunctional voiding?
column2: Habitual postponement of micturition leading to functional capacity expansion, increased PVR, and recurrent UTIs in girls.

column1: First imaging for suspected congenital posterior urethral valves (PUV)?
column2: VCUG — shows dilated posterior urethra and bladder trabeculation; cystoscopy confirms.

column1: Valve bladder syndrome sequela of PUV after ablation?
column2: Persistent bladder dysfunction with poor compliance, polyuria, and progressive renal failure even with valves resolved.
Urgency ≥1 episode/wk for ≥3 mo in toilet-trained child age ≥5; manage with urotherapy + anticholinergics if needed.
Severe proximal hypospadias with chordee >30° after degloving — staged Bracka or 2-stage Byars with preputial graft.

column1: First-line workup for "lazy bladder" (DUA) in young woman?
column2: Diary, UDS, neurologic exam; consider Fowler's syndrome and sphincter EMG.

column1: Define complete bladder neck closure indication?
column2: Devastating outlet incompetence with intractable leakage, failed AUS, or pelvic floor catastrophe — diversion through catheterizable channel.

column1: What is the typical natural history of untreated bulbar urethral stricture?
column2: Progressive scarring with worsening flow, UTIs, retention, and eventually upper-tract changes if neglected.

column1: Indication for suprapubic cystostomy over urethral catheter in chronic retention?
column2: Tight stricture, urethral fistula, large prostate with failed urethral catheterization, planned long-term diversion.

column1: Urethral stricture imaging caveat in females?
column2: MRI defines diverticulum; videourodynamics define stenosis; cystoscopy under anesthesia confirms.

column1: Define iatrogenic female urethral stricture etiologies?
column2: Repeated catheterization, urethral dilation, sling/urethrolysis, radiation, prior diverticulectomy.

column1: Threshold of female stricture for surgical reconstruction?
column2: Failure of dilation × 2 or recurrence within 6 mo — proceed to dorsal onlay graft (oral mucosa) urethroplasty.

column1: What is the "Mitrofanoff principle" applied to non-emptying bladder?
column2: Catheterizable continent channel using narrow tube (appendix) implanted into bladder via antireflux tunnel.

column1: Define BOO with concurrent DUA — clinical implication?
column2: Outlet surgery may improve symptoms partially; counsel about persistent emptying difficulty and possible CIC.

column1: Most common symptom-driven indication for re-do urethroplasty?
column2: Recurrence after initial repair at anastomosis or graft edge; 10–20% recurrence at 5 yr.

column1: What POP-Q point quantifies anterior vaginal wall apex?
column2: Ba — most dependent position of any part of upper anterior wall between vaginal cuff/anterior fornix and point Aa.

column1: What does POP-Q point C measure?
column2: Most distal edge of cervix or vaginal cuff scar.

column1: What does POP-Q point D represent?
column2: Posterior fornix (only in women with cervix); reflects level of uterosacral attachment.

column1: Distinction between cystocele and apical descent on exam?
column2: Visualize cervix/cuff with Sims speculum during Valsalva — apical descent contributes to most "cystoceles".
Level I: apical (uterosacral/cardinal); Level II: lateral (arcus tendineus); Level III: distal (perineal body, urethrovaginal fascia).

column1: Level I support defect produces what compartment prolapse?
column2: Apical — uterine prolapse or vaginal vault prolapse.

column1: Level II support defect produces what compartment prolapse?
column2: Anterior or posterior wall prolapse (paravaginal defect anteriorly, perirectal defect posteriorly).

column1: Level III support defect produces what condition?
column2: Distal prolapse, urethral hypermobility, gaping introitus, perineal-body descent.

Bulging of posterior vaginal wall and anterior rectal wall caused by defect in rectovaginal fascia/perineal body.

column1: Defecography finding suggestive of clinically significant rectocele?
column2: Anterior rectal pocket >3 cm with stool trapping requiring splinting to evacuate.

column1: Splinting maneuver clinically points to which compartment?
column2: Posterior compartment defect (rectocele) when patient supports perineum/posterior vagina to defecate.
~10% of women develop vault prolapse requiring surgical correction after hysterectomy.

column1: Why must apex be re-suspended at hysterectomy for prolapse?
column2: Apical support is essential; failure to re-suspend leads to vault prolapse in ~10%; uterosacral or McCall colpopexy reduces this risk.
All symptomatic POP patients should be offered pessary trial before surgery; successful fitting in 50–85%.

column1: Most common pessary type for stage 2–3 anterior prolapse?
column2: Ring pessary with or without support — easy self-care, allows intercourse.
Gellhorn pessary — needs clinician removal; stays best in advanced prolapse.
Vaginal erosion, fistula (vesicovaginal or rectovaginal) — schedule cleaning intervals every 3–6 mo.

column1: Imaging modality of choice for levator avulsion?
column2: 3D/4D transperineal/translabial ultrasound or MRI; "tear-drop" defect in levator attachment.

column1: Genital hiatus measurement threshold associated with prolapse recurrence?
column2: GH ≥ 4 cm at rest associated with higher POP recurrence; consider concomitant perineorrhaphy.
Distance from posterior hymen to mid-anus; normal 3–4 cm; <2 cm associated with perineal-body descent and fecal incontinence.

column1: Indication for concomitant perineorrhaphy at POP repair?
column2: Genital hiatus ≥4 cm, attenuated perineal body <2.5 cm, gaping introitus with sexual dysfunction.

column1: First-line non-surgical therapy for symptomatic POP?
column2: Pelvic floor muscle training (Hagen 2014: ≥6 mo benefit for stage 1–2 POP) + pessary.
Symptomatic bother (drag, splinting, voiding/defecatory dysfunction, sexual concerns); asymptomatic stage 3–4 usually managed expectantly.

column1: Most common cause of recurrence after native-tissue anterior repair?
column2: Inadequate apical support — recurrence ~40% if apex not addressed.
Mesh exposure ~2% laparoscopic/robotic at 5 yr; lower than transvaginal mesh and acceptable for durable apical support.

column1: Uterosacral ligament suspension (USLS) ureteral injury rate?
column2: ~1–11%; intraoperative cystoscopy after dye is mandatory; suture removal usually resolves kink.
Gluteal/buttock pain at pudendal site, usually self-limited by 6 weeks; rare nerve injury or hemorrhage.

column1: Compare SSLF vs USLS in OPTIMAL trial?
column2: 2-yr surgical success ~60% for both, no significant difference; SSLF more buttock pain, USLS more ureteric kinking.

column1: Compare sacrocolpopexy vs USLS for apical prolapse?
column2: Sacrocolpopexy more durable (~80% at 5 yr) vs ~50–60% for native-tissue; higher cost and mesh risk.

column2: Mid-anterior or apical vaginal wall; manage with local excision; complete removal for refractory pain.

column1: Define occult SUI — clinical relevance to POP repair?
column2: Continent women with stage 3–4 prolapse may leak after prolapse reduction; offer concomitant MUS (OPUS, CARE trial findings).

column1: What is the CARE trial result?
column2: Concomitant Burch at sacrocolpopexy reduced SUI at 3 mo (24% vs 44%); favored prophylactic anti-incontinence procedure.

column1: What is the OPUS trial result?
column2: Concomitant MUS at vaginal POP repair reduced postoperative SUI at 12 mo (27% vs 43%); supports shared decision-making.

column1: Most common POP recurrence pattern after sacrocolpopexy?
column2: Distal anterior or posterior wall prolapse below the mesh attachment, often grade 1–2 and asymptomatic.

column1: Define "uterine preservation" surgical options for POP?
column2: Sacrohysteropexy (mesh) or sacrospinous hysteropexy or Manchester repair — for women wishing to retain uterus.
Cervical amputation, McCall culdoplasty, anterior + posterior colporrhaphy — used for cervical elongation.

column1: Define rectal intussusception relevance to prolapse evaluation?
column2: Posterior compartment dysfunction may coexist with rectal intussusception; defecography distinguishes; needs CR consult.

column1: PFDI-20 and PFIQ-7 validated for what?
column2: POP symptom bother and impact on QoL — primary PRO endpoints in surgical trials.
PISQ-IR includes non-sexually active women; PISQ-12 short version for sexually active women with POP/UI.

column1: Difference between "anatomic" and "subjective" success after POP repair?
column2: Anatomic: POP-Q stage 0/1 or hymen-based threshold; subjective: PGI-I much/very much better — patient symptoms matter more.

column1: Define posterior compartment defect site-specific repair?
column2: Identify discrete fascial breaks (transverse/midline) and repair specifically rather than midline plication; outcomes similar.

column1: Most common new symptom after posterior repair?
column2: Dyspareunia (~15%) — counsel about levator plication tightness; minimize aggressive levatorplasty.

column1: Why avoid levatorplasty in sexually active women?
column2: Causes vaginal narrowing and dyspareunia; perineorrhaphy without levatorplasty is preferred.

column1: Indication for evaluation of fecal incontinence in POP evaluation?
column2: Posterior compartment defect with FI symptoms; obtain anorectal manometry, anal US, defecography; refer to CR.

Lateral cystocele with intact midline fascia; can be done open, laparoscopic, or vaginal; durability lower than apical repair.

column1: Difference between central and lateral cystocele on exam?
column2: Central: loss of rugae, smooth bulge midline (midline fascial break); Lateral: rugae preserved, lateral detachment.
MR defecography stages prolapse on PCL/MPL/HMO lines; less standardized than POP-Q clinically.

column1: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause relevance to prolapse?
column2: Hypoestrogenized tissue compounds prolapse symptoms; vaginal estrogen × 6 wk pre-op improves tissue handling and healing.

column1: Define recurrence after POP repair — composite definition (NIH workshop)?
column2: Anatomic recurrence (POP-Q ≥ stage 2 or beyond hymen) + symptoms of bulge + retreatment — all three for "failure" in trials.

column1: Vaginal apex hidden under sling — POP recurrence risk?
column2: Apical compartment unaddressed = recurrence risk ~40%; always evaluate apex with traction during prolapse work-up.

Stage 3–4 preoperative, levator avulsion, GH >4 cm, perineal body <2.5 cm, age <60 at primary repair, obesity, vaginal-delivery parity.
Hesitancy/incomplete emptying related to urethral kinking; resolves with prolapse reduction; rules out functional obstruction post-op.

column1: What is the Baden-Walker halfway system?
column2: Older 4-grade prolapse classification (1: halfway to hymen; 2: at hymen; 3: halfway past; 4: full procidentia); largely replaced by POP-Q.

column1: Apical descent equals total descent rule?
column2: Each cm of apical descent contributes ~1 cm to anterior wall descent — apex correction reduces cystocele.

column1: Concomitant hysterectomy at POP repair — bleeding risk?
column2: Adds bleeding risk and OR time; consider uterine preservation for low-risk patients with normal uterus.

column2: Posterior vaginal wall 3 cm proximal to hymen — range −3 to +3.

column1: Significance of POP-Q point Bp = +3 with C = −5?
column2: Isolated posterior compartment defect at hymen with well-supported apex; native-tissue posterior repair likely sufficient.
Ureteral obstruction with hydronephrosis, recurrent urinary retention, large erosive ulceration of vaginal mucosa.

column1: McGuire detrusor leak point pressure threshold predicting upper-tract damage?
column2: DLPP > 40 cm H2O — strong predictor of upper-tract deterioration in NLUTD; mandates intervention.
Massive sympathetic discharge in SCI patients with lesion at or above T6 triggered by noxious stimulus below the lesion.

column1: Most common trigger of autonomic dysreflexia?
column2: Bladder distension (CIC issue, blocked catheter, urinary stone, UDS testing); next is bowel impaction.
Sudden BP rise >20–40 mmHg above baseline, pounding headache, sweating/flushing above lesion, pallor below, bradycardia.
Sit patient upright, loosen restrictive clothing, identify and remove trigger (drain bladder, check catheter).

column1: Pharmacologic agent for AD with sustained BP elevation?
column2: Nifedipine 10 mg bite-and-swallow or topical nitroglycerin paste; remove if patient has taken sildenafil within 24 h.

column1: SCI level above which detrusor sphincter dyssynergia is common?
column2: Suprasacral SCI (T12 and above) — DSD with reflex DO is typical; below sacral cord → areflexic acontractile detrusor.

column1: SCI pattern of bladder dysfunction during spinal shock?
column2: Areflexic, atonic bladder with retention; spinal shock resolves over 6–12 weeks then reflex pattern develops above sacrum.

column1: Hallmark UDS pattern of suprasacral SCI?
column2: Neurogenic detrusor overactivity, DSD, reduced compliance — high storage pressures.

column1: Hallmark UDS pattern of sacral/infrasacral SCI?
column2: Acontractile detrusor, areflexic bladder, intact or weak sphincter — overflow incontinence with retention.

column1: Surveillance interval for upper tracts in SCI?
column2: Renal US + creatinine annually; full UDS every 1–2 yr if high-risk pattern; lifetime follow-up.
Clean intermittent catheterization (CIC) every 4–6 h to keep volumes <400–500 mL.

column1: Antimuscarinic role in SCI bladder management?
column2: Add to CIC to reduce detrusor overactivity, lower storage pressure (<40 cm H2O), and achieve continence.
200 U intradetrusor every ~6 mo; AUA-approved for refractory neurogenic DO; counsel on CIC need.
Refractory low compliance with persistent storage pressure >40 cm H2O despite anticholinergics + Botox, or recurrent upper-tract deterioration.

column1: MS phenotype of bladder dysfunction (most common pattern)?
column2: Detrusor overactivity with or without DSD (~60%); pure retention <20%; pattern reflects supraspinal vs spinal lesion mix.

column1: EDSS threshold associated with bladder dysfunction in MS?
column2: EDSS ≥ 3 — pyramidal/cerebellar dysfunction starts to correlate with NDO; nearly universal by EDSS ≥ 6.

column1: First-line urologic treatment of MS-related OAB?
column2: Behavioral + antimuscarinic; PTNS / Botox 100–200 U for refractory; SNM controversial due to relapsing course.

column1: Why is SNM less favored in MS?
column2: Disease progression can change bladder pattern; lead displacement, MRI compatibility historically limited (modern leads now MR-conditional).

column1: Parkinson disease bladder dysfunction characteristic pattern?
column2: Detrusor overactivity in ~60–70%; pseudo-DSD due to bradykinetic sphincter; "lifelong" frequency/urgency early in disease course.

column1: Distinguishing PD from MSA on UDS?
column2: MSA more often shows open bladder neck at rest, denervation EMG (Sphincter EMG with positive denervation strongly suggests MSA), and orthostatic dysfunction.
Denervation potentials with positive sharp waves and fibrillation — supportive of MSA over PD.
CIC + anticholinergics from infancy; aim to maintain low storage pressures and prevent upper-tract damage; transition urology critical.

column1: Hostile bladder definition in spina bifida?
column2: DLPP > 40 cm H2O, end-fill pressure > 40 cm H2O, poor compliance — mandates aggressive treatment to preserve kidneys.

column1: Threshold for upper-tract surveillance in spina bifida adolescent?
column2: Renal US + creatinine + UDS at transition (~18 yr); ongoing every 1–2 yr lifelong.

column1: Tethered cord recurrence after release — bladder presentation?
column2: New urinary retention or worsening incontinence with leg pain/scoliosis in adolescent with prior MMC; obtain MRI.
Detrusor overactivity with intact coordination ~60%; urinary retention initial then OAB; functional dependence often more limiting than detrusor.
Urgency incontinence from functional + neurogenic mechanism; avoid sedating anticholinergics.

column1: Cauda equina syndrome — urinary symptom triad?
column2: Painless urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, fecal incontinence/poor anal tone; surgical emergency.

column1: Time-to-decompression goal in cauda equina with retention?
column2: <48 h from onset improves bladder recovery; later compromises long-term function.
Areflexic detrusor with denervated sphincter — overflow incontinence; management with CIC ± AUS.

column1: Bladder management for areflexic detrusor with competent sphincter?
column2: CIC q4–6h is gold standard; suprapubic if hand function limits.

column1: When is indwelling Foley acceptable in NLUTD?
column2: Last resort: when CIC impractical (hand function, caregiver), short-term bridging, or palliative care; risks UTI, stones, squamous metaplasia.

column1: Long-term complication of indwelling catheter in SCI?
column2: Bladder squamous cell carcinoma — risk rises after 10 yr of indwelling catheter; surveillance cystoscopy yearly after 10 yr.

column1: Define neurogenic bowel management goals in SCI?
column2: Predictable, scheduled bowel emptying every 1–2 days; bowel program combines stimulant + bulking + digital stim.
Refractory neurogenic bowel; appendicostomy or cecostomy provides anterograde flush; success ~80%.

column1: SCI patient with new urinary symptoms — first test?
column2: Urinalysis + culture, renal US, post-void residual; AD precautions during UDS.

column1: Define MS clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) with bladder involvement?
column2: First demyelinating event with LUTS may precede MS diagnosis; refer for MRI brain/cord + neurology.
Idiopathic urinary retention (Fowler's), refractory NDO with intact sacral arc; MR-conditional devices now available.
Storage pressure >40 cm H2O, DLPP >40, severe DSD, vesicoureteral reflux, low compliance, decreased renal function.

column1: Common UDS feature in MSA early on?
column2: Open bladder neck at rest on VCUG, neurogenic DO, poor compliance, denervation EMG; orthostatic hypotension.
Optimize bladder storage pressure (CIC + anticholinergic ± Botox); reflux often resolves without ureteral reimplantation.

column1: Bladder neck closure indication in NLUTD?
column2: Severe outlet incompetence with leakage refractory to AUS/sling; combined with continent catheterizable channel.

column1: Define neurogenic LUTS in Parkinson — pseudo-DSD mechanism?
column2: Failure to relax sphincter rapidly due to bradykinesia → mimics DSD on UDS; not true neurogenic DSD.

column1: Why caution with alpha-blockers in PD/MSA?
column2: Orthostatic hypotension already common — exacerbated by alpha-blockers; use cautiously and monitor BP.

column1: Most common cause of acute urinary retention in NLUTD?
column2: UTI, constipation, anticholinergic over-titration, AD, new neurologic event.

column1: Why avoid TURP in young suprasacral SCI man with retention?
column2: Outlet reduction with intact reflex bladder produces wet, AD-prone, upper-tract-threatening incontinence; manage with CIC instead.
Selected men with refractory DSD, intact upper extremities for condom-catheter management, and willing to accept incontinence.

column1: Crede or "Valsalva" voiding caveat in NLUTD?
column2: Risk of pressure-driven VUR and upper-tract injury in patients with poor compliance or DSD; avoid in high-risk bladder.
Compliance <20 mL/cm H2O; associated with NLUTD upper-tract risk.

column1: SCI surveillance — when to add VCUG?
column2: Suspect VUR, recurrent pyelo, or new hydronephrosis; not routine if asymptomatic with normal renal US.
Inability to perform CIC, IBD/short-bowel syndrome, severe renal failure (acidosis risk), poor compliance with follow-up.
Adenocarcinoma at the bowel-bladder anastomosis after 10+ yr; controversial whether surveillance cystoscopy reduces mortality.
Not routine; treat symptomatic UTIs only; prophylaxis only for recurrent symptomatic infection per AUA.
≥3 symptomatic UTIs per year with documented bacteriuria + new urinary symptoms (fever, AD, worsening incontinence).

column1: Diagnosis of UTI in CIC patient?
column2: Symptoms + culture; asymptomatic bacteriuria is the norm and should not be treated.

column1: Bladder calculi risk factor in NLUTD?
column2: Indwelling catheter (highest), augmented bladder, struvite from chronic infection, mucus stasis.

column1: Bladder stone screening interval in chronic indwelling catheter?
column2: Yearly imaging (US or CT KUB) + cystoscopy if symptomatic; threshold to scope is low.

column1: Risk factor for AD during cystoscopy/UDS?
column2: SCI lesion ≥T6 — pretreat with topical lidocaine, nifedipine on standby, blood pressure monitoring.
Reflex, uninhibited, sensory paralytic, motor paralytic, autonomous; historical; largely replaced by ICS storage/voiding framework.
Anatomic level + completeness of SCI; modern UDS-based classification has superseded.
2x2 grid: detrusor (overactive/underactive) × sphincter (overactive/underactive). Useful clinical shorthand for NLUTD phenotype.

column1: Patient counseling priority after new SCI diagnosis?
column2: Long-term renal preservation through low-pressure storage and complete emptying; bowel program parity with bladder program.
Diabetic cystopathy: impaired sensation, increased capacity, weak detrusor; underactive bladder with high PVR.

column1: Spina bifida lipomyelomeningocele vs MMC presentation?
column2: Lipomyelomeningocele often presents later with neurogenic bladder/foot deformity; tethering common, surgery indicated for progression.
UDS baseline + renal US; reevaluate 3 mo post-detethering to document bladder pattern stability or recovery.

column1: Renal failure threshold for proceeding to diversion in NLUTD?
column2: Worsening eGFR despite optimized bladder management; consider ileal conduit or continent diversion to preserve remaining function.
Low-pressure compliant reservoir mandatory before transplant; augmentation or diversion may be required prior to listing.
Progressive lower-motor-neuron damage; mixed pattern with detrusor underactivity, sensation loss; mandate MRI in unexplained NLUTD.

column1: Vitamin B12 deficiency neurogenic bladder pattern?
column2: Subacute combined degeneration with retention, hypoesthesia, +/- DO; check B12, MMA, homocysteine.
HIV myelopathy, opportunistic infections, neuropathy from drugs; UDS individualized.
Cauda equina-like compression; retention with overflow; needs surgical decompression with urology UDS for baseline.
After spinal shock resolves (~3–6 mo); earlier UDS done with caution; document baseline + every 1–2 yr.

column1: Why is sphincterotomy fading from practice?
column2: Irreversible incontinence; alternatives (Botox 200 U, urethral stents, sacral neuromodulation) preferred.

column1: Continent catheterizable channel options in NLUTD?
column2: Mitrofanoff (appendix), Yang-Monti (ileum), Casale (tapered ileum) — anti-reflux tunnel into bladder/reservoir.

column1: Common stoma complication of catheterizable channel?
column2: Stomal stenosis ~10–25% — revision common; need lifelong dilation.

column1: Urodynamic finding mandating intervention in NDO with reflux?
column2: Storage pressure >40 cm H2O OR LPP >40 → optimize medical first; surgery if refractory.
Use higher than label doses (e.g., oxybutynin 30 mg/day) with shared decision-making — adverse effects often limit.
Compounded solution instilled via catheter; bypasses systemic anticholinergic side effects; useful in CIC.
Pubic-bone catheter exchange difficulty, AD with insertion; CIC by patient or caregiver; AUS rarely feasible.
Increased UTI, AD risk in delivery (lesion ≥T6 → epidural); plan urology + OB co-management.

column1: NLUTD-related sexual dysfunction in SCI men?
column2: ED, ejaculatory dysfunction; PDE5i first-line; PVS/EEJ for fertility; AD precautions during EEJ.
Reflex lubrication intact in upper-motor-neuron lesions; orgasm achievable; counsel against assumptions.

column1: Sphincter mechanism preferred in non-ambulatory SCI woman seeking continence?
column2: Bladder neck closure + Mitrofanoff with reservoir augmentation — definitive; sling/AUS often fail in wet leak from NDO.

column1: NLUTD-related vesicoureteral reflux indication for ureteric reimplantation?
column2: Refractory high-grade reflux with febrile UTIs/scarring despite optimized bladder management.

column1: Risk of nephrolithiasis in chronic SCI?
column2: ~7% lifetime kidney stones; immobilization hypercalciuria + UTI struvite; encourage hydration + bladder emptying.

column1: Define recurrent UTI workup in NLUTD?
column2: Imaging for stones/foreign body, cystoscopy for bladder stones, UDS to rule out high-pressure storage, consider bladder management change.

column1: What is "Brindley" sacral anterior root stimulator?
column2: Implant for bladder emptying in complete SCI with intact sacral roots; combined with posterior rhizotomy to reduce DO; rarely used now.
Approved for OAB/urinary retention; MR-conditional leads available; useful in incomplete SCI, MS, PD with intact arc.
~6 mo typical; minimum 12 wk between injections; some patients need every 4–6 mo.

column1: CIC frequency goal in adult SCI?
column2: 4–6 times/day to keep volumes <400–500 mL; minimize storage pressure × time exposure.

column1: Define decision threshold for ileal conduit in NLUTD?
column2: Failed augmentation, hostile bladder not amenable to reconstruction, severe upper-tract deterioration, poor manual dexterity for CIC.

column1: Risk of metabolic acidosis after bladder augmentation?
column2: Ileum: hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis; sigmoid: similar; monitor electrolytes + bicarbonate; supplement as needed.
Mucus retention and bladder stones; routine irrigation 1–2x/day reduces stone risk.
Acute abdomen in CIC patient who missed catheterization; CT cystogram diagnostic; surgical emergency.

column1: B12 deficiency risk after ileal augmentation?
column2: Yes, due to terminal ileum resorption; monitor annually after 5 yr; supplement if low.

column1: PVR threshold in NLUTD warranting intervention?
column2: No fixed threshold — symptom-based + upper-tract status; PVR contributing to UTI/pressures triggers CIC consideration.

column1: Suprapubic catheter long-term advantage over urethral?
column2: Less urethral erosion; allows sexual activity; preserves urethra for future surgery; still has UTI/stone risk.

column1: Common cause of new hydronephrosis in NLUTD patient?
column2: Worsening compliance, NDO breakthrough, VUR, calculi, ureteric stricture (uncommon) — workup with UDS + imaging.
Suspected VUR, anatomic anomaly, prior reconstruction, complex incontinence — adds anatomic detail to UDS.

column1: Risk of NLUTD progression in MS?
column2: ~50–80% develop LUTS over disease course; severity correlates with EDSS and disease duration.

column1: Anti-CGRP migraine prophylaxis interaction with NLUTD?
column2: No major interaction; clinical relevance is recognizing migraines triggered by AD in SCI patients with neck pain.
Restriction of urine flow from renal pelvis to ureter resulting in dilation of collecting system and potential renal damage.

column1: Most common cause of UPJ obstruction in children?
column2: Intrinsic narrowing at the UPJ due to abnormal smooth muscle development; <30% have crossing vessel.

column1: Most common cause of UPJ obstruction in adults?
column2: Crossing accessory lower-pole vessel in ~50%; intrinsic stenosis remaining.
Grades 0–4: 0 none, 1 mild pelvic dilation, 2 with calyces, 3 calyceal dilation without parenchymal thinning, 4 with parenchymal thinning.

column1: Diagnostic test of choice for UPJ obstruction?
column2: MAG3 renogram with Lasix — T1/2 washout time and differential renal function.
<10 min: non-obstructed; 10–20 min: equivocal; >20 min: obstructed.

column1: Differential renal function threshold for intervention in UPJO?
column2: DRF <40% in affected kidney + symptoms or progressive function loss → pyeloplasty.
~95% with symptom resolution and improved drainage; minimally invasive equivalent to open.
~65–80% — lower than pyeloplasty (~95%); reserve for short narrow strictures, no crossing vessel, good DRF.

column1: Define ureteropelvic vs ureterovesical junction obstruction differential on imaging?
column2: UPJO: dilated pelvis, normal ureter; UVJO: dilated ureter to UVJ with megaureter morphology.

column1: Primary obstructive megaureter — adult ureteral diameter threshold?
column2: >7 mm in adults (>10 mm distal); pediatric threshold lower; differentiate from refluxing or obstructed megaureter.

column1: Most common cause of primary megaureter in adults?
column2: Distal aperistaltic ureteric segment (adynamic juxtavesical ureter), congenital — analogous to achalasia.

column1: First-line management of asymptomatic adult primary megaureter?
column2: Observation with serial imaging + renogram; intervention only with symptoms, function decline, or stones.
Reflux into non-dilated distal ureter only.
Reflux into non-dilated ureter, pelvis, and calyces.
Reflux with mild-moderate dilation of ureter, pelvis, and calyces; minimal blunting of fornices.
Moderate dilation with blunted calyces but maintained papillary impressions.
Gross dilation and tortuosity of ureter with loss of papillary impressions.

column1: VUR with renal cortical scarring on DMSA — terminology?
column2: Reflux nephropathy — irreversible damage from repeated pyelonephritis or developmental hypoplasia.

column1: First-line management of low-grade VUR (I–III) in children?
column2: Continuous antibiotic prophylaxis + observation; spontaneous resolution rates highest in grades I–II (~80% by 5 yr).
Breakthrough febrile UTI on prophylaxis, new renal scarring, persistent high-grade reflux (IV–V) beyond age 5, non-compliance.

column1: Endoscopic VUR injection success rates by grade?
column2: ~80% for grades I–II, ~70% grade III, ~60% grade IV, ~50% grade V at first injection — open reimplant if refractory.
Cohen cross-trigonal (intravesical) or Lich-Gregoir (extravesical); 95–98% success across grades.
Right ureter passes posterior to IVC ("J-shape" or "fishhook" on imaging); rare congenital venous anomaly.

column1: Imaging of choice for retrocaval ureter?
column2: CT urography or MR urography demonstrating retrocaval segment with proximal hydroureteronephrosis.
Ureteric transection, transposition anterior to IVC, and reanastomosis; robotic approach standard.

column1: Define duplex collecting system Weigert-Meyer rule.
column2: Upper-pole ureter inserts inferomedial (often ectopic, obstructed); lower-pole ureter inserts superolateral (often refluxing).

column1: Most common indication for surgery in duplex collecting system?
column2: Upper-pole obstruction with poor function → heminephroureterectomy; or ectopic insertion causing incontinence.

column1: Where do ectopic ureters insert in females?
column2: Bladder neck, urethra, vagina, vulva, perineum — any insertion below external sphincter causes continuous incontinence.

column1: Ectopic ureter in males — clinical hallmark?
column2: Always above external sphincter (Wolffian-derived) — never causes urinary incontinence; presents with epididymitis, UTI, or obstruction.
Cystic dilation of intravesical ureter; intravesical (simple, often adult) vs ectopic (often duplex, pediatric).
Endoscopic incision/puncture to decompress; address VUR or upper-pole function later if persistent.

column1: Iatrogenic ureteric injury — most common surgical setting?
column2: Gynecologic surgery (hysterectomy) > colorectal > urologic; right at the cardinal ligament/IP ligament area.

column1: Time of recognition of ureteric injury intra-op vs post-op?
column2: Only ~30% recognized intra-op; rest present 1–14 days postop with flank pain, ileus, urinoma, fistula.
Retrograde + antegrade (loopogram) ureterogram + CT urogram; assess length, location, and renal function.

column1: Length threshold for ureteral reimplantation vs ureteroureterostomy?
column2: Ureteroureterostomy ≤2 cm; ureteric reimplant for distal lesions; psoas hitch for 6–10 cm distal; Boari flap for 10–15 cm; ileal substitution for longer.
Long ureteric loss (>15 cm) where Boari flap insufficient; contraindicated in severe renal failure (eGFR <40) or IBD.
Adds ~5 cm of bladder-to-pelvis reach; ipsilateral psoas tendon anchored; preserves antireflux.
Adds 10–15 cm of bladder tube to bridge midureteral defects; reflux risk higher; preserve antireflux tunnel.
~50–60% at 1 year for short (<2 cm) strictures with good blood supply; lower for radiated or ischemic.
Onlay for long mid-ureteric strictures avoiding reimplantation; emerging robotic technique; early success 80–90%.

column1: Most common cause of UPJ obstruction in adults — etiology beyond crossing vessel?
column2: Intrinsic stricture from prior endourologic instrumentation (stone surgery, ureteroscopy) or stones.

column1: Hydronephrosis without obstruction — most common cause?
column2: Vesicoureteral reflux, megacalycosis, or postobstructive resolution; renography distinguishes.
Non-obstructive dilation of calyces with normal pelvis and ureter; congenital, no intervention needed.
Mild: pelvis <15 mm with normal calyces; moderate: 15–25 mm with calyceal dilation; severe: >25 mm with parenchymal thinning.
Cortical imaging for scarring and split renal function; gold standard for permanent renal damage in VUR.

column1: When should radiation be added to UPJO workup?
column2: Generally avoided in children; favor US, MR urography, MAG3 for diagnostic and functional assessment.

column1: Define horseshoe kidney clinical relevance to UPJ surgery?
column2: Isthmus crosses anterior to aorta; altered vascular anatomy; pyeloplasty more complex but feasible robotically.

column1: Define crossed fused renal ectopia management?
column2: Most asymptomatic; UPJO can occur due to abnormal vessel courses; surgery as needed individualized.
Subcapsular hematoma compressing kidney → renin-mediated hypertension; secondary HTN workup includes recent renal trauma/procedure.

column1: Define renal pelvis stone composition tendency in chronic obstruction?
column2: Struvite from chronic infection (Proteus, Klebsiella); requires complete removal + treatment of obstruction.

column1: Most common organism in obstructed pyelonephritis with stone?
column2: Proteus mirabilis (struvite stones), E. coli, Klebsiella — urgent decompression with stent or nephrostomy.

column1: Urgent intervention for obstructed infected upper tract?
column2: Percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde stent; definitive stone removal deferred until sepsis resolves.

column1: Define ureteric stricture causes besides iatrogenic?
column2: Ischemic (post-radiation, vascular), inflammatory (TB, schistosoma), malignant compression, endometriosis.
Intrinsic or extrinsic compression usually at distal ureter; presents with cyclical hematuria/hydronephrosis; MR pelvis diagnostic.
Bilateral medial ureteric deviation with proximal hydronephrosis; biopsy + steroids; ureterolysis if refractory.
Flank pain, recurrent pyelonephritis, hydroureteronephrosis with normal bladder; imaging differentiates from VUR.

column1: Imaging confirmation of complete vs partial UPJ obstruction?
column2: MAG3 with Lasix — complete: no washout; partial: prolonged T1/2 with eventual washout.

column1: Define crossing vessel impact on endopyelotomy?
column2: Crossing vessel doubles risk of bleeding and failure; pyeloplasty (with vessel transposition) preferred.
Salvage for failed pyeloplasty or intrarenal pelvis with scarred UPJ; lower pole calyx anastomosed to ureter after partial polectomy.

column1: Indication for nephrectomy in obstructed nonfunctioning kidney?
column2: DRF <10% with symptomatic infections, pain, hypertension, or stone burden; preserve unless reconstruction is feasible.

column1: Define autotransplantation indication in ureteric disease?
column2: Massive ureteric loss not bridgeable by ileum; sympathetic dystrophy (loin-pain hematuria); rare modern indication.

column1: Renal pelvis dilation threshold in pregnancy (physiologic)?
column2: Up to ~2.5 cm right and 1.5 cm left in 3rd trimester is normal; persistent or symptomatic dilation requires workup.
Where renal pelvis tapers into proximal ureter; anteromedial to lower pole; site of most congenital obstructions.
Upper: branches from renal artery (medial supply); mid: aortic + gonadal + iliac (medial); distal: vesical and uterine (lateral). Skeletonization risks stricture.

column1: Ureteral stent indwelling time before stricture risk?
column2: After 3–6 mo stents encrust significantly; routine exchange q3–6 mo to prevent encrustation; lifelong rare.
Refractory benign ureteric stricture in non-surgical candidates; long-term indwelling biocompatible options.
Refluxing patulous orifice — supports VUR diagnosis; classification (golf hole, stadium, horseshoe) historical.

column1: Long-term renal outcome of treated grade III–V VUR?
column2: Reflux nephropathy may progress despite surgery; ~10–15% of severe VUR develops ESRD; lifelong surveillance for HTN and proteinuria.

column1: Renal cortical thickness threshold concerning for parenchymal loss?
column2: <5 mm cortical thickness on US correlates with substantially reduced function; consider nephrectomy vs reconstruction.

column1: Define "split function" cutoff usually requiring reconstruction over nephrectomy?
column2: DRF ≥15–20% generally preserved with reconstruction; <10% often considered for nephrectomy if obstructed and symptomatic.
UPJO: at junction; high ureteric stricture: below UPJ; both managed with reconstructive approaches but differ in technique.

column1: Risk of UPJO recurrence after successful pyeloplasty?
column2: ~5%; presents within first 2 yr; reoperation success >85% but more complex (consider buccal/ureterocalicostomy).
Postnatal US in first weeks; subsequent intervals based on SFU grade and persistence; functional studies if SFU 3–4.

column1: Define antenatal hydronephrosis threshold prompting postnatal workup?
column2: APD ≥7 mm second trimester or ≥10 mm third trimester; postnatal repeat US after 1 week to allow physiologic oliguria.
MAG3 — function + drainage curves (dynamic); DMSA — cortical imaging for scars (static).
Tracer uptake low, masking obstruction; consider antegrade Whitaker test if renography ambiguous.

column1: Define Whitaker test threshold for obstruction?
column2: Pressure differential pelvis-bladder >22 cm H2O at 10 mL/min infusion = obstruction; >15 equivocal.

column1: Define stone passage rate by ureteral location?
column2: Proximal ureteric: ~50% spontaneous passage if <5 mm; distal: ~80% if <5 mm; >10 mm: very low; consider intervention.

column1: Most common cause of vesicovaginal fistula (VVF) in developed world?
column2: Iatrogenic injury at hysterectomy (especially for benign disease) — ~75% of cases.

column1: Most common cause of VVF in low/middle-income countries?
column2: Obstetric (obstructed labor) — pressure necrosis from prolonged second stage; preventable with EmOC access.
Continuous incontinence 7–14 days postop after benign hysterectomy.

column1: Initial diagnostic test for suspected VVF?
column2: Office tampon dye test — instill methylene blue into bladder, dye on superior tampon confirms VVF.
Differentiates ureterovaginal (oral pyridium → orange staining of tampon) from vesicovaginal (intravesical blue staining).

column1: Imaging modality of choice for ureterovaginal fistula?
column2: CT urography with delayed phase or retrograde ureterogram; identifies level of ureteric injury.

column1: Timing of VVF repair after iatrogenic recognition?
column2: If recognized within 72 h: immediate repair; otherwise wait 6–12 wk (or up to 3 mo) for inflammation to resolve.

column1: Conservative management of small VVF — success rate?
column2: Foley drainage × 4–8 wk for VVF <1 cm fresh: ~10–15% spontaneous closure; most need surgery.

column1: Approach selection — vaginal vs abdominal VVF repair?
column2: Vaginal: low VVF accessible, no concomitant pathology; abdominal: high/complex, concurrent ureteric repair, augmentation needed.
Small post-hysterectomy apical VVF — partial colpocleisis; high success ~90% in selected cases.
Bulbocavernosus fat pad from labium majus; tissue interposition for VVF, RVF, urethrovaginal fistula repair.

column1: Define Goh classification of obstetric VVF?
column2: Type I–IV based on distance from external urethral meatus, fistula size, and tissue characteristics; predicts continence after repair.

column1: Continence rate after obstetric VVF repair?
column2: ~85% closed, but ~30% have persistent SUI from urethral involvement (Goh type IV).
Anti-incontinence surgery, urethral diverticulectomy, obstetric trauma, radiation; presents with continuous leak or post-coital.
Wait 3 mo for tissue healing; multilayer closure + Martius flap; success >85%.

column1: Define rectovaginal fistula (RVF) most common cause?
column2: Obstetric (3rd/4th-degree laceration breakdown) > iatrogenic (gyn or rectal surgery) > IBD > radiation > malignancy.
Optimize medical therapy (anti-TNF, antibiotics) + seton drainage; definitive repair only when bowel disease quiescent.
Diverting colostomy + ileal urinary diversion; primary repair usually fails; tissue interposition (gracilis) for select cases.
Communication between rectum and posterior urethra; post-RP (~1%) or post-radiation/HIFU/cryotherapy; gas/feces per urethra.
Cystoscopy, sigmoidoscopy, MRI pelvis; biopsy to exclude recurrent cancer in post-treatment fistulas.

column1: Most common surgical approach for non-radiated RUF?
column2: York-Mason transanal/transsphincteric; transperineal with gracilis interposition for radiated/complex cases.

column1: Timing of RUF repair after radiation?
column2: After diverting colostomy + suprapubic; wait 3–6 mo for inflammation to settle; counsel about diversion permanence in 30%.
Catheter erosion, suprapubic tube tract maturation, trauma, malignancy invading bladder; presents with urine drainage from skin.
Cystogram or CT cystogram to locate; cystoscopy and skin tract probing; resect if persistent after Foley drainage.
Diverticulitis (~70%), colon cancer (~10%), Crohn (~10%), radiation, iatrogenic; M>F due to uterine interposition in women.
Pneumaturia, fecaluria, and recurrent UTI with polymicrobial growth.

column1: Best diagnostic test for colovesical fistula?
column2: CT abdomen/pelvis with rectal or oral contrast — shows air in bladder + adjacent inflamed colonic loop; cystoscopy confirms.
Single-stage resection of involved colon segment + primary anastomosis + bladder closure; biopsy bladder edge to rule out cancer.
Enterovesical includes small bowel involvement (Crohn most common); higher diarrhea/short-bowel risk after resection.

column2: Repair of rectocele alone may not improve constipation if dyssynergia present; address pelvic floor function preoperatively.

column1: NOM success rates by AAST renal grade?
column2: Grade I–II ~100%; III ~95%; IV ~94%; V ~85%. Only absolute contraindication is persistent hemorrhagic shock from the renal injury.

column1: Renal CT — which phase is required for collecting-system injury?
column2: Delayed (excretory) 3–20 min (optimal ~10 min). Portal venous alone misses urinary extravasation. May be acquired up to ~60 min after initial contrast if patient must leave the scanner.

column1: Renal trauma — when is delayed CT for follow-up?
column2: 48–72 h for grades III–V with ongoing bleeding or urine extravasation, penetrating destructive firearm grade III+, or symptoms (fever, worsening flank pain).

column1: Pediatric renal trauma — what is a late sign of shock?
column2: Hypotension. Children compensate with tachycardia first; do not require hypotension to trigger CT — base decisions on hematuria + mechanism.

column1: Most common blunt ureteral injury pattern in children?
column2: UPJ avulsion — hyperextensible pediatric spine + less perirenal fat. Repair by ureteropyelostomy.

column1: AAST ureteral grade III vs IV?
column2: III: laceration ≥50% transection. IV: complete transection with <2 cm devascularization. V: avulsion with >2 cm devascularization.

column1: Why avoid endoscopic stenting alone for ballistic ureteral injury?
column2: Blast effect causes microvascular injury beyond visible wound; delayed necrosis at 5–7 days with stricture formation. Plan early re-evaluation and low threshold for formal repair.

column1: Damage-control options for ureteral injury in unstable polytrauma?
column2: Cutaneous ureterostomy; ureteral ligation + PCN; intubated ureterostomy (stent secured to proximal end, externalized); intraperitoneal drainage with re-look.

column1: Most common bladder trauma type in blunt mechanism?
column2: Extraperitoneal (~63%) — pelvic ring distortion / bony fragment. Intraperitoneal ~32% — hydraulic dome rupture. Combined <5%.

column1: AAST bladder grade IV vs V?
column2: IV: intraperitoneal laceration ≥2 cm. V: extension into bladder neck or ureteral orifice (trigone).

column1: Pelvic fracture pattern with highest bladder injury risk?
column2: Pubic symphysis diastasis >1 cm and obturator ring disruption with >1 cm displacement.

column1: CT cystography retrograde fill — minimum volume?
column2: 300 mL retrograde (or until patient discomfort / contrast stops flowing). Passive antegrade filling (Foley clamp) has unacceptably high false-negative rates.

column1: Complex EPB features mandating operative repair?
column2: Concomitant urethral / bladder-neck injury, vaginal or rectal injury, intravesical clot impairing drainage, intraluminal foreign body, need for anterior pelvic internal fixation.
≥18 Fr Foley × minimum 7 days; some extend 2–3 weeks. Confirm healing with repeat cystography before catheter removal.

column1: Bladder repair vs pelvic ORIF — sequencing?
column2: Repair the bladder before pelvic reduction — symphyseal reduction makes bladder repair technically impossible. SPT relatively contraindicates anterior internal fixation (infection risk).

column1: Strongest physical exam finding for testicular torsion?
column2: Absent cremasteric reflex — OR 47.6. High-riding testis with transverse lie is classic but less sensitive.

column1: Salvage rate by time-to-detorsion in torsion?
column2: <6 h ~90%; 6–8 h usually salvageable; 8–12 h variable; >12 h orchiectomy risk rises; >24 h most non-viable. ~32% of pediatric cases result in orchiectomy.

column1: Why bilateral orchiopexy in unilateral torsion?
column2: Bell-clapper anatomy is usually bilateral; contralateral testis is at high risk for asynchronous torsion. Bilateral fixation is mandatory.
Nonabsorbable (polypropylene 3-0 or 4-0) — absorbable suture associated with higher recurrence.

column1: A normal scrotal Doppler — does it exclude torsion?
column2: No. Clinical suspicion drives management. High-pretest-probability cases go to the OR, not the ultrasound suite.

Audible pop/crack at injury, immediate detumescence, severe penile pain with ecchymosis and "eggplant" deformity. Diagnosis is clinical; imaging only for indeterminate presentations.

column1: Penile fracture — concomitant urethral injury rate?
column2: ~15% of penile fractures. Evaluate (RUG or cystourethroscopy) when blood at meatus, gross hematuria, retention, or inability to pass catheter.
Within 7 days. Earlier intervention → less pain, faster convalescence, lower curvature risk, better preserved erectile function. Conservative management has higher complication rates.

column1: Penile fracture — most common tunical rupture site?
column2: Ventral / lateral surfaces of the penile shaft, distal to the suspensory ligament — thinnest portion of the tunica albuginea.

column1: Urethral involvement in penile ballistic injury?
column2: Up to 50%. Immediate exploration, conservative debridement, foreign body removal, and tension-free primary urethroplasty over a catheter.

column1: PFUI incidence relative to pelvic fractures?
column2: 1.5–10% of anterior pelvic fractures cause urethral injury. Each mm of symphysis pubis diastasis ≈ 10% relative increased risk.
Membranous urethral disruption extending below the urogenital diaphragm, involving the anterior urethra. Type II: at membranous-prostatic junction above diaphragm.
Low sensitivity and specificity — no longer recommended. Blood at the urethral meatus is the most classic sign.

Suprapubic tube placement (≥14 Fr Foley, not pigtail). Open urethral realignment has no role due to substantially increased complications. SPT followed by delayed urethroplasty achieves 84–97% success.

column1: Primary endoscopic realignment vs SPT — outcomes per TURNS?
column2: McCormick 2023 (n=69): obstruction 97% vs 94% (p=0.471); urethroplasty required 87% vs 91% (p=0.784). Comparable rates of stricture, incontinence, and ED in 2025 meta-analysis (Owen).
3–6 months — allows scar maturation. Range 6 weeks to 4 yr; Scarberry/Gómez 2018 showed early (3–6 wk) reconstruction has comparable outcomes when positioning is safe.
1) Bulbar mobilization + spatulated end-to-end (34–67% sufficient). 2) Corporal splitting (17–36%). 3) Inferior pubectomy (10–32%). 4) Supracrural rerouting (2–5%, higher failure).

column1: Pubourethral stump angle on MRI — predictor of what?
column2: Lower PUA predicts need for elaborate (vs simple perineal) approach. Horiguchi 2025: OR 0.95 per degree, AUC 0.782. Indicates proximal stump displaced superoposteriorly behind symphysis.
Pubic symphysis diastasis (OR 15.9, strongest), lateral prostatic displacement (OR 6.9), long urethral gap (OR 2.0).

column1: Narumi 1993 MRI predictors of post-PFUI permanent impotence?
column2: Avulsion of corpus cavernosum + lateral prostatic displacement = 95% probability permanent impotence; neither = 83% probability normal potency. Dorsal venous plexus disruption is the third predictor.

column1: Diagnostic corporal blood gas — ischemic priapism?
column2: pO2 <30 mmHg, pCO2 >60 mmHg, pH <7.25. Dark blood. Normal arterial: pO2 >90, pCO2 <40, pH ~7.40 (bright red).

Ischemic (~95%): rigid + painful corpora, soft glans, time-critical. Non-ischemic: partial + non-painful tumescence after perineal/straddle trauma — NOT a surgical emergency. Stuttering: recurrent <3-hr ischemic episodes.
1 mg in 10 mL saline (100 µg/mL); inject 100–500 µg q3–5 min up to 1 hour. Continuous BP/HR monitoring; risk of hypertensive crisis. Pediatric max 500 µg total.

column1: Distal vs proximal priapism shunts — initial choice?
column2: Distal shunts first: Winter (Tru-Cut), Ebbehoj (scalpel stab), T-shunt, Al-Ghorab (open excision of distal tunica — most durable). Proximal (Quackels, Grayhack, Barry) only if distal fails.
Al-Ghorab shunt + retrograde corporal tunneling with 7/8 Hegar dilator to disrupt ischemic coagulum along the corpus. Added to 2021 AUA/SMSNA guideline.

Do NOT delay urologic intervention for exchange. Exchange does not terminate priapism faster than standard care and delays effective intervention by 6+ hours. Simple transfusion to Hb 9–10 before GA is reasonable.
Association of Sickle cell, Priapism, Exchange transfusion, and Neurologic events — described after rapid exchange transfusion; argues against reflexive exchange.

column1: Early prosthesis in priapism — indication and rationale?
column2: Priapism >36–48 h with failed medical management. Implantation is substantially easier acutely than after 4–6 wk fibrosis consolidation; preserves length; only ~43% retain function after 48+ h.
Observation (spontaneous resolution common). Selective pudendal arteriography with embolization for persistent symptomatic cases; gelfoam preferred over coils to preserve future erectile function.
~7.5% population-based; tertiary referral centers 20–40%; >70% in septic shock. Time-to-debridement is the single most important determinant of survival.
FGSI >9: ~75% mortality probability (original Laor 1995). Uludag FGSI adds age + extent; score >9 → 94% mortality. AUC 0.94 (highest of available tools).
WBC, CRP, hemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, glucose. Score ≥6 → 68% sensitivity, 85% specificity for NSTI. Negative LRINEC does NOT exclude NSTI.

column1: Skin-sparing debridement in Fournier's — outcome impact?
column2: Tom 487 patients: primary closure rates 0% (traditional) → 50% (skin-sparing); mortality comparable. Modern paradigm — cutaneous vasculature preserves skin viability over necrotic subcutaneous tissue.

column1: Why is testicular salvage usually possible in Fournier's?
column2: Dartos fascia resists infection spread; testicular blood supply comes from aorta via testicular arteries, not affected by scrotal fascial necrosis.

Every 24–48 hours until wound is clean. Median 1.8–3.5 debridements in series. Areas appearing viable initially may become ischemic within 24–72 h. Re-look is mandatory.
CRP ratio (follow-up/initial) cutoff 1.78 predicts death with 86% sensitivity, 82% specificity. Rising CRP at 48–72 h → inadequate source control, return to OR.

column1: SGLT-2 inhibitors and Fournier's risk — current evidence?
column2: FDA 2018 safety alert. Subsequent high-level evidence has NOT demonstrated significant difference in FG incidence vs other diabetes treatments.

column1: Indication for diverting colostomy in Fournier's?
column2: Anorectal source identified, extensive perirectal involvement, or stool contamination threatens wound healing. Reverse at 3–6 months after recovery.

column1: Female cases as proportion of all Fournier's?
column2: 20–30%. Female mortality ~7.1% slightly higher than male ~5.7%. ~50% of FG patients sought prior medical care for same symptoms before NSTI diagnosis.

column1: AAST testicular grade IV vs V?
column2: IV: major laceration of tunica albuginea with ≥50% parenchymal loss. V: total testicular destruction or avulsion. III: <50% loss; II: subclinical tunica laceration.

column2: Interruption of the tunica albuginea — but not always visualized. Don't delay surgery for additional imaging if strongly suspected clinically.

column1: Penetrating scrotal trauma — bilateral injury rate?
column2: Unilateral testicular injury in ~50%, bilateral in ~30%, with spermatic-cord vascular or vas deferens injury in up to 9%. All require urgent exploration.

column1: Human vs animal bite — primary closure?
column2: Animal bite: copious irrigation + debridement + absorbable suture closure + amoxicillin-clavulanate + tetanus/rabies. Human bite: irrigation + debridement + antibiotics but DO NOT close primarily (high contamination/infection risk).

column1: Pediatric trauma hematuria threshold for imaging?
column2: Any degree of hematuria warrants CT — children have less perirenal fat and more pliable ribs making the kidney more vulnerable.

column1: Acute urinary retention — clamping the catheter during decompression?
column2: Not recommended — no RCT supports gradual decompression. Rapid complete emptying is safe; hematuria 2–16%, hypotension common but transient. Mayo Clinic review (Nyman).

Urine output ≥200 mL/hr × 2 consecutive hours OR >3 L over 24 hr after relief of obstruction. Physiologic <48 h; pathologic >48 h with intrinsic tubular damage.

Sacral neuromodulation — only specific treatment for idiopathic female retention with abnormal sphincter EMG. >70% therapeutic effectiveness. Associated with PCOS.
≥300 mL for symptomatic patients; ≥500 mL for asymptomatic patients. Bladder scanner is preferred diagnostic tool over catheterization for confirming retention.

column1: WPATH SOC8 hormone-therapy requirement before chest vs genital surgery?
column2: Chest surgery: no required prior hormone therapy. Most genital surgeries: ≥12 months of consistent hormone therapy. Endocrine Society also requires age of majority and persistent gender dysphoria.

column2: ~6% across all GAS. 3.5% top surgery; 8% bottom surgery; 2.1% head/neck. Vaginoplasty Clavien-Dindo ≥3 in 5.5% with no 30-day mortality.

Self-lubricating neovagina (peritoneal flaps). Used when penile skin is insufficient (prior circumcision, puberty blocker history). Castanon: 52 patients, mean depth 14.7 cm, 96% satisfaction, complications 13.5%.

column1: Most common complications after penile inversion vaginoplasty?
column2: Massie 2018 (n=117): granulation tissue (26%), intravaginal scarring (20%), prolonged pain (20%). Vaginal stenosis is most frequent across all techniques — usually from inadequate dilation.

column1: Prostate screening in transfeminine patients post-vaginoplasty?
column2: Performed VAGINALLY, not rectally — the prostate lies anterior to the constructed vagina.

column1: Most commonly performed feminizing GAS procedure?
column2: Breast augmentation — 74% of transfeminine respondents desire/have undergone it. Routine inframammary fold lowering common; transfeminine patients need larger implants (median 500 vs 350 mL).

column1: Voice surgery feminization — most reliable option?
column2: Wendler glottoplasty — anterior glottic web shortens vibrating length of vocal folds. SF0 effect size g=1.21. Combined with voice therapy is more effective than therapy alone.
99% (Djordjevic 938-patient series). Mean neophallus 4–10 cm; full erogenous sensitivity preserved (4.8/5 vs 3.4/5 for phalloplasty). 12.5% subsequently request phalloplasty.

column1: Top surgery DIFNG vs PAT — tradeoff?
column2: DIFNG (double incision + free nipple grafting) has lowest complication rate; PAT (periareolar) has significantly higher patient-satisfaction scores. Trade-off between complication risk and aesthetic outcome.

column1: Adverse effects 12 yr after prostate-cancer treatment per Unger 2024?
column2: Urethral stricture 6-fold higher; radiation cystitis 131-fold higher; radiation proctitis 88-fold higher; secondary bladder cancer nearly 3-fold higher. AUS placement 110-fold higher after prostatectomy.

column1: Radiation cystitis prevalence after pelvic RT?
column2: 5–15% of patients; presents months to decades after treatment. RICH-ART RCT: HBOT improves symptoms and QoL; long-term follow-up shows durable benefit with lower healthcare cost.

column1: Posterior urethral stenosis rate after radiotherapy vs salvage prostatectomy?
column2: 4–13% after radiotherapy; >40% after salvage prostatectomy. After RP alone: 5–10%.

column1: De novo SUI rate after urethroplasty for radiation-induced stricture?
column2: 19–40% develop new SUI. ~22% later require AUS placement. EPA success ~70–87% at 2–3 years for radiation-induced bulbomembranous strictures.

column1: Pelvic-floor disorders after pelvic RT in women — pooled prevalence?
column2: Perez 2026 meta-analysis: UI 37%, urgency incontinence 47%, OAB 42%, anal incontinence 24%, pelvic pain 30%, sexual dysfunction 19%.

column1: Secondary malignancy in urologic reconstructions — timing and histology?
column2: Median 36 years after reconstruction; predominantly adenocarcinoma; often advanced stage and aggressive. Decades-long surveillance horizon for any bowel incorporated into the urinary tract.

column1: NCCN survivorship — initiation of sexual-health discussion?
column2: A team member should initiate at diagnosis and reassess throughout follow-up — proactive clinician initiation, not waiting for patient. Validated tools: FSFI, SHIM, PROMIS SexFS.
Chronic progressive condition from declining estrogen — affects vulva, vagina, urethra, bladder. Replaces narrower term "vulvovaginal atrophy." Symptoms typically progressive without treatment.

column1: Lowest systemic absorption vaginal estrogen formulation?
column2: Estradiol vaginal ring (Estring 7.5 µg/day, replace q90 days) — most consistent + lowest systemic absorption. Preferred for breast cancer survivors. Imvexxy 4 µg insert is comparable.

column1: Vaginal DHEA mechanism and unique benefit?
column2: Intracrinology — local conversion to estrogens + androgens. Improves all 6 FSFI domains including desire and arousal (differentiates from vaginal estrogen). Serum estrogen stays below postmenopausal levels even in AI users.

column1: Vaginal estrogen in breast cancer survivors — 2025 meta?
column2: Beste 2025 (8 obs studies, >24,000 patients): no increase in breast cancer recurrence (OR 0.48), breast cancer mortality (OR 0.60), or overall mortality (OR 0.46). FDA removed boxed warnings 11/2025.
≥2 UTIs in 6 months OR ≥3 UTIs in 12 months, with at least one culture-confirmed episode. Affects ~25% of women who experience an initial UTI.

column1: Vaginal estrogen for rUTI prevention — efficacy?
column2: 58% reduction (RR 0.42; 5 RCTs, 1,936 patients). Oral estrogen shows NO benefit (RR 1.11). Tan-Kim 2023: 51.9% real-world reduction in 5,638 women.

Non-inferior to daily low-dose antibiotics for rUTI prevention (1.38 vs 0.89 episodes/person-year; within 1 UTI/PY margin). Antibiotic resistance in E. coli was higher in the antibiotic group (72% vs 56%).

column1: Network meta-analysis — strongest non-antibiotic rUTI prevention?
column2: D-mannose showed strongest effect (RR 0.34). But MERIT RCT 2024 (Hayward JAMA Intern Med) — 2 g daily for 6 months did NOT significantly reduce UTI recurrence vs placebo.

column1: Continuous antibiotic prophylaxis for rUTI — recurrence reduction?
column2: ~95% (from 2–3 to 0.1–0.2 episodes/PY). Typically initiated for 6-month trial; safely continued 2–5 years. Benefits confined to usage period.

Usually not appropriate; NPV ~93% for normal findings in women without risk factors. Imaging only when relapse <2 wk, nonresponse, persistent hematuria, or risk factors (calculi, pneumaturia, fecaluria).

Adjusted OR 1.48 (French case-control, >365 DDD) for dementia. Oxybutynin + solifenacin highest risk; trospium (does not cross BBB) shows no increased risk. AUGS recommends avoiding anticholinergics >70 yr.

column1: β3 agonists in elderly OAB — advantage?
column2: Equivalent efficacy to antimuscarinics; dry mouth at placebo rate (vs 3.8–7.9× with antimuscarinics). No anticholinergic burden. Monitor BP (3–10 mmHg systolic elevation possible).
≥15 seconds. Timed Up and Go is a recommended preoperative screen for women ≥65 before elective pelvic-floor surgery, alongside Mini-Cog and Life-Space Assessment.

Highly effective for elderly women not desiring vaginal preservation. 94.8% anatomic success; 77.5% subjective; 6.8% regret at mean 2.9 yr. No patients regret loss of sexual function. Shorter LOS vs reconstruction.

column1: Frailty impact on prolapse surgery (ASPIRe trial)?
column2: Prefrail/frail patients had no increase in immediate postop complications but 2.1× higher hazard of treatment failure. Those living alone needed enhanced social support in first 6 wks (19% vs 6%).

column1: Urethral stricture as adult hypospadias presentation — frequency?
column2: 11–47% of adults after childhood repair. Strictures significantly longer than in unoperated patients (5.5 cm vs 3.0 cm). Most common adult indication for hypospadias-related urethroplasty.

column1: Preferred graft material for adult hypospadias reconstruction?
column2: Buccal mucosa — 99% GURS member preference. Bracka technique BMG complication rate 20% vs 31% for preputial skin. Avoid hair-bearing penile skin.

Stage 1: chordee correction + urethral plate transection if needed + free graft (BMG preferred) as neourethral plate on ventral surface. Stage 2 (~6 mo later): tubularize the grafted plate. Dominant approach for severe proximal hypospadias or reoperative cases.

column1: Avoid EPA in penile post-hypospadias strictures — why?
column2: Penile shortening, chordee, and recurrence risk are high; poor outcomes reported in failed-hypospadias cohorts. Two-stage substitution with BMG is preferred.

column1: Failure-free survival after urethroplasty for failed hypospadias?
column2: 82% at 1 year → 57% at 10 years (Verla series). Mandates long-term surveillance.

column1: Oligozoospermia/azoospermia rate in adult nonsyndromic hypospadias?
column2: 18.6%; higher rates in complex hypospadias and men born small for gestational age. Offer semen analysis + endocrine eval rather than reassurance.

Glanular (mildest), penile, penopubic/complete (entire dorsal urethra open to symphysis, highest continence burden). Female: bifid clitoris + patulous urethra; incontinence common with sphincteric involvement.

Age 12–14 (AAP/AAFP/ACP "Got Transition"). Transfer typically 18–25 depending on readiness and stability. Conduct part of each visit without parents present.
