column1: Valve bladder syndrome in adult PUV?
column2: Persistent bladder dysfunction (myogenic failure, poor compliance, high-pressure chronic retention) in 38% of adults; may worsen at puberty. ED is rare; 12.5% report ejaculatory dysfunction.
Incidence 0–5.5%; mean latency 19–20 years. Adenocarcinoma most common (52%), predominantly at entero-urinary anastomosis. Often diagnosed at advanced stage (1-yr survival 56%).
Annual focused history, exam, BMP (acidosis, B12), urinary-tract imaging for all bowel-incorporating reconstructions. Routine cystoscopy debated — some advocate starting 10 yr after augmentation.

column1: Bowel issue prioritized by parents of spina bifida adolescents?
column2: Fecal incontinence — rated as the biggest issue by 50% of parents. Continence is a major factor in social participation and employment.

column1: Multidisciplinary PUV clinic — Lopez Pereira outcomes?
column2: Dedicated clinic with proactive standardized management reduced CKD progression (12% vs 27%) and need for kidney replacement therapy (3% vs 20%).
TRAQ is the most widely used generic transition readiness tool. TRAQ-SB is the spina bifida-specific version, validated up to age 25.
~10% of reproductive-age women; ~9 million in US. Most common cause of chronic pelvic pain in women; infertility in 30–50%. Diagnostic delay averages 5–12 years from symptom onset.
Nociceptive (lesion-driven inflammation), neuropathic (lesion-associated nerve fiber injury), nociplastic (central sensitization). Lesion burden correlates poorly with pain severity.

column1: Relugolix combination therapy — SPIRIT trial result?
column2: Relugolix 40 mg + estradiol 1 mg + norethindrone acetate 0.5 mg once daily. SPIRIT 1/2: 75% clinically significant improvement in dysmenorrhea vs 27–30% placebo. Sustained at 2 yr; BMD loss minimized by integrated add-back.

column1: Endometriosis recurrence rate after laparoscopic surgery?
column2: 40–45% pain recurrence; repeat surgery in 15–20% at 2 yr; up to 50% at 5–7 yr. Postoperative hormonal therapy recommended to reduce recurrence.

column1: Urologic involvement in endometriosis — bladder vs ureter?
column2: 1–2% of endometriosis cases. Bladder most affected (~85%) — cyclic dysuria, hematuria, suprapubic pain; partial cystectomy. Ureter — high silent renal loss risk; intrinsic disease requires segmental resection + reimplant (psoas hitch/Boari).
93% greater overall risk; 3.4× clear-cell, 2.3× endometrioid. Absolute lifetime risk remains low (1.8% vs 1.1%). Prophylactic oophorectomy is NOT recommended.
GnRH agonist pretreatment for 3–6 months before IVF significantly increases pregnancy likelihood. IVF is most effective treatment for moderate-severe (rASRM III–IV) disease.

column1: Primary HPV testing sensitivity vs cytology?
column2: Primary hrHPV >90% sensitivity for precancer vs 50–70% for cytology. 17% lower risk of invasive cervical cancer with primary HPV vs cytology with reflex (recent large RCT).
Primary HPV testing every 5 years. Acceptable alternatives: cotesting every 5 years or cytology every 3 years.
3 years (vs 5 yr clinician-collected) — margin of safety while US longitudinal data accrue. FDA approved self-collection at-home device (Teal Wand) May 2025.
Immediate CIN3+ risk 4–24% → colposcopy. <4% → surveillance. ≥60% → expedited treatment (excision without prior colposcopy) preferred.
Biennial mammography for ages 40–74 (B recommendation). Notable update from 2016 which individualized 40–49 decision. Insufficient evidence ≥75 or for supplemental screening in dense breasts.

BRCA1/2 carriers (ages 25–29 MRI alone, 30–75 MRI + mammography); residual lifetime risk ≥20%; prior chest radiation 10–30 yr old (begin 8–10 yr after RT or age 25). DENSE trial: ~50% reduction in interval cancers with supplemental MRI for extremely dense breasts.

column1: Why no routine endometrial cancer screening?
column2: Favorable prognosis (most stage I at presentation, 5-yr survival >88%); TVUS specificity only 35–62% at 5 mm cutoff; endometrial biopsy is invasive (7–40% inadequate sampling); no proven mortality reduction.
TVUS — endometrial thickness ≤4 mm has >99% NPV for endometrial cancer. Persistent/recurrent bleeding warrants histologic evaluation regardless of thickness.

NCCN: consider annual endometrial biopsy starting 30–35 yr. TVUS NOT preferred. Total hysterectomy reduces incidence (not mortality) — legitimate option after childbearing. MLH1/MSH2 25–60% lifetime EC risk; MSH6 up to 71%.
No routine endometrial screening per ACOG for asymptomatic women on standard 20 mg/d. The 2–3× RR does not justify routine screening. Any abnormal bleeding → prompt evaluation.
~43% of US women have a sexual concern; 12% experience distress (peak 15% in 45–64 yr). DSM-5 diagnoses require ≥6 months and clinically significant personal distress.

Female Sexual Interest/Arousal Disorder (FSIAD); Female Orgasmic Disorder; Genito-Pelvic Pain/Penetration Disorder (GPPPD; combines former vaginismus + dyspareunia); Substance-Induced Sexual Dysfunction.

FDA-approved for acquired generalized HSDD in premenopausal women only. Modest efficacy (+0.5 SSE/mo vs placebo). Avoid alcohol within 2 hours of dosing — hypotension/syncope risk. CYP3A4 contraindications.

Melanocortin-4 receptor agonist, 1.75 mg SC ~45 min before activity, premenopausal HSDD. RECONNECT phase 3: +0.35 FSFI desire vs placebo. AE: nausea 40%, flushing 21%. Uncontrolled HTN contraindication.

Only evidence-based testosterone indication per 2019 Global Consensus. Meta of 36 RCTs (n=8,480): +0.85 SSE/month. NO FDA-approved female formulation in US; fractionate male formulation; transdermal preferred (oral worsens lipids).
Annual screening for all sexually active women ≤24 yr and older women with risk factors. Vaginal specimen (clinician- or self-collected) is preferred for NAAT in women.
Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 7 days — preferred over azithromycin (superior at rectal sites). Retest in 3 months due to high reinfection rates.
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM × 1 (1 g if ≥150 kg). Azithromycin co-treatment NO LONGER recommended.
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + doxycycline 100 mg BID × 14 d + metronidazole 500 mg BID × 14 d. Metronidazole now routinely included.
8% after one PID episode; 18% after two; 38% after three. ~10% of first pregnancies after PID are ectopic. Chronic pelvic pain 3× more frequent post-PID.
Metronidazole 500 mg PO BID × 7 days. 7-day regimen superior to single 2 g dose in women (unlike in men).
Doxycycline 200 mg within 72 h of condomless sex. ~80% reduction chlamydia/syphilis; ~50% gonorrhea in MSM/TGW. NOT recommended for cisgender women — Kenyan trial showed no benefit (29% adherence).

Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million U IM. Single dose for early; weekly × 3 for late latent. Penicillin is the ONLY recommended therapy in pregnancy — desensitize if allergic. Untreated → stillbirth up to 40%.

9-valent (Gardasil 9) — ages 9–12 (2-dose); catch-up through age 26 (3-dose if initiated ≥15 yr). Ages 27–45 shared decision-making. Population-level: cervical cancer incidence ~69% decline in vaccinated women 20–24.
Grade B for DXA in all postmenopausal women ≥65 yr. Younger women: assess with FRAX and proceed to DXA if 10-yr major osteoporotic fracture probability ≥9.3% (equivalent to a 65-yr-old white woman).
T ≤ −2.5 at lumbar spine, total hip, or femoral neck. OR any low-trauma fragility fracture at hip/vertebra/other site regardless of T score. Osteopenia: T −1.0 to −2.5.
T −1.0 to −2.5 + 10-yr hip fracture risk ≥3% OR major osteoporotic fracture risk ≥20%. Use FRAX to determine treatment need within osteopenic range.

column1: GnRH agonist bone loss — magnitude over 6 months?
column2: 4–8% reduction in lumbar spine BMD. Courses >3–6 months need bone-protective co-therapy (add-back estrogen-progestin or bisphosphonate). Baseline + 12–18-mo DXA if ongoing.

Anabolic agents preferred (vs antiresorptives in high-risk): teriparatide 20 µg SC daily × 2 yr (~65% vertebral fracture reduction) or romosozumab 210 mg SC monthly × 12 mo. Follow with antiresorptive after anabolic course.
1–3% BMD loss per year. ASCO/NCCN recommend baseline + annual DXA + bisphosphonate or denosumab co-therapy for breast cancer survivors on AI.
38–62% of high-grade serous adenocarcinomas originate as STIC (serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma) in the fimbrial funnel — not on the ovarian surface. Foundation for opportunistic salpingectomy.
42–80% reduction in tubo-ovarian carcinoma (2025 Tang meta OR 0.48; Swedish Falconer HR 0.35; Danish Madsen OR 0.58). If broadly implemented, could lower US ovarian-cancer mortality by 15%.

Sectioning and Extensively Examining the Fimbriated End — amputated fimbria sectioned longitudinally + remainder of tube at 2–3 mm intervals. Detects 25% more STICs than a single H&E section. Only 74% of labs perform.

Remove tube completely from fimbriated end to uterotubal junction; interstitial portions don't need removal; cauterize/remove any fimbrial attachments on the ovary. Complete preferred over fimbriectomy because precursors are throughout tube.
Up to 1/3 require secondary surgery. Massie series 7.9% overall reoperation; cosmesis 3.8%, neovaginal stenosis 2.1%. External genital (vulvar) revisions are most common.

column1: Rectoneovaginal fistula — primary vs revision vaginoplasty?
column2: 0.8% primary vs 6.3% revision (OR 8.6). Among 1,082 patients: 25 (2.3%) developed neovaginal fistulas — 13 rectoneovaginal, 11 urethroneovaginal.

column1: Colpectomy at phalloplasty — effect on fistula?
column2: Primary colpectomy reduces fistula incidence from 48% to 21% (p<0.05). Critical adjunct in transmasculine genital surgery with urethral lengthening.

column1: Phalloplasty urethral stricture — open vs endoscopic?
column2: 82% recurrence-free at 3 yr open vs 43% endoscopic (p=0.002). Heineke-Mikulicz 78%, EPA 100%, two-stage without graft 100% in selected indications.

column1: Pelvic floor dysfunction rate after transmasculine genital surgery?
column2: Up to 94.1%. PFPT before and after surgery can substantially reduce dysfunction. Significantly impacts urinary and sexual function.

Earlier intervention → reduced postop pain, faster convalescence, lower curvature risk, higher preserved erectile function. Surgery should be within 7 days; conservative management has higher complication rates (abscess, fibrosis, Peyronie's-like plaques, ED).

Lateral glans entry at 2 and 10 o'clock; No. 10 blade incision into distal corpus; 90° rotation of blade within the corpus; Foley protects the urethra. Compatible with the Burnett Snake maneuver for retrograde tunneling.

Cavernosospongiosum shunt — perineal approach connecting corpus cavernosum to bulbar corpus spongiosum. Proximal shunt; risk of urethrocutaneous fistula (Manjunath 2015) and urethrocavernous fistula (Robbins 1984).

column1: Grayhack shunt — concept and modern status?
column2: 1964 cavernovenous concept — saphenous vein anastomosed to corpus cavernosum. EAU 2024 abandoned for primary use. Kulmala 1995: 19.2% permanent open shunt with 100% impotence reversal on shunt closure. Largely historical.
Planned 2-month elective closure of the caverno-dorsal-vein shunt with adrenaline-irrigation × 5 protocol to prevent venous-leak ED after detumescence.

column1: Early malleable penile prosthesis — Zacharakis comparison?
column2: Early MPP vs delayed: 96% vs 60% function preservation. 80% of delayed required second corporotomy + downsized cylinders. Barham 2023: 0% early vs 40.5% delayed cylinder shortening with IPP.

column1: Ralph 2010 MRI for early MPP candidate selection?
column2: 100% sensitivity for identifying nonviable corpora — supports MRI-guided patient selection for early malleable prosthesis. ISSM 2019 survey: <40% utilization gap despite evidence.

2 mg/kg of contrast IV with image obtained at 10 minutes. Confirms contralateral renal function before exploring an injured kidney. Indicated when contralateral kidney is absent or abnormal on palpation.

column1: Cesarean section — most common GU injury?
column2: Bladder injury — risk increased with adhesions from prior CS, prolonged obstructed labor, anatomic distortion. Ureteral injury rare but increased with cesarean hysterectomy or pelvic adhesions.

column1: Why doxy-PEP not recommended for cisgender women per CDC?
column2: Kenyan trial in women showed no significant benefit, likely due to low adherence (only 29% had detectable doxycycline in hair samples). CDC reserves doxy-PEP for MSM and transgender women with bacterial STI in past 12 months.
Forensic specimen collection (SANE/SART), STI testing, emergency contraception consideration, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis consideration. Chaperone for exam; consider EUA strongly.

column1: Vaginal lacerations from straddle injury — repair principles?
column2: Superficial without bleeding: local wound care. Deep/active bleeding: surgical debridement + multi-layer closure with absorbable suture. Large hematomas >5 cm: incision + drainage to prevent pressure necrosis. Refer to gyn for proximal canal / cervical injuries.

column1: Female genital straddle injury — most common mechanism?
column2: Bicycle-related (crossbar). Penetrating injuries from falls onto sharp objects, pelvic-fracture bone fragments, or sexual assault.
Assessment for child abuse is mandatory for ALL pediatric genital trauma. Examination under anesthesia is strongly recommended when abuse or intentional injury is suspected.

Tourniquet/strangulation: penile swelling + erythema in a child → evaluate for hair, thread, or rubber band → expedited removal. Zipper: mineral oil lubrication, incise cloth between teeth, cut median bar with metal cutter, or release shield with screwdriver.

column1: Hyperbaric oxygen for radiation cystitis — RICH-ART?
column2: 2019 RCT 5-yr follow-up 2025: improved macroscopic bladder appearance, symptoms, QoL with durable long-term benefit. 30–40 sessions at 2.0–2.5 ATA; 2.5 ATA may be superior for hematuria.
Conservative (hydration, anticholinergics) → intravesical (hyaluronic acid, alum, formalin) → endoscopic cautery of telangiectasia → HBOT (30–40 sessions) → urinary diversion ± cystectomy.

column1: Salvage cystectomy after pelvic RT — complication rate?
column2: 75% overall; Clavien ≥3 in 30%; mortality 2.9–6.1%. 3-fold higher rectal injury (OR 3.17). 86% receive incontinent diversion; orthotopic neobladder only in highly selected patients.

Every 3 months in year 1, every 6 months in years 2–5, then annually. Post-cystectomy: cytology + urethral wash every 6–12 mo for first 2 yr, especially with high-risk features (positive urethral margin, multifocal CIS, prostatic urethral invasion).
Universal HIV screening at least once for all adults; annual for those at increased risk. PrEP recommended for those at substantial risk of HIV acquisition.

column1: EAU 2024 priapism — early malleable prosthesis trigger?
column2: 48-hour irreversibility threshold (priapism >48 h ≈ 100% necrotic smooth muscle on biopsy). MRI-guided patient selection (Ralph 2010 100% sensitivity).
Compatible with T-shunt and Al-Ghorab shunts. INCOMPATIBLE with Winter and Ebbehoj (insufficient channel to admit a 7/8 Hegar dilator).

Rationale vs immediate MPP: 37.5% revision / 50% distal extrusion / 25% impending lateral extrusion with MPP placed too early. Fuchs penoscrotal 100% detumescence / 0% revision; Baumgarten 0% bilateral recurrence; Basile 96% detumescence.
Default to bilateral PSD. In the largest multi-institutional series, unilateral PSD had recurrence while bilateral PSD had none.
Annual B12 if ileal segment used — B12 deficiency from terminal ileum resection. Also annual basic metabolic panel for hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.

Stomal stenosis (10–50% of patients). Other: false passage formation (~9%), channel incontinence (tunnel shortening or patulousness), reservoir stones. Cystoscopy through channel identifies level and severity.

column1: Aspiration for ischemic priapism — first step?
column2: Corporal aspiration laterally — aspirate 20–30 mL of dark blood. Alone resolves subset of early-presentation priapism and decompresses corpora for subsequent phenylephrine therapy.

Hydroxyurea (standard of care for SCD; reduces priapism frequency), scheduled monthly transfusion in selected patients, pseudoephedrine at bedtime (limited evidence), low-dose daily sildenafil (paradoxical PDE5 mechanism, limited evidence).

column1: Pheochromocytoma-resistant elevated BP during phenylephrine for priapism?
column2: Risk of hypertensive crisis is meaningful — continuous BP and HR monitoring required. Particularly high risk in children and patients with cardiovascular disease.

column1: EPIC and ICIQ — comparator role in survivorship?
column2: NCCN survivorship and ASCO recommend using validated instruments (FSFI, SHIM, PROMIS SexFS, EPIC) regularly for survivors; proactive clinician initiation, not waiting for patient.

column1: SIU/ICUD bulbar urethral stricture EPA success?
column2: 93.8% pooled (Wessells/Webster 2014; 1,234 patients). Gold standard for short (≤2 cm) bulbar strictures.
Long-term improvement in macroscopic bladder appearance, symptom burden, QoL after HBOT for radiation cystitis. Lower healthcare costs in the HBOT arm. Durable benefit established.

Penile prosthesis implantation complications systematic review — guides counseling around prosthesis selection in fibrotic corpora after priapism, post-radiation, or following gender-affirming phalloplasty.

All Type III FGM/C — universal recommendation. Includes menstrual obstruction/hematocolpos, painful neuromas, dyspareunia, recurrent UTI, pregnancy, gynecologic exam access. Re-infibulation prohibited.

column1: Defibulation timing — first stage of labor option?
column2: Acceptable in late-presenting pregnant patients. Spinal anesthesia preferred in pregnant women; AAP-vs-WHO local-anesthesia divergence (flashback risk).
n=3,166: emergency CD OR 0.16 (0.06–0.42); lacerations OR 0.48 (0.29–0.79). Berg 2017 SR: 50–100% satisfaction across studies.
36.9% pooled prevalence; Somalia 99.2%; >500k US women/girls at risk. PTSD ~55%; obstructed labor OR 2.04; dyspareunia OR 2.47.

Urinary leakage persists after prostatectomy; sexual function declines across all arms; fecal leakage worsens long-term after radiotherapy. Treatment-choice counseling should include late bowel and sexual sequelae.

column1: Posterior urethral valves in adults — sexual function?
column2: ED is rare; 12.5% report ejaculatory dysfunction. Fertility generally preserved though lower paternity rates reported.
Multidisciplinary clinic with proactive standardized management reduced CKD progression (12% vs 27%, p=0.02) and need for kidney replacement therapy (3% vs 20%, p<0.05).
76% require >1 continence surgery; ~83% achieve diurnal continence after typically multiple procedures.

column1: SBA 2023 spina bifida transition packet contents?
column2: Medical summary; action plans for common complications (shunt malfunction, UTI, constipation, skin ulcers); supply/equipment information; latex allergy status.

column1: What is the "femalehealth" cancer screening rule for hysterectomy without history of CIN2+?
column2: No further cervical screening required if hysterectomy included cervix removal and no history of CIN2+ or cervical cancer. Applies to both USPSTF and ACS.
Kim 2024: first interventional study of genetically enhanced bacteriophage cocktail (LBP-EC01, CRISPR-Cas3-enhanced 6-phage cocktail) for uncomplicated UTI from E. coli. Favorable safety profile.

column1: ABA test — meaning of negative bladder scanner result?
column2: If <300 mL symptomatic OR <500 mL asymptomatic, retention is not present and catheterization is not warranted (URECA algorithm; RAND/UCLA).

column1: Highest-yield indication for HBOT in late RT injury?
column2: Hemorrhagic radiation cystitis (RICH-ART RCT). Also chronic radiation-induced fistula (low-certainty Cochrane). 30–40 sessions at 2.0–2.5 ATA.
Low-dose vaginal estrogen. Alternatives: vaginal DHEA, ospemifene, CO2 laser. Consider survivorship context in breast-cancer survivors per NCCN.
One-stage TIP (Snodgrass) is the default for distal/glandular/coronal adults — distal complication rate ~7%; 620-patient adult series 12.7% overall.

column1: FRAX threshold for proceeding to DXA in younger postmenopausal women?
column2: 10-yr major osteoporotic fracture probability ≥9.3% — threshold equivalent to a 65-yr-old white woman without additional risk factors.

column1: What is the rectoprostatic fascia reinforcement flap?
column2: Pansritum 2022: interposition flap for intraoperative rectal injury during vaginoplasty when primary repair is tenuous. 100% success and no recurrence at 1-yr follow-up.

column1: ProtecT findings on radiation arm bowel function?
column2: Fecal leakage worsens long-term after radiotherapy — should be incorporated into prostate-cancer treatment-decision counseling.

column1: KIDS-COVE or vaginal-rugae loss postmenopausal — what condition?
column2: GSM examination findings: thin/pale/erythematous vulvar-vaginal epithelium; loss of rugae; introital narrowing; decreased tissue elasticity; urethral caruncle; resorption of labia minora.
Up to 3% of all civilian trauma patients have GU injuries. >90% from blunt mechanisms. Renal is the most common GU injury overall.

column1: Why bilateral orchiopexy in unilateral testicular torsion?
column2: Bell-clapper deformity is bilateral in most cases. Contralateral testis is at high risk for asynchronous torsion. Sutureless dartos pouch or sutured (nonabsorbable preferred) — comparable success.

column1: Sutureless dartos pouch orchiopexy series outcome?
column2: Kozminski 1,104 cases (155 for torsion): 98.7% success, 14 adverse outcomes. Sub-dartos pouch + obliterate tunica vaginalis sac; tissue adherence secures without transparenchymal sutures.

column1: Endometrial Cancer Survivorship — Pipelle biopsy performance?
column2: Sensitivity 75–100%, specificity ~100% for endometrial cancer. Office-based, preferred diagnostic in postmenopausal bleeding after TVUS ≥4 mm or persistent bleeding regardless of thickness.

Non-neurogenic neurogenic bladder. Dysfunctional voiding (learned external-sphincter co-contraction during voiding) without neurologic lesion; often pediatric. Behavioral retraining + biofeedback + α-blockers; surgery only for refractory secondary upper-tract injury.

Allows scar maturation, hematoma resorption, and full extent of stricture to declare. Earlier repair compromises planning. Scarberry/Gómez 2018: early 3–6 wk reconstruction has comparable outcomes when positioning is safe.

column1: Pelvic-floor PT effect on chronic pelvic pain?
column2: SMD -1.69 for short-term pain in women (high-certainty evidence). Recommended by ACOG, AUA, EAU. Also effective in CP/CPPS in men.

column1: Vaginal pH normal range in premenopausal women?
column2: 3.5–4.5 — Lactobacillus-dominant. >4.5 in untreated postmenopausal women supports GSM diagnosis.

column1: Estrogen receptors in lower urinary tract?
column2: ERα and ERβ are present throughout vagina, urethra, bladder trigone, and pelvic-floor musculature — explaining the broad GSM symptom profile.

CAPP2 in Lynch syndrome: 7 vs 17 endometrial cancers (HR 0.50; 0.22–1.11). Pooled obesity analysis: weekly aspirin ~15% reduced EC risk in overweight/obese women (OR 0.86); no association in normal-weight women.
5–22% lifetime risk. NCCN: consider endometrial cancer screening starting age 35; biopsy q1–2 yr. Discuss hysterectomy after childbearing. Oophorectomy NOT indicated for Cowden alone.

column1: USPSTF cervical screening — what about under 21?
column2: No screening recommended. ACS recommends no screening before age 25. USPSTF 21–24 cytology every 3 yr; ACS 25–29 primary HPV every 5 yr.
Negative primary HPV (preferred) OR negative cotesting at ages 60 AND 65 = discontinue screening. Two consecutive negative tests within the prior 10 years required.
More frequent screening. Should NOT use self-collection — require both HPV and cytology testing. Includes HIV, organ transplant, HSCT, SLE, IBD on immunosuppressive therapy.

column1: TVUS endometrial thickness cutoff in postmenopausal bleeding?
column2: ≤4 mm has >99% NPV for endometrial cancer. ≤5 mm cutoff: sensitivity 90–97% but specificity only 35–62% in asymptomatic screening (not recommended). Persistent bleeding warrants histologic evaluation regardless of thickness.

COCs (10-yr use → absolute risk before 75 from 2.3 to 1.3 per 100; persisting 30+ yr after cessation). Progesterone-containing IUDs (pooled OR 0.81). Parity (~25% reduction per pregnancy). Physical activity.

column1: Why hysterectomy alone does not eliminate ovarian cancer risk in Lynch?
column2: Endometrial cancer is the most common extraintestinal sentinel cancer in Lynch but hysterectomy reduces incidence not mortality. Discuss after childbearing as legitimate risk-reducing option.

column1: WISDOM trial — risk-based vs annual breast cancer screening?
column2: Risk-based noninferior for stage ≥IIB detection (rate difference −18.0 per 100,000 person-yr). 89% of participants in observational cohort preferred risk-based screening.

column1: BCSC vs Gail vs Tyrer-Cuzick (IBIS) — best use case?
column2: BCSC: highest AUC when breast density data available. Gail: drives 5-yr risk ≥1.7% threshold; widely used but lower discrimination. Tyrer-Cuzick (IBIS): preferred for most comprehensive high-risk assessments. BOADICEA: known BRCA or complex pedigrees.
Biennial mammography for ages 50–74; shared decision-making for ages 40–49 and ≥75. Supports DBT for dense breasts but recommends AGAINST supplemental MRI or US in average-risk dense-breast patients.
Annual mammography starting at age 40, continuing as long as life expectancy >5–7 yr. Lower age limit than USPSTF and continuation criterion differs.

Supplemental MRI in extremely dense breasts → ~50% reduction in interval cancers. Category 1 evidence for ages 50–75. NCCN recommends MRI for extremely dense breasts starting age 50 (may consider 40).

column1: Why ACP recommends against supplemental MRI/US in average-risk dense breasts?
column2: Increases false positives without proven mortality benefit; reserved for elevated-risk per other criteria. NCCN now recognizes extremely dense breasts as their own increased-risk category supported by DENSE.

column1: Pretreatment urinary biomarker for radiation cystitis monitoring?
column2: None routinely validated. Cystoscopy + symptom monitoring + correction of coagulopathy + catheter drainage form the workup. HBOT mainstays for persistent disease.

column1: Pediatric trauma — bladder more intraabdominal in children — implication?
column2: Greater IPB risk for a given pelvic fracture in pediatric trauma. Smaller capacity requires more precise catheter sizing. High index of suspicion even with microhematuria.

column1: Pediatric trauma — perirenal fat / rib protection differences?
column2: Children have less perirenal fat and more pliable ribs — kidney is more vulnerable. Hematuria threshold for imaging is lower (any degree warrants CT).

Reverse for hemodynamically unstable patients or those with significant blood loss. Do not withhold contrast CT based on age alone — evidence linking age to contrast-induced nephropathy is inconclusive.

Skin-lined and colonized by skin + vaginal flora. Discharge/odor often dead skin, sebum, or retained lubricant. Douching with dilute vinegar/betadine adequate. Persistent odor: 5-day vaginal metronidazole.

column1: Voice therapy effect on speaking fundamental frequency?
column2: Effect size g = 0.86 for SF0 increase. Wendler glottoplasty g = 1.21. Combined approach significantly more effective than therapy alone.

column1: What does endometriosis ASRM staging predict — and not predict?
column2: Stage I–II vs III–IV. Correlates poorly with symptoms and prognosis. Newer frameworks: ENZIAN classification for deep endometriosis; Endometriosis Fertility Index for fertility decisions.

column1: What is the Endometriosis Fertility Index used for?
column2: After endometriosis surgery — predicts spontaneous pregnancy likelihood. Guides decision between expectant management, IUI, or moving to IVF.

~25% experience recurrent pelvic pain after hysterectomy for endometriosis; 10% require additional surgery. Ovarian preservation recommended in premenopausal women when possible (surgical menopause contributes to elevated CV disease risk).

column1: LNG-IUD (52 mg) effect on endometriosis pain?
column2: 17.7 points VAS reduction vs placebo. Does not suppress ovulation. Used in chemoprevention for high-risk women and for fertility-sparing treatment of atypical hyperplasia / early endometrial cancer.

column1: Elagolix dosing range and BMD considerations?
column2: Low-dose 150 mg daily (up to 24 months); high-dose 200 mg BID (up to 6 months without add-back). High-dose with add-back (estradiol 1 mg + norethindrone acetate 0.5 mg) sustained efficacy at 12 mo with preserved BMD.

column1: What screening for women with HIV regarding STIs?
column2: Screen gonorrhea, chlamydia, syphilis, trichomoniasis at entry to care and at least annually; every 3–6 months for those with multiple partners.
Only in symptomatic women with persistent cervicitis — NOT for routine screening. FDA-cleared NAATs available. Macrolide resistance >50% in many regions.
Doxycycline 100 mg BID × 7 d → azithromycin (resistance-guided sequential). Macrolide-resistant or unknown: doxycycline × 7 d → moxifloxacin 400 mg daily × 7 d.

column1: Syphilis serologic-test gap in primary syphilis?
column2: Both treponemal and nontreponemal tests may be nonreactive in ~30% of primary syphilis cases. Sequential algorithm (treponemal followed by nontreponemal, or vice versa).
Associated with increased risk of PID and reproductive sequelae. Retest at 3 months due to high reinfection rates.
Type-specific PCR of lesions is preferred over culture. Two-step serologic testing when serology is used. Daily suppression reduces recurrences and transmission risk by ~50%.

column1: Daily suppressive therapy for genital herpes — quantitative?
column2: Reduces recurrences AND transmission risk by ~50%. Acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir.

First prenatal visit, ~28 weeks (third trimester), and at delivery. Penicillin only therapy — desensitize if allergic. Untreated → stillbirth in up to 40%; congenital syphilis cases +106% from 2019 to 2023.

column1: Hypospadias as part of testicular dysgenesis syndrome — workup?
column2: Severe/proximal hypospadias, cryptorchidism, or infertility concern → offer semen analysis + endocrine evaluation. 18.6% oligo/azoospermia in nonsyndromic adult cohort; higher rates in complex hypospadias.

column1: Verla failure-free survival post-urethroplasty in failed hypospadias?
column2: 82% at 1 yr → 57% at 10 yr — mandates prolonged surveillance. LUTS twice as common as controls; paternity rates modestly lower (~24% vs ~29%).
Meatal advancement and glanuloplasty for glanular distal hypospadias with minimal chordee. Most distal variants only — limited adult applicability.
Default single-stage approach. Distal complication rate ~7%; large adult series (n=620) 12.7% overall complications; lowest urethrocutaneous fistula rate vs Mathieu in SR.
99% prefer buccal mucosa as primary graft site. BMG favored over fasciocutaneous flaps for penile urethroplasty regardless of circumcision status.

column1: Bracka technique — BMG vs preputial skin?
column2: BMG 20% complication rate vs 31% preputial skin. Skin grafts significantly associated with stricture recurrence vs BMG in complex cohorts (Morrison series).

Legitimate definitive option for elderly, multiply failed repairs, or patient preference. AUA 2023 endorses PU as long-term alternative to urethroplasty in high-risk populations. 13.8% of adult hypospadias-related strictures in one series.
Bifid clitoris + patulous urethra. Incontinence common when bladder neck/sphincteric mechanism involved. Adult reconstruction focuses on continence + sexual function/pain.
Rare variant with intact prepuce, later diagnosis, generally milder anatomy than complete penopubic epispadias.

column1: What does a smaller PUA on MRI imply?
column2: Proximal urethral stump displaced superiorly and posteriorly behind pubic symphysis ("hiding") → inaccessible from simple perineal approach without pubectomy. Predictive of elaborate approach during PFUI reconstruction.
Gap length / total urethral length on urethrography. Cutoff >0.35 → elaborate PFUI approach. AUC 0.979; 91% specificity, 95% PPV.
Proximal urethral stump position above (vs below) the inferior pubic symphysis on RGU/VCUG. Above → elaborate approach (OR 66). 2026 Scherñuk: 100% sensitivity, 42.3% specificity.

column1: Iatrogenic ureteral injury — intraoperative detection rate?
column2: Only 17.6%–50% are identified during primary surgery. Delayed recognition has pooled OR 0.22 (0.12–0.41) for complication management failure vs intraoperative detection.

column1: Intraoperative bladder injury — long-term success of consultant repair?
column2: 98.4% long-term success when performed by a consultant urologist. ~1% complication rate; no significant difference between 7–10 days and longer catheterization.

column1: Damage-control IUTI strategy ("drain now, fix later")?
column2: PCN for upper tract; large Foley ± SPT for lower; ligate proximal ureteral stump if transected (prevents uroperitoneum); wide retroperitoneal/pelvic drain. Definitive repair in 5–7 days after resuscitation.

column1: Skokan algorithm for postoperative ureteral injury?
column2: Imaging (CT urogram first-line; RPG confirms level/character) → PCN ± antegrade stent for immediate decompression → delayed definitive reconstruction at 6–12 weeks. Temporizing drainage is almost always the right first move.
Energy damage extends 1–2 cm beyond visible lesion; declares itself 3–10 days later as urinoma or stricture. Requires aggressive debridement back to healthy tissue.

column1: Most common iatrogenic ureteral injury type?
column2: Complete occlusion (ligation or clipping). Often recognized only postoperatively from hydronephrosis + flank pain. Retrograde stent passage often resolves a partial ligature intraoperatively.

column1: Indigo carmine dose for intraoperative ureteral assessment?
column2: 40 mg slow IV infusion — observe for blue dye leaking into surgical field or visibly absent ureteral jet on cystoscopy. Alternatives: methylene blue, sodium fluorescein, direct renal pelvis injection.

column1: Prophylactic ureteral stenting — gynecologic vs colorectal?
column2: Gynecologic: reduces ureteric injury (OR 0.61; NNT 224). Colorectal: does NOT reduce risk of injury. Lighted stents aid identification but no RCT benefit on injury rate.
Diverticular disease (OR 2.12), T4 malignancy (OR 1.80), open surgery (OR 1.32), prior radiotherapy, locally advanced colorectal cancers, visceral obesity, prior colorectal/gyn surgery.

34 injuries over 7 yr; 20/34 occurred during teams' first 8 cases. 22% conversion to open; 8% unplanned APR/Hartmann; 26% repair complication; 9% permanent diversion; 18% persistent urinary dysfunction.

column1: Bladder injury location near trigone — operative implication?
column2: Place bilateral ureteral stents/retrograde catheters before closure to protect orifices. If ureteral orifice directly involved → ureteroneocystostomy into healthy bladder wall rather than closing over orifice.

column1: GU injury overview — Zone 1 retroperitoneal hematoma — management?
column2: Always explore — aorta/IVC injury. Zone 2 (perinephric): explore only if pulsatile/expanding in blunt trauma. Zone 3 (pelvic): do NOT explore in blunt trauma — pack and angiography.

column1: Hematuria sensitivity for ureteral trauma — clinical implication?
column2: Absent in up to 55% of cases. Mechanism-driven imaging essential. Standard portal-venous trauma CT misses most ureteral injuries — must explicitly add delayed-phase acquisition (5–10 min).

Palpate the contralateral kidney before exploring the injured kidney. If absent or abnormal (polycystic, atrophic) → single-shot IV pyelogram (2 mg/kg contrast at 10 min) confirms function and guides salvage decision.

column1: Genital scrotal trauma — Dartos fascia role in Fournier's?
column2: Resistant to spread of infection into testicular blood supply (which arises from aorta via testicular arteries). Explains why testicular salvage is usually possible despite extensive scrotal involvement.

column1: Recurrent UTI behavioral interventions with evidence?
column2: Adequate hydration (one RCT: +1.5 L water/day reduced UTI ~50%). Urge-initiated voiding and postcoital voiding. Avoid spermicidal contraceptives.

column1: Mannose / cranberry NMA findings vs MERIT RCT?
column2: NMA: D-mannose strongest effect RR 0.34; cranberry RR 0.72; probiotics RR 0.69. BUT MERIT RCT 2024 found D-mannose 2 g daily for 6 months did NOT reduce recurrence vs placebo.

column1: Pharmacologic UTI prevention for postcoital infections?
column2: TMP-SMX 40/200 or 80/400 mg single dose post-intercourse; nitrofurantoin 50–100 mg single dose; ciprofloxacin 125 mg single dose. Similar recurrence reduction as continuous prophylaxis with less total exposure.

column1: What does the OPNet OBS algorithm predict?
column2: Not a standard algorithm. Geriatric assessment principles: TUG ≥15 sec, CFS-9, Mini-Cog, Robinson Frailty Index, Life-Space Assessment recommended before elective pelvic-floor surgery in patients ≥65.

A woman in advanced postmenopausal age (typically ≥75) with multiple comorbidities seeking urogynecologic care. 2026 J Clin Med paper coined term to describe emerging cohort. By 2050 elderly woman population expected to grow 46%.
GnRH agonist for 3–6 months before IVF significantly increases pregnancy likelihood — the one exception to "medical therapy is contraceptive" rule before conception attempts.

9–12 years (2-dose series). Catch-up through age 26 (3-dose series if initiated ≥15 yr). Shared decision-making 27–45. Population-level: cervical cancer incidence ~69% decline in vaccinated 20–24 yr olds.

column1: Single-cell concept of cervical screening exit?
column2: Two consecutive negative tests within prior 10 years (USPSTF/ACS). ACS adds forward-looking: negative primary HPV (preferred) OR negative cotesting at ages 60 AND 65.

column1: TVUS sensitivity for symptomatic vs asymptomatic patients — endometrial cancer?
column2: Symptomatic: ≤4 mm has >99% NPV (initial workup standard). Asymptomatic screening: insufficient specificity (35–62% at 5 mm cutoff) — high false-positive rate makes it inappropriate for population screening.
60% — highest of all flap types. ALT 20%; pedicled abdominal 9.1%. RFFF is preferred for aesthetic outcomes despite this.

column1: ALT vs RFFF phalloplasty operative time?
column2: 290 min ALT vs 516 min RFFF. ALT requires significantly less operative time. Comparable flap survival and patient satisfaction (~78% vs 76%).

Two-stage phalloplasty-first approach. Long-term urologic outcomes: 27% total complication rate, 96% achieve standing urination, 96% would undergo again. Lower complication rate than single-stage approaches.
Series n=52: mean depth 14.7 cm; 96% satisfaction; complication rate 13.5%. Used when penile skin is insufficient (prior circumcision, puberty blocker use). Self-lubricating neovagina.

column1: Penile inversion vaginoplasty rectoneovaginal fistula rate?
column2: Primary 0.8%; revision 6.3% (OR 8.6). 13/25 rectoneovaginal among 1,082 patients (Van der Sluis). Intraoperative rectal injury 3–7%.
Garcia (n=22 revision cases): 100% satisfaction. Complications: neovaginal prolapse (5/22), introital stenosis (4/22) — all successfully managed.

column1: RSV (robot-assisted sigmoid vaginoplasty) for stenosis revision?
column2: Sljivich n=25: depth improved 3.4 → 17.6 cm. No fistulas; most patients satisfied. Two developed sigmoid-skin anastomotic strictures requiring intervention.

column1: Robotic peritoneal flap revision for stenosis (Dy 2021)?
column2: 24 patients with stenotic/absent canals after PIV: mean depth 13.6 cm, width 3.6 cm at 410-day mean follow-up. No rectal injuries, minimal complications.
Hydraulic 39%; malleable 31%. Secondary implantations carry 3.5× higher complication risk; urethral lengthening increases late complication risk (HR 2.6).

column1: Briles single-surgeon penile prosthesis in transmen — infrapubic infrequency?
column2: 40% required surgical revision at mean 35 months. Common: device detachment (7/30), malposition (3/30), infection (1/30). No neophallus erosions or flap losses.
Effective January 2027 — requires insurance coverage without cost-sharing.

column1: False-negative TVUS in Black women — endometrial cancer?
column2: Retrospective study of 1,494 Black women: 9.5% false-negative rate at 4 mm threshold — concerns about racial disparities in diagnostic accuracy.

column1: Methenamine hippurate dosing for rUTI prevention?
column2: 1 g BID — converts to formaldehyde in acidic urine, acts as urinary antiseptic without promoting antibiotic resistance. ALTAR trial: non-inferior to daily low-dose antibiotics.

column1: ImpresU trial — methenamine in older women?
column2: Heltveit-Olsen 2025: n=289 women ≥70 yr; methenamine reduced antibiotic UTI treatments by 25% during 6-month treatment (IRR 0.75, p=0.049). After discontinuation, higher UTI incidence (IRR 1.7).
Formaldehyde-resistant E. coli in 5.8% of ALTAR-derived isolates, mediated by non-functional frmR variants. Methenamine has its own resistance risks.

column1: Endometrial cancer pre-surgical workup — Pipelle adequacy rate?
column2: Inadequate sample rates 7–40% in postmenopausal women — too invasive for population-based screening. Pipelle sensitivity 75–100%, specificity ~100%.

column1: Tamoxifen and EC — biological-aggressiveness at standard 20 mg/d?
column2: Stage and grade similar to sporadic EC at 20 mg/d. Higher doses (40 mg/d) may produce more biologically aggressive tumors. Routine endometrial screening NOT recommended for asymptomatic women.

column1: WID-qEC test for endometrial cancer detection?
column2: DNA methylation of ZSCAN12 and GYPC from cervicovaginal samples. Compared favorably to sonography in EPI-SURE prospective UK cohort for detecting uterine cancers in women with abnormal bleeding.

1st sensate osteocutaneous free fibula flap for transmasculine reconstruction (n=18). Built-in rigidity from fibular bone allows penetration without separate prosthesis. Significant donor-site morbidity.
Penile-inversion vaginoplasty with cranially pedicled U-flaps + V-Y advancement + 90° medial rotation + fat-pad relocation. Most common feminizing genital surgery.
Dreher 2018: 14.4% (range 4–40%). Most common urethral complication after feminizing vaginoplasty. Stepwise management: office dilation → dorsal meatotomy → Y-V meatoplasty.
Overall 20.8% (n=206, mean 11.5-yr follow-up). Drops to 11.5% with modern Hoebeke V-Y scrotoplasty. Smoking is dominant modifiable risk factor.
Detubularized ileum reconfigured perpendicular over a wire → retubularized as a narrow catheterizable channel. Used when appendix is unavailable for Mitrofanoff or for substitute ureter.

column1: McGuire LPP threshold for upper-tract injury — original paper?
column2: McGuire 1981 J Urol — myelodysplastic patients. End-filling detrusor pressure >40 cm H2O correlates with high risk of upper-tract deterioration. Validated for adults with SCI, MS, other neurogenic etiologies.

Acute uncontrolled sympathetic discharge in SCI above T6 from noxious stimulus below lesion. SBP rise >20 mmHg above baseline. Immediate: sit patient up, remove trigger (catheterize for retention #1), nifedipine SL if persistent.

column1: Why is SNM contraindicated in dementia and severe NLUTD?
column2: Patient cannot reliably report sensory/efficacy feedback; settings require iterative titration. Also avoid in pregnancy (potential fetal nerve stimulation). Relative contraindication in severe SCI.
Weekly 30-min sessions × 12 weeks induction → monthly maintenance. Comparable continence response to anticholinergic monotherapy in OAB. Well-tolerated alternative for medication-intolerant patients.
Refractory OAB / urge incontinence. Office-based delivery without weekly visits. Comparable outcomes to SNM for OAB but no DUA / fecal incontinence indication.

column1: Pelvic floor PT — first-line for stress UI women?
column2: Cure or improvement in ~70% of women with mild-moderate SUI. Best evidence-based conservative management. Also effective for urgency and mixed UI; ~50% satisfaction at 1 year for stress-predominant UI.

column1: Pessaries — utility in very frail patients?
column2: Effective even in severely frail or demented patients. Caregivers should be aware of need for regular pessary changes (every 4–6 weeks) to avoid complications.

column1: What constitutes a satisfactory PSA Castro change vs baseline post-RP?
column2: Biochemical recurrence: PSA ≥0.2 ng/mL with subsequent confirmatory rise. Surveillance interval: every 6–12 months for first 5 years, then annually. Ultrasensitive PSA enables earlier detection but does not change AUA threshold.

column1: Sponge testing or surveillance after augmentation cystoplasty?
column2: Surveillance cystoscopy controversial. AUA/SUFU recommends annual focused H&P + BMP + urinary tract imaging — not mandatory routine surveillance cystoscopy. Cystoscopy promptly for new hematuria, recurrent unexplained UTIs, or suprapubic pain.
Approximately 1.5% (often signet-ring adenocarcinoma at augment-bladder anastomosis). 10-year cystoscopy after augmentation is debated; Higuchi 15-year prospective found no cancer.
100% sensitivity, 95% specificity — potentially outperforms conventional cytology. Limited prospective evidence in this setting. Primary clinical utility is NPV.

column1: Stone formation rate in augmented bladders at 10 years?
column2: 28–36%. 44% recurrence rate. Antegrade flexible URS via percutaneous access sheath preferred — Stuurman achieved 80% stone-free rate after single session.

column1: Cystic fibrosis in spina bifida — vector?
column2: Latex allergy is highly prevalent in spina bifida patients (often documented). Must be communicated to adult providers. Implant choice (silicone implants, latex-free materials) must reflect this.

column1: Pediatric trauma straddle injury — bicycle most common?
column2: Yes — most common unintentional female pelvic-perineal trauma mechanism. Toilet-seat crush, falls onto sharp objects also common. Always assess for child abuse.

Cystoscopy through channel identifies level + severity. Stomal dilation under local anesthesia or formal open revision required. False passage formation (~9%) — endoscopic eval identifies false tract.

Mildest form; many achieve daytime continence without major surgery, sometimes with pelvic floor therapy. Adult care centers on cosmesis and sexual function rather than major continence reconstruction.

Entire dorsal urethra open to symphysis — highest continence burden. Bladder neck reconstruction typically required; bladder neck closure + catheterizable channel if outlet continence cannot be salvaged.

column1: Adult EEC LUTS prevalence in questionnaire studies?
column2: 80% report moderate or severe LUTS, involving both storage and voiding domains. Often underrecognized without questionnaires.
Single-stage extended TIP (with or without dorsal inlay graft) reserved for no/mild chordee + intact urethral plate. Proximal hypospadias series report ≥50% complication and up to 30% fistula rate.
83% initial success at 9.5-year median follow-up. BMG two-stage used in 90% of reoperative cases. Skin grafts significantly associated with stricture recurrence vs BMG.

column1: Phenylephrine for ICI test pediatric dosing?
column2: 100 µg doses, maximum 500 µg total. Consider cardiology monitoring. Continuous BP/HR monitoring; meaningful risk of hypertensive crisis especially in children.

Endometrioma — characteristic ovarian cyst with hemorrhagic content. Often visible on TVUS or MRI. Endometriotic phenotype: superficial peritoneal, ovarian endometriomas, deep infiltrating endometriosis.
Failed primary PIV with depth loss; persistent mucus-secreting depth desired (14–17.6 cm); penile skin insufficient for primary. Higher morbidity than PIV.
Highly suggestive but not universal. Triad: pop/crack, immediate detumescence, severe pain + ecchymosis ("eggplant" or "rolled sausage" deformity). Penile US or MRI when clinical exam is equivocal.

column1: Why never blindly catheterize after blood at meatus?
column2: Can convert a partial urethral tear into a complete disruption. Always perform retrograde urethrogram first if urethral injury is suspected.

column1: TIP success in pediatric vs adult hypospadias?
column2: Comparable when surgeon is experienced. Adult repair achieves complication rates comparable to pediatric repair but reoperation status (~33% complication vs ~14% primary), proximal anatomy, and severe scarring increase complication risk.
Associated with faster CKD progression. Median eGFR decline 2.6 mL/min/1.73m²/yr. Annual proteinuria + creatinine + upper-tract imaging surveillance; ACE inhibitors for progressive CKD.
Long mid-to-lower ureteral defects beyond psoas hitch range. Technically demanding — defer acutely if expertise unavailable; ileal ureter alternative if defect too long.
Partial transection at laparotomy — convert longitudinal tear to transverse repair over stent. Maintains length without segmental resection.
UPJ avulsion — anastomose proximal ureter directly into renal pelvis. Most common blunt ureteral injury in children due to hyperextensible spine.
Mitrofanoff: appendix-based continent catheterizable channel (the original). Yang-Monti: detubularized ileum retubularized perpendicular over a wire. Used when appendix unavailable.

column1: Most common cause of pediatric obstructive uropathy?
column2: Posterior urethral valves (PUV). 28.5% lifetime ESRD risk. "Valve bladder" syndrome in 38% adults (myogenic failure, poor compliance, high-pressure chronic retention).

column1: Pediatric vs adult bladder injury — anatomic difference?
column2: Bladder is more intraabdominal in children → greater IPB risk for given pelvic fracture. Smaller capacity requires more precise catheter sizing. High index of suspicion even with microhematuria.
Tunica albuginea disruption (discontinuity of hyperechoic tunica). Differentiates intracavernosal from extracavernosal hematomas. Routine US not required when diagnosis is clinically clear.

column1: Most common ureteric injury during gynecologic surgery?
column2: Iatrogenic ureteric injury during pelvic surgery (hysterectomy, colorectal resection, aortoiliac surgery) is numerically more common than traumatic ureteral injury overall.

column1: Common congenital condition in transitional urology highest volume?
column2: Spina bifida / neurogenic bladder — most common condition requiring transitional urology care. Lifelong management of CIC, anticholinergics (or β3 agonists), upper-tract surveillance.

column1: ADHD-like presentation in pediatric voiding dysfunction — Hinman?
column2: Non-neurogenic neurogenic bladder. Dysfunctional voiding (learned EAS co-contraction); often pediatric. Behavioral retraining + biofeedback + α-blockers; surgery only for refractory secondary upper-tract injury.

column1: Cancer surveillance in pelvic exenteration survivors?
column2: Multidisciplinary follow-up: stoma/pouch/augmented bladder review, sexual rehabilitation, expectation-setting. Quality of life can be high despite severely impaired sexual function (Assi 2021).

column1: What flap is most commonly used after exenteration in females?
column2: VRAM (vertical rectus abdominis myocutaneous), gracilis, IGAP, lotus petal. 77.6% used simpler techniques (direct closure, secondary healing, skin grafts, local flaps); 22.4% required complex loco-regional flaps.
102-patient series of concurrent gynecologic oncology + urogynecology: 9.8% complication rate without major morbidity events. Conservative management is recommended before surgical escalation.

Densely fibrotic, necrotic, fistulized, intolerably painful, or refractory-incontinent posterior urethra. Urinary diversion with or without cystectomy may be the most restorative operation rather than a failure of reconstruction.

column1: Woodle 2026 — urinary diversion for pelvic radiation injury?
column2: Prospective n=55: PROMIS Global Health, GU pain, and QoL improved with low decision regret. Survivorship-version diversion counseling endpoint.

Largely abandoned for primary use. Bypassed for proximal shunts toward Quackels for cavernospongiosum or, in modern practice, T-shunt/Al-Ghorab + Burnett snake maneuver as preferred distal salvage. Grayhack reserved for very specific historical/limited cases.
Brant 92%, Zacharakis 100% if <48h, Ortaç 84.2% ED, Unal/Burnett 92.3% vs 53.6% (T-shunt + snake vs T-shunt alone). 4-shunt comparison shows superior T-shunt durability.

column1: Al-Ghorab shunt — what makes it durable?
column2: Largest tunical window, direct vision, lowest reoperation rate. 1973 origin. Shiraishi-Matsuyama blunt cavernosotomy salvage with Pean forceps for 5–7-day priapism extends its utility.

column1: Hyperbaric oxygen sessions for hemorrhagic radiation cystitis?
column2: 30–40 sessions at 2.0–2.5 ATA. 2.5 ATA may be superior for hematuria specifically. RICH-ART 5-yr durable benefit with lower healthcare costs. Yang 2024 meta-analysis confirmed efficacy.

column1: Cocci 2025 PPI SR — Cocci penile prosthesis SR?
column2: Penile prosthesis implantation complications systematic review across populations. Guides counseling around prosthesis selection in fibrotic corpora (priapism, post-radiation, gender-affirming phalloplasty).
$83,818 preop cost analysis for delayed IPP after priapism. Early MPP at the time of acute priapism is more cost-effective due to ease of acute placement vs cavernotome-required delayed surgery.

column1: Dighero 2025 — long-term QoL after early MPP?
column2: 100% no-regret in patients who received early malleable penile prosthesis for prolonged priapism. Supports the strategy as the modern standard.
70.9% of ISSM members more comfortable with MPP than shunt for prolonged priapism, yet ~80% still favor shunts first-line. Reveals practice-pattern vs evidence gap.
Specialized cavernotome toolkit, Carter-Trost technique, downsized cylinders for fibrosed corpora after delayed presentation. Inferior length outcomes vs early placement.

column1: Most common cause of post-cystectomy female sexual dysfunction?
column2: Anatomic disruption + estrogen deprivation + body image distress. After radical cystectomy: many women receive little or no information about sexual dysfunction; qualitative work shows desire for more complete counseling including self-pleasure and non-intercourse intimacy.

column1: NCCN survivorship — initiation of pelvic-floor PT?
column2: Recommended as multidisciplinary component for pelvic pain after cancer treatment. Should be offered before and after reconstruction, not only after the patient asks. CBT, dilators, vaginal moisturizers as adjuncts.

7/8 Hegar dilator passed retrograde through Al-Ghorab corporotomy to disrupt ischemic coagulum along the corpus. Provides physical removal of organized clot at the proximal corpus that smaller distal shunts cannot achieve.

Original: longitudinal or transverse incision at penoscrotal junction (familiar to implant surgeons). Modified: proximal penile shaft incision or degloving (analogous to fracture repair). Both approaches require bilateral corporotomies on ventrolateral surface.
Foley catheter placed before dissection allows urethra/corpus spongiosum to be palpated and protected. Corporotomies on ventrolateral surface — away from dorsal NVB and urethra (6 o'clock).

19.2% permanent open shunt rate. 100% impotence reversal on shunt closure. Critical evidence that proximal-shunt physiology underlies long-term ED — supports Micoogullari planned 2-month closure of Barry shunts.
Combined urethrocutaneous + urethrocavernous fistula after Quackels — required suprapubic diversion. Specific Quackels risk: urethral injury and fistula formation.

column1: Robbins 1984 — late urethrocavernous fistula after Quackels?
column2: Late presentation of fistula formation after proximal cavernospongiosal shunt. Underpins counseling re: long-term fistula risk after proximal shunt.

Prevents distal erosion of malleable prosthesis after early placement for priapism — 0% erosion in 11/12 prior-failed-shunt patients. Modifies traditional MPP technique to address erosion risk in fibrotic corpora.

column1: Calopedos 2025 guideline positioning of early MPP?
column2: Aligns with EAU 2024 / AUA-SMSNA 2022 endorsement of early malleable penile prosthesis as the modern standard for prolonged ischemic priapism (>36–48 h) with failed medical management.

Early outcome series of proximal cavernospongiosal shunts. Quackels-vs-Grayhack head-to-head historically: lower urethral-injury risk than Quackels, but Grayhack has higher persistent shunt and PE risk.

column1: Manuscripts: 47-reference priapism atlas — significance of Schifano 2025?
column2: Schifano 2025 contributes to the reference list (refs 1–47) of the WARWIKI priapism-shunts-decompression atlas page. Aligned with EAU 2024 framework on early prosthesis.

column1: Pubic symphysis diastasis predicting PFUI risk?
column2: Each mm of symphysis pubis diastasis (or inferomedial pubic bone fracture displacement) ≈ 10% relative increased risk of urethral injury. Largest PFUI risk factor.

Bladder neck injury with extension into the proximal urethra. Type IVa: injury to the base of the bladder with periurethral extravasation simulating Type IV. Most associated with post-op incontinence.
11 studies, 769 patients. Comparable rates of stricture (OR 1.23, p=0.80), incontinence (OR 1.02, p=0.94), ED (OR 0.97, p=0.88) between PER and SPT with delayed urethroplasty.

column1: Step 2 corporal body separation success rate in PFUI?
column2: 17–36% of cases benefit from crural splitting. Fu/Xu series 86.5% success. Provides additional 1–2 cm effective length by shortening course between separated corpora.

column1: Sa et al 2021 PFUI — largest series?
column2: n=1,637 — 92.4% success rate (1,363/1,475 with follow-up). Used progressive transperineal anastomotic strategy. Largest single-center PFUI series in the literature.
90–98% over 27 years. Standard pathway: SPT-first → delayed anastomotic urethroplasty at 3 months → perineal approach.

Li 2025 (n=37): 91.2% success (31/34 with follow-up) using one-sided rerouting via perineal approach + inferior pubectomy. Advocated for young patients and children to minimize secondary trauma to corpora cavernosa.

column1: What is the recommended SPT size for PFUI?
column2: ≥14 Fr Foley (not pigtail). Bladder may be displaced by pelvic hematoma — ultrasound, fluoroscopy, or needle aspiration may be needed for localization. Open urethral realignment has no role.

column1: Foreign-body or stone in augmented bladder management?
column2: Cystoscopic lithotripsy (holmium laser) via urethra or catheterizable channel. Stones occur in 28–36% of augmented bladders at 10 years (44% recurrence).

Soergel et al. — 3 patients with TCC after AC for neuropathic bladder, all died of metastatic disease. Recommended endoscopic surveillance beginning 10 years after surgery. Controversial; not universally adopted.

column1: Why bremelanotide for HSDD vs flibanserin?
column2: Mechanism: melanocortin-4 receptor agonist (vs serotonin/dopamine modulator for flibanserin). On-demand SC vs daily oral. RECONNECT trials showed +0.35 FSFI desire. Less alcohol/CYP3A4 issues but uncontrolled HTN contraindication + 40% nausea.
Standard for female SUI. Retropubic (TVT) or transobturator (TVT-O). Long-term success 80–90%. Outcomes similar to autologous fascial sling for primary SUI but lower morbidity.

column1: Tab Bladder cyclic dysuria with hematuria + suprapubic pain — diagnosis?
column2: Bladder endometriosis. Cyclic symptoms = pathognomonic. Bladder is the most common urinary endometriosis site (~85%). Deep detrusor involvement requires partial cystectomy with primary closure.

Insufficient evidence that removal improves IVF success; surgery considered for endometriomas >4 cm to confirm histology and improve follicle access. Counsel about potential ovarian-reserve compromise.
Predicts spontaneous pregnancy likelihood after endometriosis surgery. Guides decision between expectant management, IUI (limit 3–4 cycles), or IVF (most effective for moderate-severe disease).
Recommended in premenopausal women when possible. Surgical menopause contributes to ~half of the 60% elevated cardiovascular disease risk observed in women with endometriosis.

~25% experience recurrent pelvic pain; 10% require additional surgery. Approximately 1 in 4 minor / 1 in 5 major conservative surgery patients require additional endometriosis surgery (Bougie n=84,885).

column1: ASRM committee opinion on endometriosis and infertility?
column2: Surgical excision/ablation may improve spontaneous pregnancy rates in stage I–II disease. Ovulation induction with IUI increases fecundity (limit 3–4 cycles). IVF most effective for moderate-severe.

column1: Endometriosis and ovarian cancer risk in absolute terms?
column2: 1.8% absolute lifetime risk vs 1.1% general population. 93% relative increase overall; 3.4× clear-cell, 2.3× endometrioid. Prophylactic oophorectomy NOT recommended.

column1: What is the SHAEZ technique for ureteral injury repair?
column2: Not a standard acronym. Core repair principles: spatulation, tension-free closure, single-layer interrupted absorbable, double-J stent for 4–6 weeks, closed-suction retroperitoneal drain near (not on) anastomosis.

column1: Persistent CRP elevation in Fournier's at 48–72 h — implication?
column2: Rising CRP indicates inadequate source control and should prompt early return to OR. CRP ratio 1.78 cutoff predicts death with 86% sensitivity, 82% specificity (survivors 6.7 ± 6.6 vs non-survivors 1.2 ± 0.8).

column1: Why omit primary skin closure in human bite?
column2: Human bites carry high polymicrobial infection risk. Animal bites can be primarily closed with absorbable suture after thorough irrigation and amoxicillin-clavulanate prophylaxis. Both require tetanus update.

High-probability necrotizing fasciitis / Fournier's. Score ≥6 has ~68% sensitivity, ~85% specificity. Negative LRINEC does NOT exclude NSTI — operate on clinical diagnosis if systemic sepsis and crepitus / necrosis present.
